I wonder how the king escap'd our hands.
I wonder how the king slipped through our fingers.

While we pursued the horsemen of the North, / He slyly stole away and left his men, / Whereat the great Lord of Northumberland, / Whose warlike ears could never brook retreat, / Cheer'd up the drooping army; and himself, / Lord Clifford, and Lord Stafford, all abreast, / Charg'd our main battle's front, and breaking in, / Were by the swords of common soldiers slain.

While we were chasing the northern cavalry, he quietly crept away and abandoned his men. Then the great Lord Northumberland, whose fighting spirit could never stand a retreat, rallied the sagging army; and he himself, Lord Clifford and Lord Stafford charged side by side into the front of our main force, broke into it, and were killed by ordinary soldiers' swords.
Lord Stafford's father, Duke of Buckingham, / Is either slain or wounded dangerously; / I cleft his beaver with a downright blow. / That this is true, father, behold his blood.
Lord Stafford's father, the Duke of Buckingham, is either dead or badly wounded. I split his visor with a straight downward blow. Here's his blood on my sword, father, to prove it.
And, brother, here's the Earl of Wiltshire's blood,
And here, brother, is the Earl of Wiltshire's blood,
Whom I encounter'd as the battles join'd.
whom I fought when the armies met.
Speak thou for me, and tell them what I did.
Let this speak for me and tell them what I did.
Richard hath best deserv'd of all my sons.— / But is your grace dead, my Lord of Somerset?
Richard has earned the most praise of all my sons. But are you really dead, my Lord of Somerset?
Such hope have all the line of John of Gaunt!
May all of John of Gaunt's descendants end the same way!
Thus do I hope to shake King Henry's head.
That's how I hope to shake King Henry's head off.

And so do I.—Victorious Prince of York, / Before I see thee seated in that throne / Which now the house of Lancaster usurps, / I vow by heaven these eyes shall never close. / This is the palace of the fearful king, / And this the regal seat; possess it, York, / For this is thine, and not King Henry's heirs'.

So do I. Victorious Prince of York, I swear by heaven I won't close my eyes until I see you sitting on the throne that the house of Lancaster has stolen. This is the timid king's palace and this is the royal seat. Take it, York; it belongs to you, not to King Henry's heirs.
Assist me, then, sweet Warwick, and I will; / For hither we have broken in by force.
Help me, then, dear Warwick, and I will, since we've broken in here by force.
We'll all assist you; he that flies shall die.
We'll all help you. Anyone who runs away will die.
Thanks, gentle Norfolk.—Stay by me, my lords;— / And, soldiers, stay and lodge by me this night.
Thank you, good Norfolk. Stay by me, my lords; and soldiers, stay and camp here with me tonight.
And when the king comes, offer him no violence, / Unless he seek to thrust you out perforce.
And when the king comes, don't use violence on him unless he tries to throw you out by force.
The queen this day here holds her parliament, / But little thinks we shall be of her council. / By words or blows here let us win our right.
The queen is holding her parliament here today, but she has no idea we'll be sitting in on it. With words or with blows, let's win our rights here.
Arm'd as we are, let's stay within this house.
Let's stay in this building armed as we are.
The bloody parliament shall this be call'd, / Unless Plantagenet, Duke of York, be king, / And bashful Henry depos'd, whose cowardice / Hath made us bywords to our enemies.
This will be called the bloody parliament unless Plantagenet, Duke of York, becomes king and timid Henry is deposed; his cowardice has made us a joke among our enemies.
Then leave me not, my lords; be resolute. / I mean to take possession of my right.
Then don't desert me, my lords; stand firm. I mean to take what's mine.

Neither the king, nor he that loves him best, / The proudest he that holds up Lancaster, / Dares stir a wing if Warwick shake his bells. / I'll plant Plantagenet, root him up who dares.— / Resolve thee, Richard; claim the English crown.

Neither the king, nor his most loyal friend, nor the proudest man who supports Lancaster dares flap a wing while Warwick shakes his falcon bells. I'll plant Plantagenet here; let anyone who dares try to pull him up. Make up your mind, Richard: claim the English crown.

My lords, look where the sturdy rebel sits, / Even in the chair of state! belike he means, / Back'd by the power of Warwick, that false peer, / To aspire unto the crown and reign as king.— / Earl of Northumberland, he slew thy father; / And thine, Lord Clifford; and you both have vow'd revenge / On him, his sons, his favourites, and his friends.

My lords, look where the bold rebel sits, right on the throne! It seems he means, with the backing of that traitor Warwick, to grab the crown and rule as king. Earl of Northumberland, he killed your father, and yours, Lord Clifford; you have both sworn revenge on him, his sons, his favourites and his friends.
If I be not, heavens be reveng'd on me!
If I don't take it, let heaven take revenge on me!
The hope thereof makes Clifford mourn in steel.
The hope of revenge is why Clifford mourns in armour instead of black.
What! shall we suffer this? let's pluck him down; / My heart for anger burns; I cannot brook it.
What! Are we going to put up with this? Let's drag him down. I'm burning with anger; I can't stand it.
Be patient, gentle Earl of Westmoreland.
Be patient, good Earl of Westmoreland.
Patience is for poltroons, such as he; / He durst not sit there had your father liv'd. / My gracious lord, here in the parliament / Let us assail the family of York.
Patience is for cowards like him. He wouldn't dare sit there if your father were alive. My gracious lord, let's attack the York family right here in parliament.
Well hast thou spoken, cousin; be it so.
Well said, cousin; let's do it.
Ah, know you not the city favours them, / And they have troops of soldiers at their beck?
Ah, don't you know the city of London is on their side, and they have troops of soldiers ready at a word?
But when the duke is slain, they'll quickly fly.
But once the duke is dead, they'll soon run.
Far be the thought of this from Henry's heart, / To make a shambles of the parliament-house! / Cousin of Exeter, frowns, words, and threats / Shall be the war that Henry means to use.—
Henry would never dream of turning the parliament house into a slaughterhouse! Cousin Exeter, frowns, words and threats are the only war Henry means to wage.
Thou factious Duke of York, descend my throne, / And kneel for grace and mercy at my feet; / I am thy sovereign.
You rebellious Duke of York, get down from my throne and kneel at my feet for pardon and mercy. I am your sovereign.
For shame, come down; he made thee Duke of York.
Shame on you, come down. He made you Duke of York.
'T was my inheritance, as the earldom was.
It was my inheritance, just as the earldom was.
Thy father was a traitor to the crown.
Your father was a traitor to the crown.
Exeter, thou art a traitor to the crown / In following this usurping Henry.
Exeter, you're the traitor to the crown, following this usurper Henry.
Whom should he follow, but his natural king?
Who else should he follow but his rightful king?
True, Clifford; and that's Richard, Duke of York.
Quite right, Clifford, and that's Richard, Duke of York.
And shall I stand, and thou sit in my throne?
And am I to stand while you sit on my throne?
It must and shall be so. / Content thyself.
It must and will be so. Accept it.
Be Duke of Lancaster; let him be king.
Be Duke of Lancaster and let him be king.
He is both king and Duke of Lancaster; / And that the Lord of Westmoreland shall maintain.
He is both king and Duke of Lancaster, and the Lord of Westmoreland will defend that.
And Warwick shall disprove it. You forget / That we are those which chas'd you from the field, / And slew your fathers, and with colours spread / March'd through the city to the palace gates.
And Warwick will prove it false. You forget that we're the ones who chased you off the battlefield, killed your fathers, and marched through the city to the palace gates with our flags flying.
Yes, Warwick, I remember it to my grief; / And, by his soul, thou and thy house shall rue it.
Yes, Warwick, I remember it, to my sorrow; and by my father's soul, you and your family will regret it.
Plantagenet, of thee, and these thy sons, / Thy kinsmen, and thy friends, I'll have more lives / Than drops of blood were in my father's veins.
Plantagenet, I'll take more lives from you, your sons, your relatives and your friends than there were drops of blood in my father's veins.
Urge it no more; lest that instead of words / I send thee, Warwick, such a messenger / As shall revenge his death before I stir.
Say no more, or instead of words I'll send you, Warwick, a messenger that will avenge his death before I move from this spot.
Poor Clifford! how I scorn his worthless threats!
Poor Clifford! How I despise his empty threats!
Will you we show our title to the crown? / If not, our swords shall plead it in the field.
Do you want us to show our claim to the crown? If not, our swords will argue it on the battlefield.

What title hast thou, traitor, to the crown? / Thy father was, as thou art, Duke of York; / Thy grandfather, Roger Mortimer, Earl of March. / I am the son of Henry the Fifth, / Who made the Dauphin and the French to stoop, / And seiz'd upon their towns and provinces.

What claim do you have to the crown, traitor? Your father was Duke of York, as you are; your grandfather was Roger Mortimer, Earl of March. I am the son of Henry the Fifth, who made the Dauphin and the French bow down and seized their towns and provinces.
Talk not of France, sith thou hast lost it all.
Don't talk about France, since you've lost all of it.
The lord protector lost it, and not I; / When I was crown'd I was but nine months old.
The Lord Protector lost it, not me. I was only nine months old when I was crowned.
You are old enough now, and yet, methinks, you lose.— / Father, tear the crown from the usurper's head.
You're old enough now, and still you seem to be losing. Father, tear the crown off the usurper's head.
Sweet father, do so; set it on your head.
Dear father, do it; put it on your own head.
Good brother, as thou lov'st and honourest arms, / Let's fight it out and not stand cavilling thus.
Good brother, as you love and respect the profession of arms, let's fight it out instead of standing here quibbling.
Sound drums and trumpets, and the king will fly.
Sound the drums and trumpets, and the king will run.
Peace thou, and give King Henry leave to speak.
Quiet yourself, and let King Henry speak.
Plantagenet shall speak first; hear him, lords, / And be you silent and attentive too, / For he that interrupts him shall not live.
Plantagenet will speak first. Listen to him, lords, and stay silent and attentive, because anyone who interrupts him will die.

Think'st thou that I will leave my kingly throne, / Wherein my grandsire and my father sat? / No! first shall war unpeople this my realm; / Ay, and their colours—often borne in France, / And now in England, to our heart's great sorrow— / Shall be my winding sheet.—Why faint you, lords? / My title's good, and better far than his.

Do you think I'll give up my royal throne, where my grandfather and father sat? No! War will empty this kingdom of people first; and the flags so often carried in France, and now in England to our great sorrow, will be my burial shroud. Why are you losing heart, lords? My claim is good, far better than his.
Prove it, Henry, and thou shalt be king.
Prove it, Henry, and you'll be king.
Henry the Fourth by conquest got the crown.
Henry the Fourth won the crown by conquest.
'T was by rebellion against his king.
It was by rebellion against his king.
[Aside] I know not what to say; my title's weak.— / Tell me, may not a king adopt an heir?
(Aside) I don't know what to say; my claim is weak. (Aloud) Tell me, can't a king adopt an heir?
An if he may, then am I lawful king; / For Richard, in the view of many lords, / Resign'd the crown to Henry the Fourth, / Whose heir my father was, and I am his.
If he can, then I'm the lawful king; for Richard the Second, in front of many lords, handed the crown to Henry the Fourth, whose heir was my father, and I am his.
He rose against him, being his sovereign, / And made him to resign his crown perforce.
Henry rebelled against him, his sovereign, and forced him to give up his crown.
Suppose, my lords, he did it unconstrain'd, / Think you 't were prejudicial to his crown?
Suppose, my lords, he gave it up freely: do you think that would cancel his line's right to the crown?
No; for he could not so resign his crown / But that the next heir should succeed and reign.
No; he couldn't give up his crown in a way that stopped the next heir from succeeding and reigning.
Art thou against us, Duke of Exeter?
Are you against us, Duke of Exeter?
His is the right, and therefore pardon me.
The right is on his side, so forgive me.
Why whisper you, my lords, and answer not?
Why are you whispering, my lords, instead of answering?
My conscience tells me he is lawful king.
My conscience tells me he is the lawful king.
[Aside] All will revolt from me and turn to him.
(Aside) They'll all desert me and go over to him.
Plantagenet, for all the claim thou lay'st, / Think not that Henry shall be so depos'd.
Plantagenet, whatever claim you make, don't think Henry will be deposed so easily.
Depos'd he shall be, in despite of all.
He will be deposed, whatever anyone does.
Thou art deceiv'd; 't is not thy southern power, / Of Essex, Norfolk, Suffolk, nor of Kent, / Which makes thee thus presumptuous and proud, / Can set the duke up in despite of me.
You're mistaken. It isn't your southern army from Essex, Norfolk, Suffolk or Kent, which makes you so arrogant, that can put the duke on the throne against my will.
King Henry, be thy title right or wrong, / Lord Clifford vows to fight in thy defence. / May that ground gape and swallow me alive, / Where I shall kneel to him that slew my father!
King Henry, whether your claim is right or wrong, Lord Clifford swears to fight for you. May the ground open and swallow me alive where I kneel to the man who killed my father!
O Clifford, how thy words revive my heart!
O Clifford, how your words lift my heart!
Henry of Lancaster, resign thy crown.— / What mutter you, or what conspire you, lords?
Henry of Lancaster, give up your crown. What are you muttering and plotting, lords?
Do right unto this princely Duke of York, / Or I will fill the house with armed men, / And over the chair of state where now he sits / Write up his title with usurping blood.
Give this princely Duke of York his rights, or I'll fill this hall with armed men and write his claim above the throne where he sits in the usurper's blood.
My Lord of Warwick, hear but one word: / Let me for this my lifetime reign as king.
My Lord of Warwick, hear just one thing: let me reign as king for the rest of my life.
Confirm the crown to me, and to mine heirs, / And thou shalt reign in quiet while thou liv'st.
Settle the crown on me and my heirs, and you can reign in peace as long as you live.
I am content; Richard Plantagenet, / Enjoy the kingdom after my decease.
I agree. Richard Plantagenet, have the kingdom after my death.
What wrong is this unto the prince your son!
What a wrong this does to the prince your son!
What good is this to England and himself!
What a good thing this is for England and for him!
How hast thou injur'd both thyself and us!
How you've harmed yourself and us!
I cannot stay to hear these articles.
I can't stay to hear the terms of this deal.
Come, cousin, let us tell the queen these news.
Come, cousin, let's take this news to the queen.
Farewell, faint-hearted and degenerate king, / In whose cold blood no spark of honour bides.
Goodbye, faint-hearted, unworthy king, with not a spark of honour in your cold blood.
Be thou a prey unto the house of York, / And die in bands for this unmanly deed!
May you fall prey to the house of York and die in chains for this unmanly act!
In dreadful war mayst thou be overcome, / Or live in peace abandon'd and despis'd!
May you be defeated in terrible war, or live in peace, abandoned and despised!
Turn this way, Henry, and regard them not.
Turn this way, Henry, and ignore them.
They seek revenge, and therefore will not yield.
They want revenge, so they won't give in.
Why should you sigh, my lord?
Why are you sighing, my lord?

Not for myself, Lord Warwick, but my son, / Whom I unnaturally shall disinherit.— / But be it as it may, I here entail / The crown to thee, and to thine heirs for ever; / Conditionally, that here thou take an oath / To cease this civil war, and whilst I live / To honour me as thy king and sovereign, / And neither by treason nor hostility / To seek to put me down and reign thyself.

Not for myself, Lord Warwick, but for my son, whom I am unnaturally going to disinherit. But let it be: I here settle the crown on you and your heirs for ever, on condition that you swear an oath here to end this civil war, to honour me as your king and sovereign while I live, and never to try to overthrow me and reign yourself, by treason or by force.
This oath I willingly take and will perform.
I take this oath willingly and will keep it.
Long live King Henry!—Plantagenet, embrace him.
Long live King Henry! Plantagenet, embrace him.
And long live thou, and these thy forward sons!
And long live you, and these eager sons of yours!
Now York and Lancaster are reconcil'd.
Now York and Lancaster are reconciled.
Accurs'd be he that seeks to make them foes!
Cursed be anyone who tries to make them enemies!
Farewell, my gracious lord; I'll to my castle.
Goodbye, my gracious lord; I'm going to my castle.
And I'll keep London with my soldiers.
And I'll hold London with my soldiers.
And I to Norfolk with my followers.
And I'll go to Norfolk with my followers.
And I unto the sea from whence I came.
And I'll go back to the sea where I came from.
And I, with grief and sorrow, to the court.
And I'll go to court, with grief and sorrow.
Here comes the queen, whose looks bewray her anger. / I'll steal away.
Here comes the queen; her face shows her anger. I'll slip away.
Nay, go not from me; I will follow thee.
No, don't leave me; I'll follow you.
Be patient, gentle queen, and I will stay.
Calm down, dear queen, and I'll stay.

Who can be patient in such extremes? / Ah, wretched man! would I had died a maid, / And never seen thee, never borne thee son, / Seeing thou hast prov'd so unnatural a father! / Hath he deserv'd to lose his birthright thus? / Hadst thou but lov'd him half so well as I, / Or felt that pain which I did for him once, / Or nourish'd him as I did with my blood, / Thou wouldst have left thy dearest heart-blood there / Rather than have made that savage duke thine heir / And disinherited thine only son.

Who can be calm in such extremes? Ah, miserable man! I wish I'd died a virgin and never seen you or borne you a son, since you've turned out such an unnatural father! Has he done anything to deserve losing his birthright like this? If you had loved him half as much as I do, or felt the pain I felt for him once, or fed him with my blood as I did, you would have given your own heart's blood rather than make that savage duke your heir and disinherit your only son.
Father, you cannot disinherit me. / If you be king, why should not I succeed?
Father, you can't disinherit me. If you're king, why shouldn't I succeed you?
Pardon me, Margaret;—pardon me, sweet son; / The Earl of Warwick and the duke enforc'd me.
Forgive me, Margaret; forgive me, dear son. The Earl of Warwick and the duke forced me.

Enforc'd thee! art thou king, and wilt be forc'd? / I shame to hear thee speak. Ah, timorous wretch! / Thou hast undone thyself, thy son, and me, / And given unto the house of York such head / As thou shalt reign but by their sufferance. / To entail him and his heirs unto the crown, / What is it but to make thy sepulchre / And creep into it far before thy time? / Warwick is chancellor and the lord of Calais; / Stern Falconbridge commands the narrow seas; / The duke is made protector of the realm; / And yet shalt thou be safe? such safety finds / The trembling lamb environed with wolves. / Had I been there, which am a silly woman, / The soldiers should have toss'd me on their pikes / Before I would have granted to that act. / But thou prefer'st thy life before thine honour; / And seeing thou dost, I here divorce myself, / Both from thy table, Henry, and thy bed, / Until that act of parliament be repeal'd / Whereby my son is disinherited. / The northern lords that have forsworn thy colours / Will follow mine if once they see them spread; / And spread they shall be to thy foul disgrace / And utter ruin of the house of York. / Thus do I leave thee.—Come, son, let's away: / Our army is ready; come, we'll after them.

Forced you! Are you a king and you let yourself be forced? I'm ashamed to hear you speak. Ah, timid wretch! You've ruined yourself, your son and me, and given the house of York so much power that you'll reign only because they allow it. To settle the crown on him and his heirs is just digging your own grave and crawling into it long before your time. Warwick is Chancellor and lord of Calais; stern Falconbridge controls the Channel; the duke is made Protector of the realm; and you think you'll be safe? That's the safety of a trembling lamb surrounded by wolves. If I'd been there, silly woman that I am, the soldiers would have tossed me on their spears before I agreed to that act. But you value your life above your honour; and since you do, I here separate myself from your table and your bed, Henry, until that act of parliament that disinherits my son is repealed. The northern lords who have abandoned your flag will follow mine once they see it unfurled; and it will be unfurled, to your shame and the complete ruin of the house of York. So I leave you. Come, son, let's go. Our army is ready; come, we'll go after them.
Stay, gentle Margaret, and hear me speak.
Wait, gentle Margaret, and hear me speak.
Thou hast spoke too much already; get thee gone.
You've said too much already; go away.
Gentle son Edward, thou wilt stay with me?
My dear son Edward, you'll stay with me?
Ay, to be murther'd by his enemies.
Yes, to be murdered by his enemies.
When I return with victory from the field / I'll see your grace; till then I'll follow her.
When I come back victorious from the battlefield I'll see your grace; until then I'll follow her.
Come, son, away! we may not linger thus.
Come, son, away! We can't hang about like this.

Poor queen! how love to me and to her son / Hath made her break out into terms of rage! / Reveng'd may she be on that hateful duke / Whose haughty spirit, winged with desire, / Will cost my crown, and like an empty eagle / Tire on the flesh of me and of my son. / The loss of those three lords torments my heart; / I'll write unto them, and entreat them fair.— / Come, cousin, you shall be the messenger.

Poor queen! How her love for me and her son has made her burst out in rage! May she get her revenge on that hateful duke, whose proud ambition, flying on desire, will cost me my crown and, like a starving eagle, tear at my flesh and my son's. Losing those three lords torments me. I'll write to them and ask them kindly to return. Come, cousin, you'll be the messenger.
And I, I hope, shall reconcile them all.
And I hope I'll reconcile them all.
Brother, though I be youngest, give me leave.
Brother, I may be the youngest, but let me speak.
No; I can better play the orator.
But I have reasons strong and forcible.
But I have strong, convincing reasons.
Why, how now, sons and brother! at a strife? / What is your quarrel? how began it first?
What's this, sons and brother? Arguing? What's the quarrel? How did it start?
No quarrel, but a slight contention.
It's not a quarrel, just a small disagreement.
About that which concerns your grace and us— / The crown of England, father, which is yours.
About something that concerns your grace and us: the crown of England, father, which is yours.
Mine, boy? not till King Henry be dead.
Mine, boy? Not until King Henry is dead.
Your right depends not on his life or death.
Your right doesn't depend on whether he lives or dies.
Now you are heir, therefore enjoy it now; / By giving the house of Lancaster leave to breathe, / It will outrun you, father, in the end.
You're the heir now, so enjoy it now. If you give the house of Lancaster time to breathe, it will overtake you in the end, father.
I took an oath that he should quietly reign.
I swore an oath that he would reign in peace.
But for a kingdom any oath may be broken; / I would break a thousand oaths to reign one year.
But any oath can be broken for a kingdom. I'd break a thousand oaths to reign for one year.
No; God forbid your grace should be forsworn.
No; God forbid your grace should break your word.
I shall be, if I claim by open war.
I will be breaking it if I claim the crown by open war.
I'll prove the contrary if you'll hear me speak.
I'll prove the opposite if you'll hear me out.
Thou canst not, son; it is impossible.

An oath is of no moment, being not took / Before a true and lawful magistrate / That hath authority over him that swears. / Henry had none, but did usurp the place; / Then, seeing 't was he that made you to depose, / Your oath, my lord, is vain and frivolous. / Therefore, to arms! And, father, do but think / How sweet a thing it is to wear a crown, / Within whose circuit is Elysium / And all that poets feign of bliss and joy. / Why do we linger thus? I cannot rest / Until the white rose that I wear be dyed / Even in the lukewarm blood of Henry's heart.

An oath means nothing unless it's sworn before a true and lawful authority with power over the one who swears. Henry had no such power; he stole the place. So, since he was the one you swore to, your oath, my lord, is empty and worthless. So, to arms! And father, just think how sweet it is to wear a crown; inside its circle lies paradise and every bliss and joy the poets invent. Why are we hanging about? I can't rest until the white rose I wear is dyed in the warm blood of Henry's heart.

Richard, enough; I will be king, or die.— / Brother, thou shalt to London presently, / And whet on Warwick to this enterprise.— / Thou, Richard, shalt to the Duke of Norfolk, / And tell him privily of our intent.— / You, Edward, shall unto my Lord Cobham, / With whom the Kentishmen will willingly rise. / In them I trust; for they are soldiers, / Witty, courteous, liberal, full of spirit.— / While you are thus employ'd, what resteth more / But that I seek occasion how to rise, / And yet the king not privy to my drift, / Nor any of the house of Lancaster?

Enough, Richard; I will be king or die. Brother, go to London at once and spur Warwick on to this enterprise. Richard, go to the Duke of Norfolk and tell him our plan secretly. Edward, go to my Lord Cobham; the men of Kent will gladly rise with him. I trust them, for they're soldiers: clever, courteous, generous and full of spirit. While you're busy with this, all that's left for me is to find an opportunity to rise up, without the king or anyone of the house of Lancaster knowing my plan.
But stay.—What news? Why com'st thou in such post?
But wait. What news? Why have you come in such a hurry?
The queen, with all the northern earls and lords, / Intend here to besiege you in your castle. / She is hard by with twenty thousand men, / And therefore fortify your hold, my lord.
The queen, with all the northern earls and lords, intends to besiege you here in your castle. She's close by with twenty thousand men, so strengthen your defences, my lord.

Ay, with my sword. What! think'st thou that we fear them?— / Edward and Richard, you shall stay with me; / My brother Montague shall post to London. / Let noble Warwick, Cobham, and the rest, / Whom we have left protectors of the king, / With powerful policy strengthen themselves, / And trust not simple Henry nor his oaths.

Yes, with my sword. What! Do you think we're afraid of them? Edward and Richard, you'll stay with me; my brother Montague will ride to London. Let noble Warwick, Cobham and the rest we left to guard the king strengthen themselves with clever policy, and not trust simple Henry or his oaths.
Brother, I go; I'll win them, fear it not: / And thus most humbly I do take my leave.
Brother, I'm going. I'll win them over, don't worry. And so I humbly take my leave.
Sir John and Sir Hugh Mortimer, mine uncles, / You are come to Sandal in a happy hour; / The army of the queen mean to besiege us.
Sir John and Sir Hugh Mortimer, my uncles, you've come to Sandal at a lucky moment. The queen's army means to besiege us.
She shall not need; we'll meet her in the field.
She won't need to; we'll meet her in the field.
Ay, with five hundred, father, for a need. / A woman-general! what should we fear?
Yes, with five hundred if need be, father. A woman general! What do we have to fear?
I hear their drums; let's set our men in order, / And issue forth and bid them battle straight.
I can hear their drums. Let's put our men in order, march out and fight them at once.

Five men to twenty!—though the odds be great, / I doubt not, uncle, of our victory. / Many a battle have I won in France / Whenas the enemy hath been ten to one; / Why should I not now have the like success?
Five men against twenty! Though the odds are great, I don't doubt we'll win, uncle. I won many battles in France when the enemy outnumbered us ten to one; why shouldn't I have the same success now?
Ah! whither shall I fly to scape their hands? / Ah, tutor! look where bloody Clifford comes.
Ah! Where can I run to escape them? Ah, tutor! Look, here comes bloody Clifford.
Chaplain, away! thy priesthood saves thy life. / As for the brat of this accursed duke / Whose father slew my father, he shall die.
Chaplain, go! Your priesthood saves your life. But this cursed duke's brat, whose father killed my father, will die.
And I, my lord, will bear him company.
And I'll die with him, my lord.
Ah, Clifford, murder not this innocent child, / Lest thou be hated both of God and man.
Ah, Clifford, don't murder this innocent child, or you'll be hated by God and man.
How now! is he dead already? Or is it fear / That makes him close his eyes?—I'll open them.
What's this? Is he dead already? Or is it fear that makes him shut his eyes? I'll open them.

So looks the pent-up lion o'er the wretch / That trembles under his devouring paws; / And so he walks, insulting o'er his prey, / And so he comes to rend his limbs asunder.— / Ah, gentle Clifford, kill me with thy sword, / And not with such a cruel threat'ning look. / Sweet Clifford, hear me speak before I die: / I am too mean a subject for thy wrath; / Be thou reveng'd on men, and let me live.

That's how a caged lion looks at the trembling wretch under its devouring paws; that's how it paces, gloating over its prey; and that's how it comes to tear the limbs apart. Ah, gentle Clifford, kill me with your sword, not with such a cruel threatening look. Sweet Clifford, hear me before I die: I'm too lowly a target for your anger. Take your revenge on men, and let me live.
In vain thou speak'st, poor boy; my father's blood / Hath stopp'd the passage where thy words should enter.
You're wasting your words, poor boy. My father's blood has blocked the way your words would enter.
Then let my father's blood open it again; / He is a man, and, Clifford, cope with him.
Then let my father's blood open it again. He's a man; fight him, Clifford.

Had I thy brethren here, their lives and thine / Were not revenge sufficient for me. / No; if I digg'd up thy forefathers' graves / And hung their rotten coffins up in chains, / It could not slake mine ire nor ease my heart. / The sight of any of the house of York / Is as a fury to torment my soul; / And till I root out their accursed line / And leave not one alive, I live in hell. / Therefore—

If I had your brothers here, their lives and yours would not be revenge enough for me. No; if I dug up your ancestors' graves and hung their rotting coffins up in chains, it couldn't quench my anger or ease my heart. The sight of anyone from the house of York is like a Fury tormenting my soul, and until I root out their cursed family and leave not one alive, I'm living in hell. So—
O, let me pray before I take my death!— / To thee I pray; sweet Clifford, pity me!
O, let me pray before I die! I pray to you: sweet Clifford, pity me!
Such pity as my rapier's point affords.
The only pity you'll get is my sword's point.
I never did thee harm; why wilt thou slay me?
I never did you any harm; why will you kill me?

But 't was ere I was born. / Thou hast one son; for his sake pity me, / Lest in revenge thereof, sith God is just, / He be as miserably slain as I. / Ah, let me live in prison all my days, / And when I give occasion of offence, / Then let me die, for now thou hast no cause.

But that was before I was born. You have a son; for his sake pity me, or in revenge for this, since God is just, he may be killed as miserably as I am. Ah, let me live in prison all my life, and if I ever give you cause for offence, then let me die; but now you have no reason.
No cause? / Thy father slew my father; therefore, die. [Clifford stabs him]
No reason? Your father killed my father; so die. (He stabs him.)
Dii faciant laudis summa sit ista tuae! [Dies]
May the gods grant that this be the height of your glory! (He dies.)
Plantagenet! I come, Plantagenet! / And this thy son's blood cleaving to my blade / Shall rust upon my weapon till thy blood / Congeal'd with this, do make me wipe off both.
Plantagenet! I'm coming, Plantagenet! And your son's blood sticking to my blade will rust on my weapon until your blood, dried together with it, makes me wipe both off.

The army of the queen hath got the field. / My uncles both are slain in rescuing me; / And all my followers to the eager foe / Turn back and fly like ships before the wind, / Or lambs pursu'd by hunger-starved wolves. / My sons—God knows what hath bechanced them; / But this I know,—they have demean'd themselves / Like men born to renown by life or death. / Three times did Richard make a lane to me, / And thrice cried 'Courage, father! fight it out!' / And full as oft came Edward to my side / With purple falchion painted to the hilt / In blood of those that had encount'red him; / And when the hardiest warriors did retire / Richard cried 'Charge! and give no foot of ground!' / And cried 'A crown, or else a glorious tomb! / A sceptre, or an earthly sepulchre!' / With this, we charg'd again; but, out, alas! / We budg'd again, as I have seen a swan / With bootless labour swim against the tide / And spend her strength with overmatching waves.

The queen's army has won the field. Both my uncles are killed trying to rescue me, and all my followers turn their backs on the eager enemy and run, like ships before the wind or lambs chased by starving wolves. My sons: God knows what has happened to them; but I do know they have behaved like men born to win fame in life or death. Three times Richard cut a path through to me and three times shouted, 'Courage, father! Fight it out!' And just as often Edward came to my side with his sword stained red to the hilt with the blood of the men who had fought him. And when the toughest soldiers fell back, Richard shouted, 'Charge! Don't give an inch!' and 'A crown, or else a glorious tomb! A sceptre, or a grave on earth!' With that, we charged again; but, alas, we were pushed back again, like a swan I've seen swimming uselessly against the tide and wearing herself out against waves too strong for her.

Ah, hark! the fatal followers do pursue, / And I am faint and cannot fly their fury; / And were I strong, I would not shun their fury. / The sands are number'd that make up my life; / Here must I stay, and here my life must end.—

Ah, listen! The deadly pursuers are coming, and I'm too weak to escape their fury; and if I were strong, I wouldn't run from it. The sands of my life are counted out; here I must stay, and here my life must end.
Come, bloody Clifford, rough Northumberland, / I dare your quenchless fury to more rage. / I am your butt, and I abide your shot.
Come, bloody Clifford, rough Northumberland; I dare your endless fury to rage even more. I'm your target, and I'll stand and take your shots.
Yield to our mercy, proud Plantagenet.
Surrender to our mercy, proud Plantagenet.
Ay, to such mercy as his ruthless arm / With downright payment show'd unto my father. / Now Phaethon hath tumbled from his car, / And made an evening at the noontide prick.
Yes, the kind of mercy his ruthless arm showed my father, paid in full. Now Phaethon has fallen from his chariot and turned noon into evening.

My ashes, as the phoenix, may bring forth / A bird that will revenge upon you all; / And in that hope I throw mine eyes to heaven / Scorning whate'er you can afflict me with. / Why come you not?—what! multitudes, and fear?

My ashes, like the phoenix's, may produce a bird that will take revenge on you all; and in that hope I lift my eyes to heaven, scorning whatever torment you can give me. Why don't you come on? What! So many of you, and afraid?
So cowards fight when they can fly no further; / So doves do peck the falcon's piercing talons; / So desperate thieves, all hopeless of their lives, / Breathe out invectives 'gainst the officers.
That's how cowards fight when they can't run any further; that's how doves peck at the falcon's sharp claws; that's how desperate thieves with no hope of life hurl insults at the officers.

O Clifford, but bethink thee once again, / And in thy thought o'errun my former time; / And, if thou canst for blushing, view this face, / And bite thy tongue, that slanders him with cowardice / Whose frown hath made thee faint and fly ere this.

O Clifford, just think back and run over my past in your mind; and if you can look at this face without blushing, bite your tongue for calling a coward the man whose frown has made you faint and run before now.
I will not bandy with thee word for word, / But buckle with thee blows, twice two for one.
I won't trade words with you; I'll trade blows with you, four for every one.
Hold, valiant Clifford! for a thousand causes / I would prolong awhile the traitor's life.— / Wrath makes him deaf; speak thou, Northumberland.
Stop, brave Clifford! For a thousand reasons I want to keep the traitor alive a little longer. Anger has made him deaf; you speak to him, Northumberland.

Hold, Clifford! do not honour him so much / To prick thy finger, though to wound his heart. / What valour were it, when a cur doth grin, / For one to thrust his hand between his teeth, / When he might spurn him with his foot away? / It is war's prize to take all vantages, / And ten to one is no impeach of valour.

Stop, Clifford! Don't do him the honour of pricking your finger, even to wound his heart. What bravery is there in putting your hand between a snarling dog's teeth when you could kick it away? In war it's fair to take every advantage, and ten against one is no slur on courage.
Ay, ay; so strives the woodcock with the gin.
Yes, yes; that's how the woodcock struggles in the trap.
So doth the cony struggle in the net.
That's how the rabbit struggles in the net.
So triumph thieves upon their conquer'd booty; / So true men yield, with robbers so o'ermatch'd.
That's how thieves gloat over the loot they've captured; that's how honest men give in when robbers outnumber them.
What would your grace have done unto him now?
What would your grace like done with him now?

Brave warriors, Clifford and Northumberland, / Come, make him stand upon this molehill here, / That raught at mountains with outstretched arms, / Yet parted but the shadow with his hand.— / What! was it you that would be England's king? / Was 't you that revell'd in our Parliament, / And made a preachment of your high descent? / Where are your mess of sons to back you now? / The wanton Edward and the lusty George? / And where's that valiant crook-back prodigy, / Dicky your boy, that with his grumbling voice / Was wont to cheer his dad in mutinies? / Or, with the rest, where is your darling Rutland? / Look, York; I stain'd this napkin with the blood / That valiant Clifford with his rapier's point / Made issue from the bosom of the boy, / And, if thine eyes can water for his death, / I give thee this to dry thy cheeks withal. / Alas, poor York! but that I hate thee deadly / I should lament thy miserable state. / I prithee, grieve to make me merry, York; / Stamp, rave, and fret, that I may sing and dance. / What, hath thy fiery heart so parch'd thine entrails / That not a tear can fall for Rutland's death? / Why art thou patient, man? thou shouldst be mad; / And I, to make thee mad, do mock thee thus. / Thou wouldst be feed, I see, to make me sport; / York cannot speak unless he wear a crown.— / A crown for York!—and, lords, bow low to him.— / Hold you his hands whilst I do set it on.—

Brave warriors, Clifford and Northumberland, come and make him stand on this molehill here, the man who reached for mountains with outstretched arms but only grasped their shadow. What! Was it you who wanted to be King of England? Was it you who made merry in our parliament and preached a sermon about your noble descent? Where's your pack of sons to back you now? The wanton Edward and the lusty George? And where's that brave hunchbacked freak, your boy Dicky, who used to cheer his dad on in rebellions with his growling voice? Or, along with the rest, where's your darling Rutland? Look, York: I stained this handkerchief with the blood that brave Clifford, with his sword's point, made flow from the boy's chest; and if your eyes can weep for his death, I give you this to dry your cheeks with. Alas, poor York! If I didn't hate you to death, I'd pity your miserable state. Please, grieve to make me merry, York; stamp, rave and fret, so I can sing and dance. What, has your fiery heart so dried up your insides that not a tear can fall for Rutland's death? Why are you so calm, man? You should be mad; and I'm mocking you like this to make you mad. I see you want to be paid to entertain me. York can't speak unless he wears a crown. A crown for York! And, lords, bow low to him. Hold his hands while I put it on.

Ay, marry, sir, now looks he like a king. / Ay, this is he that took King Henry's chair; / And this is he was his adopted heir.— / But how is it that great Plantagenet / Is crown'd so soon and broke his solemn oath? / As I bethink me, you should not be king / Till our King Henry had shook hands with Death. / And will you pale your head in Henry's glory, / And rob his temples of the diadem, / Now in his life, against your holy oath? / O, 't is a fault too too unpardonable.— / Off with the crown, and with the crown his head! / And whilst we breathe take time to do him dead.

Yes, indeed, sir, now he looks like a king. Yes, this is the man who took King Henry's throne, and this is the one who was his adopted heir. But how is it that great Plantagenet is crowned so soon and has broken his solemn oath? As I remember, you weren't to be king until our King Henry had shaken hands with Death. And will you wrap your head in Henry's glory and rob his brows of the crown now, while he's alive, against your holy oath? O, it's a fault far too unforgivable. Off with the crown, and with the crown his head! And while we catch our breath, let's take time to kill him.
That is my office, for my father's sake.
That's my job, for my father's sake.
Nay, stay; let's hear the orisons he makes.
No, wait; let's hear the prayers he says.

She-wolf of France, but worse than wolves of France, / Whose tongue more poisons than the adder's tooth, / How ill-beseeming is it in thy sex / To triumph, like an Amazonian trull, / Upon their woes whom fortune captivates! / But that thy face is, vizard-like, unchanging, / Made impudent with use of evil deeds, / I would assay, proud queen, to make thee blush. / To tell thee whence thou cam'st, of whom deriv'd, / Were shame enough to shame thee, wert thou not shameless. / Thy father bears the type of King of Naples, / Of both the Sicils and Jerusalem, / Yet not so wealthy as an English yeoman. / Hath that poor monarch taught thee to insult? / It needs not, nor it boots thee not, proud queen; / Unless the adage must be verified, / That beggars mounted run their horse to death. / 'T is beauty that doth oft make women proud; / But, God he knows, thy share thereof is small. / 'T is virtue that doth make them most admir'd; / The contrary doth make thee wond'red at. / 'T is government that makes them seem divine; / The want thereof makes thee abominable. / Thou art as opposite to every good / As the Antipodes are unto us, / Or as the south to the Septentrion. / O tiger's heart wrapp'd in a woman's hide! / How couldst thou drain the life-blood of the child, / To bid the father wipe his eyes withal, / And yet be seen to bear a woman's face? / Women are soft, mild, pitiful, and flexible; / Thou stern, obdurate, flinty, rough, remorseless. / Bid'st thou me rage? why, now thou hast thy wish: / Wouldst have me weep? why, now thou hast thy will; / For raging wind blows up incessant showers, / And when the rage allays the rain begins. / These tears are my sweet Rutland's obsequies, / And every drop cries vengeance for his death, / 'Gainst thee, fell Clifford, and thee, false Frenchwoman.

She-wolf of France, but worse than the wolves of France, whose tongue is more poisonous than an adder's fang! How unfitting it is for your sex to gloat like an Amazon whore over the sorrows of those whom fortune has taken prisoner! If your face weren't like a mask, unchanging and hardened shameless by habitual evil, I'd try to make you blush, proud queen. Just to tell you where you came from and who your family is would shame you, if you weren't shameless. Your father has the title of King of Naples, of both Sicilies and Jerusalem, yet he's not as rich as an English farmer. Did that poor monarch teach you to gloat? There's no need for it, and it does you no good, proud queen, unless it's to prove the saying that a beggar on horseback rides his horse to death. It's beauty that often makes women proud, but God knows you have little of it. It's virtue that makes them most admired; the lack of it makes you a freak. It's self-control that makes them seem divine; the lack of it makes you hateful. You're as opposite to every good thing as the other side of the world is to us, or as the south is to the north. O tiger's heart wrapped in a woman's skin! How could you draw the child's life-blood and tell the father to wipe his eyes with it, and still have the face of a woman? Women are soft, mild, compassionate and yielding; you are stern, hard, flinty, rough and pitiless. You tell me to rage? Well, now you have your wish. You want me to weep? Well, now you have your way; for raging wind whips up endless showers, and when the rage dies down the rain begins. These tears are my sweet Rutland's funeral rites, and every drop cries for revenge for his death, against you, cruel Clifford, and you, treacherous Frenchwoman.
Beshrew me, but his passion moves me so / That hardly can I check my eyes from tears.
Curse me, but his grief moves me so much I can hardly hold back my tears.

That face of his the hungry cannibals / Would not have touch'd, would not have stain'd with blood; / But you are more inhuman, more inexorable, / O, ten times more, than tigers of Hyrcania. / See, ruthless queen, a hapless father's tears; / This cloth thou dipp'dst in blood of my sweet boy, / And I with tears do wash the blood away. / Keep thou the napkin, and go boast of this; / And if thou tell'st the heavy story right, / Upon my soul, the hearers will shed tears, / Yea, even my foes will shed fast-falling tears / And say 'Alas! it was a piteous deed!'— / There, take the crown, and with the crown my curse; / And in thy need such comfort come to thee / As now I reap at thy too cruel hand!— / Hard-hearted Clifford, take me from the world; / My soul to heaven, my blood upon your heads!

Even starving cannibals wouldn't have touched that face of his or stained it with blood; but you are more inhuman, more pitiless, ten times more than the tigers of Hyrcania. See, ruthless queen, an unlucky father's tears. You dipped this cloth in my sweet boy's blood, and I'm washing the blood away with tears. Keep the handkerchief and go and boast about this; and if you tell the sad story truthfully, I swear the listeners will weep; yes, even my enemies will shed streams of tears and say, 'Alas, it was a pitiful deed!' There, take the crown, and with the crown my curse; and when you're in need, may you get the same comfort I'm now getting from your cruel hand! Hard-hearted Clifford, take me out of this world; my soul to heaven, my blood on your heads!
Had he been slaughter-man to all my kin, / I should not, for my life, but weep with him, / To see how inly sorrow gripes his soul.
Even if he had butchered all my family, I couldn't, to save my life, help weeping with him, seeing how deeply sorrow grips his soul.
What! weeping-ripe, my Lord Northumberland? / Think but upon the wrong he did us all, / And that will quickly dry thy melting tears.
What! On the verge of tears, Lord Northumberland? Just think of the wrong he did us all, and that will soon dry your melting tears.
Here's for my oath, here's for my father's death.
This is for my oath; this is for my father's death.
And here's to right our gentle-hearted king.
And this is to avenge our gentle-hearted king.
Open thy gate of mercy, gracious God! / My soul flies through these wounds to seek out thee.
Open your gate of mercy, gracious God! My soul flies out through these wounds to find you.
Off with his head, and set it on York gates; / So York may overlook the town of York.
Cut off his head and set it on the gates of York, so York can look out over the town of York.

I wonder how our princely father scap'd, / Or whether he be scap'd away or no / From Clifford's and Northumberland's pursuit. / Had he been ta'en, we should have heard the news; / Had he been slain, we should have heard the news; / Or had he scap'd, methinks we should have heard / The happy tidings of his good escape.— / How fares my brother? why is he so sad?

I wonder how our princely father got away, or whether he escaped Clifford and Northumberland's pursuit at all. If he'd been captured we'd have heard the news; if he'd been killed we'd have heard the news; and if he'd escaped, I think we'd have heard the happy news of his escape. How is my brother? Why is he so sad?

I cannot joy until I be resolv'd / Where our right valiant father is become. / I saw him in the battle range about, / And watch'd him how he singled Clifford forth. / Methought he bore him in the thickest troop / As doth a lion in a herd of neat; / Or as a bear, encompass'd round with dogs, / Who having pinch'd a few and made them cry, / The rest stand all aloof and bark at him. / So far'd our father with his enemies; / So fled his enemies my warlike father. / Methinks 'tis pride enough to be his son.— / See how the morning opes her golden gates / And takes her farewell of the glorious sun. / How well resembles it the prime of youth, / Trimm'd like a younker prancing to his love!

I can't be happy until I know what has become of our brave father. I saw him ranging about in the battle and watched him single out Clifford. I thought he carried himself in the thick of the troops like a lion among a herd of cattle, or like a bear surrounded by dogs: after he has bitten a few and made them yelp, the rest keep their distance and bark at him. That's how our father dealt with his enemies; that's how his enemies fled from my warlike father. I think it's honour enough to be his son. Look how the morning opens her golden gates and says goodbye to the glorious sun. How like it is to the springtime of youth, dressed up like a young gallant prancing off to his girl!
Dazzle mine eyes, or do I see three suns?
Are my eyes dazzled, or do I see three suns?

Three glorious suns, each one a perfect sun; / Not separated with the racking clouds, / But sever'd in a pale clear-shining sky. / See, see! they join, embrace, and seem to kiss, / As if they vow'd some league inviolable; / Now are they but one lamp, one light, one sun. / In this the heaven figures some event.

Three glorious suns, each a perfect sun; not separated by drifting clouds, but apart in a pale, clear, shining sky. Look, look! They join, embrace and seem to kiss, as if they were swearing some unbreakable alliance. Now they're only one lamp, one light, one sun. Heaven is foretelling some event in this.

'T is wondrous strange, the like yet never heard of. / I think it cites us, brother, to the field, / That we, the sons of brave Plantagenet, / Each one already blazing by our meeds, / Should, notwithstanding, join our lights together, / And overshine the earth, as this the world. / Whate'er it bodes, henceforward will I bear / Upon my target three fair shining suns.

It's wonderfully strange; nobody's ever heard of such a thing. I think it calls us to the battlefield, brother, so that we, the sons of brave Plantagenet, each already shining by his own merits, should still join our lights together and outshine the earth, as this outshines the world. Whatever it means, from now on I'll carry three bright shining suns on my shield.
Nay, bear three daughters; by your leave I speak it, / You love the breeder better than the male.—
No, carry three daughters; with your permission, I'll say it: you like the breeders better than the males.
But what art thou, whose heavy looks foretell / Some dreadful story hanging on thy tongue?
But who are you? Your gloomy looks warn of some dreadful story hanging on your tongue.
Ah, one that was a woeful looker-on / When as the noble Duke of York was slain, / Your princely father and my loving lord.
Ah, someone who sadly watched when the noble Duke of York was killed, your princely father and my loving lord.
O, speak no more, for I have heard too much!
O, say no more, I've heard too much!
Say how he died, for I will hear it all.
Tell how he died; I'll hear all of it.

Environed he was with many foes, / And stood against them as the hope of Troy / Against the Greeks that would have ent'red Troy. / But Hercules himself must yield to odds; / And many strokes, though with a little axe, / Hew down and fell the hardest-timber'd oak. / By many hands your father was subdu'd, / But only slaught'red by the ireful arm / Of unrelenting Clifford and the queen, / Who crown'd the gracious duke in high despite, / Laugh'd in his face, and when with grief he wept / The ruthless queen gave him, to dry his cheeks, / A napkin steeped in the harmless blood / Of sweet young Rutland, by rough Clifford slain. / And, after many scorns, many foul taunts, / They took his head, and on the gates of York / They set the same; and there it doth remain, / The saddest spectacle that e'er I view'd.

He was surrounded by many enemies and stood against them as Hector, the hope of Troy, stood against the Greeks who would have entered Troy. But even Hercules must give way when outnumbered, and many strokes, even with a small axe, cut down the hardest oak. Your father was overpowered by many hands, but killed only by the angry arm of merciless Clifford and the queen. She crowned the gracious duke in mockery and laughed in his face, and when he wept with grief the ruthless queen gave him a handkerchief soaked in the innocent blood of sweet young Rutland, killed by rough Clifford, to dry his cheeks. And after many insults and foul taunts, they took his head and put it on the gates of York, and there it remains, the saddest sight I've ever seen.

Sweet Duke of York! our prop to lean upon, / Now thou art gone, we have no staff, no stay. / O Clifford! boisterous Clifford! thou hast slain / The flower of Europe for his chivalry; / And treacherously hast thou vanquish'd him, / For hand to hand he would have vanquish'd thee. / Now my soul's palace is become a prison. / Ah, would she break from hence, that this my body / Might in the ground be closed up in rest! / For never henceforth shall I joy again, / Never, O, never, shall I see more joy!

Sweet Duke of York, our support to lean on! Now you're gone, we have no staff, no prop. O Clifford, violent Clifford! You've killed the flower of Europe's knighthood; and you beat him treacherously, for in single combat he would have beaten you. Now my body, the palace of my soul, has become a prison. Ah, if only my soul would break out, so my body could be shut away in the ground to rest! For I'll never be happy again; never, O never, will I see joy again!

I cannot weep, for all my body's moisture / Scarce serves to quench my furnace-burning heart; / Nor can my tongue unload my heart's great burthen, / For selfsame wind that I should speak withal / Is kindling coals that fires all my breast / And burns me up with flames that tears would quench. / To weep is to make less the depth of grief; / Tears, then, for babes, blows and revenge for me!— / Richard, I bear thy name; I'll venge thy death, / Or die renowned by attempting it.

I can't weep, for all the moisture in my body is hardly enough to cool my furnace-hot heart; nor can my tongue unload my heart's great burden, because the very breath I should speak with is fanning the coals that burn in my chest and consume me with flames that tears would put out. To weep is to make grief less deep. So tears are for babies; blows and revenge are for me! Richard, I bear your name; I'll avenge your death or die famous in the attempt.
His name that valiant duke hath left with thee; / His dukedom and his chair with me is left.
That brave duke left his name to you; his dukedom and his seat are left to me.
Nay, if thou be that princely eagle's bird, / Show thy descent by gazing 'gainst the sun; / For chair and dukedom, throne and kingdom say: / Either that is thine, or else thou wert not his.
No, if you're really that princely eagle's chick, prove your descent by staring at the sun. Instead of seat and dukedom, say throne and kingdom: either that's yours, or you were never his son.
How now, fair lords! What fare? what news abroad?
What's this, fair lords? How are things? What news?

Great Lord of Warwick, if we should recount / Our baleful news, and at each word's deliverance / Stab poniards in our flesh till all were told, / The words would add more anguish than the wounds. / O valiant lord, the Duke of York is slain!

Great Lord of Warwick, if we told our terrible news and stabbed daggers into our flesh at every word until it was all told, the words would hurt more than the wounds. O brave lord, the Duke of York is dead!
O, Warwick, Warwick! that Plantagenet / Which held thee dearly as his soul's redemption / Is by the stern Lord Clifford done to death.
O Warwick, Warwick! That Plantagenet, who loved you as dearly as the salvation of his soul, has been killed by stern Lord Clifford.

Ten days ago I drown'd these news in tears, / And now, to add more measure to your woes, / I come to tell you things sith then befallen. / After the bloody fray at Wakefield fought, / Where your brave father breath'd his latest gasp, / Tidings, as swiftly as the posts could run, / Were brought me of your loss and his depart. / I, then in London, keeper of the king, / Muster'd my soldiers, gather'd flocks of friends, / And very well appointed, as I thought, / March'd toward Saint Alban's to intercept the queen, / Bearing the king in my behalf along; / For by my scouts I was advertised / That she was coming with a full intent / To dash our late decree in parliament / Touching King Henry's oath and your succession. / Short tale to make, we at Saint Alban's met, / Our battles join'd, and both sides fiercely fought; / But, whether 't was the coldness of the king, / Who look'd full gently on his warlike queen, / That robb'd my soldiers of their heated spleen, / Or whether 't was report of her success, / Or more than common fear of Clifford's rigour, / Who thunders to his captives blood and death, / I cannot judge; but, to conclude with truth, / Their weapons like to lightning came and went, / Our soldiers',—like the night-owl's lazy flight, / Or like an idle thrasher with a flail— / Fell gently down, as if they struck their friends. / I cheer'd them up with justice of our cause, / With promise of high pay and great rewards, / But all in vain; they had no heart to fight, / And we in them no hope to win the day; / So that we fled: the king unto the queen; / Lord George your brother, Norfolk, and myself, / In haste, post-haste, are come to join with you; / For in the marches here, we heard, you were / Making another head to fight again.

Ten days ago I drowned this news in tears; and now, to add to your sorrows, I've come to tell you what has happened since. After the bloody battle at Wakefield, where your brave father breathed his last, news of your loss and his death was brought to me as fast as messengers could ride. I was in London, guarding the king. I gathered my soldiers and crowds of friends and, well equipped as I thought, marched towards St Albans to cut off the queen, bringing the king along on my side; my scouts had told me she was coming with every intention of overturning our recent decree in parliament about King Henry's oath and your succession. To cut a long story short, we met at St Albans, our armies engaged and both sides fought fiercely. But whether it was the king's coolness, looking very gently on his warlike queen, that robbed my soldiers of their hot anger, or the news of her success, or an unusual fear of Clifford's cruelty, who thunders blood and death at his prisoners, I can't say; but to tell the truth, their weapons came and went like lightning, while our soldiers' weapons, like an owl's lazy flight or a lazy thresher's flail, fell gently, as if they were hitting their friends. I encouraged them with the justice of our cause and promises of high pay and great rewards, but it was no use. They had no heart to fight, and we had no hope of winning with them, so we ran: the king to the queen; Lord George your brother, Norfolk and I have rushed here at top speed to join you, since we heard you were here in the Welsh borders raising another army to fight again.
Where is the Duke of Norfolk, gentle Warwick? / And when came George from Burgundy to England?
Where's the Duke of Norfolk, good Warwick? And when did George come from Burgundy to England?
Some six miles off the duke is with the soldiers; / And for your brother, he was lately sent / From your kind aunt, Duchess of Burgundy, / With aid of soldiers to this needful war.
The duke is about six miles away with the soldiers; and as for your brother, he was recently sent by your kind aunt, the Duchess of Burgundy, with troops to help in this necessary war.
'T was odds, belike, when valiant Warwick fled; / Oft have I heard his praises in pursuit, / But ne'er till now his scandal of retire.
The odds must have been great if brave Warwick ran. I've often heard his praises in pursuit, but never till now the disgrace of his retreat.

Nor now my scandal, Richard, dost thou hear; / For thou shalt know, this strong right hand of mine / Can pluck the diadem from faint Henry's head / And wring the awful sceptre from his fist, / Were he as famous and as bold in war / As he is fam'd for mildness, peace, and prayer.

You're not hearing of my disgrace now, Richard; for you'll learn that this strong right hand of mine can pluck the crown from feeble Henry's head and wrench the awesome sceptre from his fist, even if he were as famous and bold in war as he is famous for gentleness, peace and prayer.

I know it well, Lord Warwick, blame me not; / 'T is love I bear thy glories makes me speak. / But in this troublous time what's to be done? / Shall we go throw away our coats of steel / And wrap our bodies in black mourning-gowns, / Numbering our Ave-Maries with our beads? / Or shall we on the helmets of our foes / Tell our devotion with revengeful arms? / If for the last, say ay, and to it, lords.

I know it well, Lord Warwick; don't blame me. It's my love for your glory that makes me speak. But what's to be done in these troubled times? Shall we throw away our steel armour, wrap ourselves in black mourning gowns and count our Hail Marys on our rosary beads? Or shall we show our devotion with vengeful arms on our enemies' helmets? If you choose the second, say yes, and let's get on with it, lords.

Why, therefore Warwick came to seek you out, / And therefore comes my brother Montague. / Attend me, lords. The proud insulting queen, / With Clifford and the haught Northumberland, / And of their feather many moe proud birds, / Have wrought the easy-melting king like wax. / He swore consent to your succession, / His oath enrolled in the parliament; / And now to London all the crew are gone, / To frustrate both his oath and what beside / May make against the house of Lancaster. / Their power, I think, is thirty thousand strong; / Now, if the help of Norfolk and myself, / With all the friends that thou, brave Earl of March, / Amongst the loving Welshmen canst procure, / Will but amount to five and twenty thousand, / Why, Via! to London will we march amain, / And once again bestride our foaming steeds, / And once again cry 'Charge upon our foes!' / But never once again turn back and fly.

Why, that's why Warwick came to find you, and why my brother Montague is here. Listen, lords. The proud, insolent queen, with Clifford and the arrogant Northumberland and many more proud birds of their kind, have melted the soft king like wax. He swore to agree to your succession, and his oath is recorded in parliament; and now that whole gang has gone to London to cancel both his oath and anything else that works against the house of Lancaster. Their army is about thirty thousand strong, I think. Now, if Norfolk's help and mine, together with all the friends you can raise among the loyal Welsh, brave Earl of March, comes to just twenty-five thousand, then forward! We'll march at full speed to London, mount our foaming horses once again, and once again shout, 'Charge the enemy!' but never again turn back and run.
Ay, now, methinks, I hear great Warwick speak. / Ne'er may he live to see a sunshine day / That cries 'Retire,' if Warwick bid him stay.
Yes, now I think I hear the great Warwick speaking. May the man who cries 'Retreat' when Warwick tells him to stand never live to see a sunny day.
Lord Warwick, on thy shoulder will I lean; / And when thou fail'st—as God forbid the hour!— / Must Edward fall, which peril heaven forfend!
Lord Warwick, I'll lean on your shoulder; and if you fail, which God forbid, Edward must fall, a danger heaven prevent!

No longer Earl of March, but Duke of York. / The next degree is England's royal throne; / For King of England shalt thou be proclaim'd / In every borough as we pass along, / And he that throws not up his cap for joy / Shall for the fault make forfeit of his head. / King Edward,—valiant Richard,—Montague,— / Stay we no longer dreaming of renown, / But sound the trumpets and about our task.

No longer Earl of March, but Duke of York. The next step up is England's royal throne; for you will be proclaimed King of England in every town we pass through, and anyone who doesn't throw his cap in the air for joy will lose his head for it. King Edward, brave Richard, Montague: let's stop dreaming of glory, sound the trumpets and get to work.
Then, Clifford, were thy heart as hard as steel, / As thou hast shown it flinty by thy deeds, / I come to pierce it, or to give thee mine.
Then, Clifford, even if your heart is as hard as steel, as your flinty deeds have shown it, I'm coming to pierce it, or to give you mine.
Then strike up, drums!—God and Saint George for us!
Then strike up, drums! God and Saint George for us!
The Duke of Norfolk sends you word by me, / The queen is coming with a puissant host, / And craves your company for speedy counsel.
The Duke of Norfolk sends word through me that the queen is coming with a powerful army, and he asks you to come quickly to discuss it.
Why then it sorts; brave warriors, let's away.
Why, then, it all fits. Brave warriors, let's go.
Welcome, my lord, to this brave town of York. / Yonder's the head of that arch-enemy / That sought to be encompass'd with your crown; / Doth not the object cheer your heart, my lord?
Welcome, my lord, to this fine town of York. Over there is the head of that arch-enemy who tried to wear your crown. Doesn't the sight cheer your heart, my lord?
Ay, as the rocks cheer them that fear their wreck; / To see this sight, it irks my very soul.— / Withhold revenge, dear God! 't is not my fault, / Nor wittingly have I infring'd my vow.
Yes, the way rocks cheer sailors afraid of shipwreck. It sickens my very soul to see it. Hold back your revenge, dear God! It's not my fault, and I haven't knowingly broken my vow.

My gracious liege, this too much lenity / And harmful pity must be laid aside. / To whom do lions cast their gentle looks? / Not to the beast that would usurp their den. / Whose hand is that the forest bear doth lick? / Not his that spoils her young before her face. / Who scapes the lurking serpent's mortal sting? / Not he that sets his foot upon her back. / The smallest worm will turn, being trodden on, / And doves will peck in safeguard of their brood. / Ambitious York did level at thy crown, / Thou smiling while he knit his angry brows. / He, but a duke, would have his son a king, / And raise his issue like a loving sire; / Thou, being a king, blest with a goodly son, / Didst yield consent to disinherit him, / Which argu'd thee a most unloving father. / Unreasonable creatures feed their young; / And though man's face be fearful to their eyes, / Yet, in protection of their tender ones, / Who hath not seen them, even with those wings / Which sometime they have us'd with fearful flight, / Make war with him that climb'd unto their nest, / Offering their own lives in their young's defence? / For shame, my liege! make them your precedent. / Were it not pity that this goodly boy / Should lose his birthright by his father's fault, / And long hereafter say unto his child, / 'What my great-grandfather and grandsire got, / My careless father fondly gave away?' / Ah, what a shame were this! Look on the boy, / And let his manly face, which promiseth / Successful fortune, steel thy melting heart / To hold thine own, and leave thine own with him.

My gracious lord, this excessive leniency and harmful pity must be put aside. Who do lions look gently at? Not at the beast that would steal their den. Whose hand does the forest bear lick? Not the man who kills her cubs in front of her. Who escapes the hidden snake's deadly sting? Not the man who steps on its back. The smallest worm will turn when it's trodden on, and doves will peck to protect their young. Ambitious York aimed at your crown, while you smiled as he frowned angrily. He, only a duke, wanted his son to be king and tried to raise up his children like a loving father; you, a king blessed with a fine son, agreed to disinherit him, which showed you to be a most unloving father. Even animals without reason feed their young; and though they fear the sight of a man, who hasn't seen them use the very wings they sometimes flee with to attack someone climbing up to their nest, risking their own lives to defend their young? For shame, my lord! Let them be your example. Wouldn't it be a pity if this fine boy lost his birthright through his father's fault, and in years to come said to his own child, 'What my great-grandfather and grandfather won, my careless father foolishly gave away'? Ah, what a disgrace that would be! Look at the boy, and let his manly face, which promises good fortune, harden your melting heart to keep what's yours and leave it to him.

Full well hath Clifford play'd the orator, / Inferring arguments of mighty force. / But, Clifford, tell me, didst thou never hear / That things ill got had ever bad success? / And happy always was it for that son / Whose father for his hoarding went to hell? / I'll leave my son my virtuous deeds behind, / And would my father had left me no more; / For all the rest is held at such a rate / As brings a thousand-fold more care to keep / Than in possession any jot of pleasure.— / Ah, cousin York! would thy best friends did know / How it doth grieve me that thy head is here!

Clifford has played the speaker very well, presenting very powerful arguments. But, Clifford, tell me, haven't you ever heard that things got wrongly always turn out badly? And was it always lucky for the son whose father went to hell for his hoarding? I'll leave my son my good deeds, and I wish my father had left me nothing more; for everything else costs a thousand times more worry to keep than it gives even a scrap of pleasure to own. Ah, cousin York! I wish your best friends knew how it grieves me that your head is here!

My lord, cheer up your spirits; / our foes are nigh, / And this soft courage makes your followers faint. / You promis'd knighthood to our forward son; / Unsheathe your sword and dub him presently.— / Edward, kneel down.
My lord, cheer up; our enemies are near, and this softness makes your followers lose heart. You promised to knight our eager son; draw your sword and dub him now. Edward, kneel.
Edward Plantagenet, arise a knight; / And learn this lesson,—draw thy sword in right.
Edward Plantagenet, rise a knight; and learn this lesson: draw your sword only for what is right.
My gracious father, by your kingly leave, / I'll draw it as apparent to the crown, / And in that quarrel use it to the death.
My gracious father, with your royal permission, I'll draw it as heir to the crown and use it in that cause to the death.
Why, that is spoken like a toward prince.
Why, that's spoken like a promising prince.

Royal commanders, be in readiness; / For with a band of thirty thousand men / Comes Warwick, backing of the Duke of York, / And in the towns, as they do march along, / Proclaims him king, and many fly to him. / Darraign your battle, for they are at hand.

Royal commanders, be ready; Warwick is coming with an army of thirty thousand men, supporting the Duke of York, and in every town they march through he proclaims him king, and many go over to him. Set out your battle lines, for they're close.
I would your highness would depart the field; / The queen hath best success when you are absent.
I wish your highness would leave the battlefield. The queen does best when you're not there.
Ay, good my lord, and leave us to our fortune.
Yes, my good lord, and leave us to our fortune.
Why, that's my fortune too; therefore I'll stay.
Why, that's my fortune too, so I'll stay.
Be it with resolution then to fight.
Then let it be with a firm resolve to fight.
My royal father, cheer these noble lords, / And hearten those that fight in your defence. / Unsheathe your sword, good father; cry 'Saint George!'
My royal father, encourage these noble lords and put heart into those fighting for you. Draw your sword, good father, and cry 'Saint George!'
Now, perjur'd Henry, wilt thou kneel for grace / And set thy diadem upon my head, / Or bide the mortal fortune of the field?
Now, oath-breaking Henry, will you kneel for mercy and put your crown on my head, or face the deadly chances of battle?
Go, rate thy minions, proud insulting boy! / Becomes it thee to be thus bold in terms / Before thy sovereign and thy lawful king?
Go and scold your favourites, you proud, insolent boy! Is it right for you to speak so boldly to your sovereign and lawful king?

I am his king, and he should bow his knee. / I was adopted heir by his consent; / Since when, his oath is broke; for, as I hear, / You, that are king, though he do wear the crown, / Have caus'd him by new act of parliament / To blot out me and put his own son in.

I am his king, and he should bow to me. I was made his adopted heir with his consent; and since then he has broken his oath, for I hear that you, who are the real king though he wears the crown, have made him cut me out by a new act of parliament and put his own son in.
And reason, too; / Who should succeed the father but the son?
And with good reason. Who should succeed the father but the son?
Are you there, butcher?—O, I cannot speak!
Are you there, butcher? O, I can't speak for rage!
Ay, crook-back; here I stand, to answer thee, / Or any he the proudest of thy sort.
Yes, hunchback; here I stand to answer you, or the proudest man of your kind.
'T was you that kill'd young Rutland, was it not?
It was you who killed young Rutland, wasn't it?
Ay, and old York, and yet not satisfied.
Yes, and old York, and I'm still not satisfied.
For God's sake, lords, give signal to the fight.
For God's sake, lords, give the signal to fight.
What say'st thou, Henry, wilt thou yield the crown?
What do you say, Henry? Will you give up the crown?
Why, how now, long-tongued Warwick! dare you speak? / When you and I met at Saint Alban's last, / Your legs did better service than your hands.
Well, well, big-mouthed Warwick! Do you dare to speak? When you and I last met at St Albans, your legs served you better than your hands.
Then 't was my turn to fly, and now 't is thine.
Then it was my turn to run, and now it's yours.
You said so much before, and yet you fled.
You said that before, and you still ran.
'T was not your valour, Clifford, drove me thence.
It wasn't your courage that drove me off, Clifford.
No, nor your manhood that durst make you stay.
No, nor was it your manliness that made you dare to stay.
Northumberland, I hold thee reverently. / Break off the parley; for scarce I can refrain / The execution of my big-swoln heart / Upon that Clifford, that cruel child-killer.
Northumberland, I respect you. Break off this talk, for I can hardly stop my swollen heart from taking it out on that Clifford, that cruel child-killer.
I slew thy father; call'st thou him a child?
I killed your father; do you call him a child?
Ay, like a dastard and a treacherous coward, / As thou didst kill our tender brother Rutland, / But ere sunset I'll make thee curse the deed.
Yes, you killed him like a sneak and a treacherous coward, as you killed our young brother Rutland; but before sunset I'll make you curse the deed.
Have done with words, my lords, and hear me speak.
Stop this talk, my lords, and hear me speak.
Defy them then, or else hold close thy lips.
Defy them, then, or keep your mouth shut.
I prithee, give no limits to my tongue; / I am a king, and privileg'd to speak.
Please don't restrict my tongue. I'm a king and have the right to speak.
My liege, the wound that bred this meeting here / Cannot be cur'd by words; therefore be still.
My lord, the wound that caused this meeting can't be cured by words, so keep quiet.
Then, executioner, unsheathe thy sword. / By him that made us all, I am resolv'd / That Clifford's manhood lies upon his tongue.
Then, executioner, draw your sword. By God who made us all, I'm sure Clifford's manhood is all in his tongue.
Say, Henry, shall I have my right, or no? / A thousand men have broke their fasts to-day / That ne'er shall dine unless thou yield the crown.
