Tell me, Henry, will I have my right or not? A thousand men have eaten breakfast today who will never eat dinner unless you give up the crown.
If thou deny, their blood upon thy head; / For York in justice puts his armour on.
If you refuse, their blood is on your head, for York puts on his armour in a just cause.
If that be right which Warwick says is right, / There is no wrong, but every thing is right.
If what Warwick says is right really is right, then nothing is wrong and everything is right.
Whoever got thee, there thy mother stands; / For, well I wot, thou hast thy mother's tongue.
Whoever your father was, there stands your mother; I can tell you have your mother's tongue.
But thou art neither like thy sire nor dam, / But like a foul misshapen stigmatic, / Mark'd by the destinies to be avoided, / As venom toads or lizards' dreadful stings.
But you're like neither your father nor your mother; you're like a foul, deformed, branched creature, marked by fate to be avoided like poisonous toads or lizards' dreadful stings.

Iron of Naples hid with English gilt, / Whose father bears the title of a king,— / As if a channel should be call'd the sea,— / Sham'st thou not, knowing whence thou art extraught, / To let thy tongue detect thy base-born heart?

You're Naples iron covered with English gilding, whose father calls himself a king, as if a gutter were called the sea. Aren't you ashamed, knowing where you come from, to let your tongue reveal your low-born heart?

A wisp of straw were worth a thousand crowns / To make this shameless callat know herself.— / Helen of Greece was fairer far than thou, / Although thy husband may be Menelaus; / And ne'er was Agamemmon's brother wrong'd / By that false woman as this king by thee. / His father revell'd in the heart of France, / And tam'd the king, and made the dauphin stoop; / And, had he match'd according to his state, / He might have kept that glory to this day; / But when he took a beggar to his bed, / And grac'd thy poor sire with his bridal day, / Even then that sunshine brew'd a shower for him / That wash'd his father's fortunes forth of France / And heap'd sedition on his crown at home. / For what hath broach'd this tumult but thy pride? / Hadst thou been meek, our title still had slept; / And we, in pity of the gentle king, / Had slipp'd our claim until another age.

A bunch of straw, the badge of a scold, would be worth a thousand crowns to make this shameless trollop know what she is. Helen of Greece was far more beautiful than you, though your husband may be a Menelaus; and Agamemnon's brother was never wronged by that unfaithful woman as much as this king has been by you. His father made merry in the heart of France, tamed its king and made the Dauphin bow; and if he had married according to his rank, he might have kept that glory to this day. But when he took a beggar to his bed and honoured your poor father with his wedding day, that sunshine brewed up a storm that washed his father's fortunes out of France and heaped rebellion on his crown at home. For what has started this uproar except your pride? If you'd been humble, our claim would still be asleep; and out of pity for the gentle king, we'd have let our claim pass to another generation.

But when we saw our sunshine made thy spring, / And that thy summer bred us no increase, / We set the axe to thy usurping root; / And though the edge hath something hit ourselves, / Yet, know thou, since we have begun to strike, / We'll never leave till we have hewn thee down / Or bath'd thy growing with our heated bloods.

But when we saw that our sunshine made your springtime, and your summer gave us no harvest, we took the axe to your usurping root; and though the edge has hit us a little too, know that since we've started to strike, we'll never stop until we've cut you down or watered your growth with our hot blood.

And in this resolution I defy thee; / Not willing any longer conference, / Since thou deniest the gentle king to speak.— / Sound trumpets;—let our bloody colours wave, / And either victory or else a grave!
And with that resolve, I defy you. I want no more talk, since you won't let the gentle king speak. Sound the trumpets! Let our bloody flags wave: either victory or a grave!
No, wrangling woman, we'll no longer stay; / These words will cost ten thousand lives this day.
No, quarrelling woman, we'll wait no longer. These words will cost ten thousand lives today.

Forspent with toil, as runners with a race, / I lay me down a little while to breathe; / For strokes receiv'd, and many blows repaid, / Have robb'd my strong-knit sinews of their strength, / And, spite of spite, needs must I rest awhile.

Exhausted by effort, like runners after a race, I'll lie down for a while to get my breath back. The blows I've taken, and the many I've returned, have drained my strong muscles of their strength, and like it or not, I must rest a while.
Smile, gentle heaven, or strike, ungentle death! / For this world frowns and Edward's sun is clouded.
Smile, kind heaven, or strike, unkind death! This world frowns, and Edward's sun is clouded over.
How now, my lord? what hap? what hope of good?
What's this, my lord? What luck? What hope?
Our hap is lost, our hope but sad despair; / Our ranks are broke and ruin follows us. / What counsel give you? whither shall we fly?
Our luck is gone, our hope is only sad despair. Our ranks are broken and ruin is chasing us. What do you advise? Where shall we run?
Bootless is flight, they follow us with wings; / And weak we are and cannot shun pursuit.
Running is useless; they chase us as if on wings, and we're too weak to escape.

Ah, Warwick, why hast thou withdrawn thyself? / Thy brother's blood the thirsty earth hath drunk, / Broach'd with the steely point of Clifford's lance; / And in the very pangs of death he cried, / Like to a dismal clangor heard from far, / 'Warwick, revenge! brother, revenge my death!' / So, underneath the belly of their steeds / That stain'd their fetlocks in his smoking blood, / The noble gentleman gave up the ghost.

Ah, Warwick, why have you pulled back? The thirsty earth has drunk your brother's blood, let out by the steel point of Clifford's lance; and in the very agony of death he cried, like a grim trumpet heard from far away, 'Warwick, revenge! Brother, avenge my death!' And so, under the bellies of their horses, whose legs were stained with his steaming blood, the noble gentleman died.

Then let the earth be drunken with our blood; / I'll kill my horse, because I will not fly. / Why stand we like soft-hearted women here, / Wailing our losses whiles the foe doth rage, / And look upon, as if the tragedy / Were play'd in jest by counterfeiting actors? / Here on my knee I vow to God above, / I'll never pause again, never stand still, / Till either death hath clos'd these eyes of mine, / Or fortune given me measure of revenge.

Then let the earth get drunk on our blood. I'll kill my horse, because I will not run. Why are we standing here like soft-hearted women, wailing over our losses while the enemy rages, and watching as if the tragedy were being acted for fun by pretend actors? Here on my knee I swear to God above that I'll never pause again or stand still until death has closed my eyes or fortune has given me my share of revenge.

O Warwick, I do bend my knee with thine, / And in this vow do chain my soul to thine!— / And, ere my knee rise from the earth's cold face, / I throw my hands, mine eyes, my heart to thee, / Thou setter-up and plucker-down of kings, / Beseeching thee, if with thy will it stands / That to my foes this body must be prey, / Yet that thy brazen gates of heaven may ope, / And give sweet passage to my sinful soul.— / Now, lords, take leave until we meet again, / Where'er it be, in heaven or in earth.

O Warwick, I kneel with you and chain my soul to yours in this vow! And before my knee rises from the cold earth, I lift my hands, eyes and heart to you, God, who sets up and pulls down kings, begging you, if it's your will that this body must be prey to my enemies, at least to open your bronze gates of heaven and let my sinful soul pass sweetly in. Now, lords, let's say goodbye until we meet again, wherever it may be, in heaven or on earth.
Brother, give me thy hand;—and, gentle Warwick, / Let me embrace thee in my weary arms. / I, that did never weep, now melt with woe, / That winter should cut off our spring-time so.
Brother, give me your hand; and, gentle Warwick, let me hug you in my tired arms. I, who never wept, now melt with sorrow that winter should cut short our spring like this.
Away, away! Once more, sweet lords, farewell.
Away, away! Once more, sweet lords, farewell.

Yet let us all together to our troops, / And give them leave to fly that will not stay, / And call them pillars that will stand to us; / And if we thrive, promise them such rewards / As victors wear at the Olympian games. / This may plant courage in their quailing breasts, / For yet is hope of life and victory.— / Forslow no longer; make we hence amain.

But let's all go to our troops together. Let those who won't stay run, and call those who stand by us pillars; and if we win, promise them rewards like those the winners wear at the Olympic games. This may put courage in their sinking hearts, for there's still hope of life and victory. Don't delay any longer; let's go at full speed.
Now, Clifford, I have singled thee alone. / Suppose this arm is for the Duke of York, / And this for Rutland; both bound to revenge, / Wert thou environ'd with a brazen wall.
Now, Clifford, I've cut you out from the herd. Imagine this arm is for the Duke of York and this one for Rutland; both are bound to take revenge, even if you were surrounded by a wall of brass.

Now, Richard, I am with thee here alone. / This is the hand that stabbed thy father York, / And this the hand that slew thy brother Rutland; / And here's the heart that triumphs in their death, / And cheers these hands that slew thy sire and brother / To execute the like upon thyself; / And so have at thee!

Now, Richard, I'm here alone with you. This is the hand that stabbed your father York, and this is the hand that killed your brother Rutland; and here's the heart that rejoices in their deaths and urges these hands, which killed your father and brother, to do the same to you. So, have at you!
Nay, Warwick, single out some other chase; / For I myself will hunt this wolf to death.
No, Warwick, find some other prey; I'll hunt this wolf to death myself.

This battle fares like to the morning's war, / When dying clouds contend with growing light, / What time the shepherd, blowing of his nails, / Can neither call it perfect day nor night. / Now sways it this way, like a mighty sea / Forc'd by the tide to combat with the wind; / Now sways it that way, like the selfsame sea / Forc'd to retire by fury of the wind. / Sometime the flood prevails, and then the wind, / Now one the better, then another best, / Both tugging to be victors, breast to breast, / Yet neither conqueror nor conquered; / So is the equal poise of this fell war. / Here on this molehill will I sit me down. / To whom God will, there be the victory! / For Margaret my queen, and Clifford too, / Have chid me from the battle, swearing both / They prosper best of all when I am thence. / Would I were dead! if God's good will were so; / For what is in this world but grief and woe? / O God! methinks it were a happy life, / To be no better than a homely swain; / To sit upon a hill, as I do now, / To carve out dials quaintly, point by point, / Thereby to see the minutes how they run, / How many make the hour full complete, / How many hours brings about the day, / How many days will finish up the year, / How many years a mortal man may live. / When this is known, then to divide the times; / So many hours must I tend my flock; / So many hours must I take my rest; / So many hours must I contemplate; / So many hours must I sport myself; / So many days my ewes have been with young; / So many weeks ere the poor fools will ean; / So many years ere I shall shear the fleece. / So minutes, hours, days, months, and years, / Pass'd over to the end they were created, / Would bring white hairs unto a quiet grave. / Ah, what a life were this! how sweet! how lovely! / Gives not the hawthorn bush a sweeter shade / To shepherds looking on their silly sheep / Than doth a rich embroider'd canopy / To kings that fear their subjects' treachery? / O, yes, it doth; a thousand-fold it doth! / And to conclude, the shepherd's homely curds, / His cold thin drink out of his leather bottle, / His wonted sleep under a fresh tree's shade, / All which secure and sweetly he enjoys, / Is far beyond a prince's delicates, / His viands sparkling in a golden cup, / His body couched in a curious bed, / When care, mistrust, and treason wait on him.

This battle is like the struggle at dawn, when the fading clouds fight the growing light and the shepherd, blowing on his fingers, can't call it either full day or night. Now it sways this way, like a mighty sea forced by the tide to fight the wind; now it sways that way, like the same sea forced back by the fury of the wind. Sometimes the tide wins, then the wind; now one is ahead, then the other, both straining to win, chest to chest, yet neither conquers nor is conquered. That's how evenly balanced this cruel war is. I'll sit down here on this molehill. Let God give the victory to whoever he wants! For Margaret my queen, and Clifford too, have scolded me away from the battle, both swearing they do best when I'm not there. I wish I were dead, if it were God's will; for what is there in this world but grief and sorrow? O God! I think it would be a happy life to be nothing more than a simple shepherd; to sit on a hill as I'm doing now, carving sundials carefully, line by line, to watch the minutes run: how many make a whole hour, how many hours make a day, how many days complete a year, how many years a man may live. Once I knew that, I'd divide up my time: so many hours I must tend my flock; so many hours I must rest; so many hours I must think; so many hours I must play; my ewes have been pregnant so many days; so many weeks before the poor things give birth; so many years before I shear the fleece. So minutes, hours, days, months and years, spent in the way they were made for, would bring white hair to a quiet grave. Ah, what a life that would be! How sweet! How lovely! Doesn't the hawthorn bush give a sweeter shade to shepherds watching their innocent sheep than a rich embroidered canopy gives to kings who fear their subjects' treachery? O yes, it does, a thousand times sweeter! And in short, the shepherd's simple curds, his cold thin drink from his leather bottle, his usual sleep in the shade of a fresh tree, all of which he enjoys safely and sweetly, are far better than a prince's delicacies, his food served in a sparkling gold cup and his body laid in an elaborate bed, when worry, mistrust and treason wait on him.

Ill blows the wind that profits nobody. / This man, whom hand to hand I slew in fight, / May be possessed with some store of crowns; / And I, that haply take them from him now, / May yet ere night yield both my life and them / To some man else, as this dead man doth me.— / Who's this?—O God! it is my father's face, / Whom in this conflict I unwares have kill'd. / O heavy times, begetting such events! / From London by the king was I press'd forth; / My father, being the Earl of Warwick's man, / Came on the part of York, press'd by his master; / And I, who at his hands receiv'd my life, / Have by my hands of life bereaved him.— / Pardon me, God, I knew not what I did;— / And pardon, father, for I knew not thee.— / My tears shall wipe away these bloody marks, / And no more words till they have flow'd their fill.

It's an ill wind that blows nobody any good. This man, whom I killed in hand-to-hand combat, may have some money on him; and I, who perhaps take it from him now, may before nightfall give up both my life and the money to someone else, as this dead man does to me. Who is this? O God! It's my father's face, whom I've killed in this fight without knowing it. O terrible times, that produce such things! I was drafted out of London by the king; my father, being the Earl of Warwick's man, came to fight for York, drafted by his master; and I, who received my life from him, have taken his life with my own hands. Forgive me, God, I didn't know what I was doing; and forgive me, father, for I didn't know you. My tears will wash away these bloody marks, and I'll say no more until they've flowed their fill.

O piteous spectacle! O bloody times! / Whiles lions war and battle for their dens, / Poor harmless lambs abide their enmity. / Weep, wretched man, I'll aid thee tear for tear; / And let our hearts and eyes, like civil war, / Be blind with tears and break o'ercharg'd with grief.

O pitiful sight! O bloody times! While lions make war and fight over their dens, poor harmless lambs suffer from their hatred. Weep, poor man; I'll help you, tear for tear; and let our hearts and eyes, like a civil war, be blinded with tears and burst, overloaded with grief.

Thou that so stoutly hath resisted me, / Give me thy gold, if thou hast any gold, / For I have bought it with an hundred blows.— / But let me see;—is this our foeman's face? / Ah, no, no, no! it is mine only son!— / Ah, boy, if any life be left in thee, / Throw up thine eye; see, see what showers arise, / Blown with the windy tempest of my heart, / Upon thy wounds that kill mine eye and heart!— / O, pity, God, this miserable age!— / What stratagems, how fell, how butcherly, / Erroneous, mutinous, and unnatural, / This deadly quarrel daily doth beget!— / O boy, thy father gave thee life too soon, / And hath bereft thee of thy life too late!

You who resisted me so stubbornly, give me your gold if you have any, for I've paid for it with a hundred blows. But let me see: is this our enemy's face? Ah, no, no, no! It's my only son! Ah, boy, if there's any life left in you, lift up your eyes; see, see what showers rise, blown by the windy storm of my heart, onto your wounds, which kill my eyes and heart! O God, pity this miserable age! What cruel, butchering, unnatural, rebellious deeds this deadly quarrel produces every day! O boy, your father gave you life too soon, and took your life too late!

Woe above woe! grief more than common grief! / O that my death would stay these ruthful deeds!— / O pity, pity! gentle heaven, pity!— / The red rose and the white are on his face, / The fatal colours of our striving houses; / The one his purple blood right well resembles, / The other his pale cheeks, methinks, presenteth. / Wither one rose, and let the other flourish! / If you contend, a thousand lives must wither.

Sorrow on sorrow! Grief beyond ordinary grief! O, if only my death would stop these pitiful deeds! O pity, pity, gentle heaven, pity! The red rose and the white are on his face, the deadly colours of our warring houses: his red blood looks just like one, and his pale cheeks, I think, show the other. Let one rose wither and the other flourish! If you keep fighting, a thousand lives must wither.
How will my mother, for a father's death, / Take on with me and ne'er be satisfied!
How my mother will grieve at me for my father's death, and never be consoled!
How will my wife, for slaughter of my son, / Shed seas of tears and ne'er be satisfied!
How my wife will shed seas of tears for the killing of my son, and never be consoled!
How will the country, for these woeful chances, / Misthink the king and not be satisfied!
How the country will think badly of the king for these sad events, and never be satisfied!
Was ever son so rued a father's death?
Did a son ever regret a father's death so much?
Was ever father so bemoan'd his son?
Did a father ever mourn his son so much?
Was ever king so griev'd for subjects' woe? / Much is your sorrow, mine ten times so much.
Did a king ever grieve so much for his subjects' sorrow? Your sorrow is great; mine is ten times greater.
I'll bear thee hence, where I may weep my fill.
I'll carry you away to where I can weep my fill.

These arms of mine shall be thy winding-sheet; / My heart, sweet boy, shall be thy sepulchre, / For from my heart thine image ne'er shall go; / My sighing breast shall be thy funeral bell; / And so obsequious will thy father be, / Even for the loss of thee, having no more, / As Priam was for all his valiant sons. / I'll bear thee hence; and let them fight that will, / For I have murder'd where I should not kill.

These arms of mine will be your shroud; my heart, sweet boy, will be your tomb, for your image will never leave my heart. My sighing chest will be your funeral bell; and your father will mourn you as devotedly, losing you, his only son, as Priam mourned all his brave sons. I'll carry you away; let those fight who want to, for I have murdered where I should not have killed.
Sad-hearted men, much overgone with care, / Here sits a king more woeful than you are.
Sad-hearted men, overwhelmed with sorrow, here sits a king more miserable than you.
Fly, father, fly! for all your friends are fled, / And Warwick rages like a chafed bull. / Away! for death doth hold us in pursuit.
Run, father, run! All your friends have run, and Warwick is raging like an angry bull. Away! Death is chasing us.

Mount you, my lord; towards Berwick post amain. / Edward and Richard, like a brace of greyhounds, / Having the fearful flying hare in sight, / With fiery eyes, sparkling for very wrath, / And bloody steel grasp'd in their ireful hands, / Are at our backs; and therefore hence amain.

Get on your horse, my lord, and ride fast to Berwick. Edward and Richard, like a pair of greyhounds with the frightened hare in sight, eyes flashing with anger and bloody swords in their furious hands, are right behind us; so away, quickly.
Away! for vengeance comes along with them. / Nay, stay not to expostulate; make speed, / Or else come after; I'll away before.
Away! Revenge is coming with them. No, don't stop to argue; hurry, or else follow on; I'll go ahead.
Nay, take me with thee, good sweet Exeter; / Not that I fear to stay, but love to go / Whither the queen intends. Forward! away!
No, take me with you, good sweet Exeter. Not that I'm afraid to stay, but I want to go wherever the queen is going. Forward! Away!

Here burns my candle out; ay, here it dies, / Which whiles it lasted gave King Henry light. / O Lancaster! I fear thy overthrow / More than my body's parting with my soul! / My love and fear glued many friends to thee; / And, now I fall, thy tough commixtures melt, / Impairing Henry, strengthening mis-proud York. / The common people swarm like summer flies; / And whither fly the gnats but to the sun? / And who shines now but Henry's enemies? / O Phoebus, hadst thou never given consent / That Phaethon should check thy fiery steeds, / Thy burning car never had scorch'd the earth! / And, Henry, hadst thou sway'd as kings should do, / Or as thy father and his father did, / Giving no ground unto the house of York, / They never then had sprung like summer flies; / I, and ten thousand in this luckless realm, / Had left no mourning widows for our death, / And thou this day hadst kept thy chair in peace. / For what doth cherish weeds but gentle air? / And what makes robbers bold but too much lenity? / Bootless are plaints, and cureless are my wounds; / No way to fly, nor strength to hold out flight. / The foe is merciless and will not pity, / For at their hands I have deserv'd no pity. / The air hath got into my deadly wounds, / And much effuse of blood doth make me faint.— / Come, York and Richard, Warwick, and the rest; / I stabb'd your fathers' bosoms, split my breast.

Here my candle burns out; yes, here it dies, the candle that gave King Henry light while it lasted. O Lancaster! I fear your downfall more than my soul's parting from my body! Love and fear of me held many friends to you; and now that I fall, those strong bonds melt, weakening Henry and strengthening arrogant York. The common people swarm like summer flies; and where do gnats fly but to the sun? And who is the sun now but Henry's enemies? O Phoebus, if you had never let Phaethon drive your fiery horses, your burning chariot would never have scorched the earth! And Henry, if you had ruled as kings should, or as your father and his father did, giving no ground to the house of York, they would never have sprung up like summer flies; I and ten thousand others in this unlucky kingdom would have left no widows mourning our deaths, and you would have kept your throne in peace today. For what makes weeds grow but mild weather? And what makes robbers bold but too much leniency? Complaints are useless, and my wounds can't be cured; there's no way to escape, and no strength to keep running. The enemy is merciless and will show no pity, for I've deserved no pity from them. The air has got into my deadly wounds, and losing so much blood makes me faint. Come, York and Richard, Warwick and the rest; I stabbed your fathers' chests; now split mine.

Now breathe we, lords; good fortune bids us pause, / And smooth the frowns of war with peaceful looks.— / Some troops pursue the bloody-minded queen / That led calm Henry, though he were a king, / As doth a sail, fill'd with a fretting gust, / Command an argosy to stem the waves. / But think you, lords, that Clifford fled with them?

Now let's catch our breath, lords. Good fortune tells us to pause and smooth war's frowns with peaceful looks. Some troops are chasing the bloodthirsty queen, who led calm Henry, though he was the king, the way a sail filled with a gusty wind forces a great ship to plough against the waves. But do you think, lords, that Clifford escaped with them?
No, 't is impossible he should escape; / For, though before his face I speak the words, / Your brother Richard mark'd him for the grave, / And whereso'er he is he's surely dead.
No, it's impossible he escaped; for, though I say it to his face, your brother Richard marked him for the grave, and wherever he is, he's surely dead.
Whose soul is that which takes her heavy leave?
Whose soul is that, taking its heavy leave?
A deadly groan, like life and death's departing.
A deadly groan, like life parting from death.
See who it is; and, now the battle's ended, / If friend or foe, let him be gently us'd.
See who it is; and now the battle is over, friend or enemy, let him be treated kindly.

Revoke that doom of mercy, for 't is Clifford, / Who, not contented that he lopp'd the branch, / In hewing Rutland when his leaves put forth, / But set his murthering knife unto the root / From whence that tender spray did sweetly spring; / I mean our princely father, Duke of York.

Take back that merciful order, for it's Clifford, who, not satisfied with lopping off the branch by cutting down Rutland just as his leaves were budding, put his murdering knife to the root that tender shoot grew from, I mean our princely father, the Duke of York.
From off the gates of York fetch down the head, / Your father's head, which Clifford placed there; / Instead whereof, let this supply the room. / Measure for measure must be answered.
Take down the head from the gates of York, your father's head, which Clifford put there, and let this one take its place. Measure must be paid back with measure.
Bring forth that fatal screech-owl to our house, / That nothing sung but death to us and ours; / Now death shall stop his dismal threatening sound, / And his ill-boding tongue no more shall speak.
Bring out that deadly screech-owl to our family, who sang nothing but death to us and ours. Now death will stop his dismal threatening noise, and his tongue that foretold evil will speak no more.
I think his understanding is bereft.— / Speak, Clifford, dost thou know who speaks to thee?— / Dark cloudy death o'ershades his beams of life, / And he nor sees nor hears us, what we say.
I think he has lost his senses. Speak, Clifford: do you know who's speaking to you? Dark, cloudy death is overshadowing the light of his life, and he neither sees us nor hears what we say.
O, would he did! and so, perhaps, he doth; / 'T is but his policy to counterfeit, / Because he would avoid such bitter taunts / Which in the time of death he gave our father.
O, I wish he did! And perhaps he does. It's just his trick to pretend, to avoid the kind of bitter taunts he gave our father as he died.
If so thou think'st, vex him with eager words.
If you think so, torment him with sharp words.
Clifford, ask mercy, and obtain no grace.
Clifford, beg for mercy, and get no pardon.
Clifford, devise excuses for thy faults.
Clifford, think up excuses for your crimes.
While we devise fell tortures for thy faults.
While we think up cruel tortures for your crimes.
Thou didst love York, and I am son to York.
You loved York, and I am York's son.
Thou pitiedst Rutland, I will pity thee.
You pitied Rutland; I will pity you.
Where's Captain Margaret to fence you now?
Where's Captain Margaret to defend you now?
They mock thee, Clifford; swear as thou wast wont.
They're mocking you, Clifford; swear as you used to.

What! not an oath? nay then, the world goes hard / When Clifford cannot spare his friends an oath.— / I know by that he's dead; and, by my soul, / If this right hand would buy two hours' life, / That I in all despite might rail at him, / This hand should chop it off, and with the issuing blood / Stifle the villain whose unstanched thirst / York and young Rutland could not satisfy.

What! Not one oath? Well, things are bad when Clifford can't spare his friends an oath. That tells me he's dead; and by my soul, if this right hand could buy him two hours of life so that I could insult him with all my scorn, I'd chop it off and choke the villain with the gushing blood, the villain whose endless thirst York and young Rutland couldn't satisfy.

Ay, but he's dead. Off with the traitor's head, / And rear it in the place your father's stands.— / And now to London with triumphant march, / There to be crowned England's royal king; / From whence shall Warwick cut the sea to France, / And ask the Lady Bona for thy queen. / So shalt thou sinew both these lands together, / And, having France thy friend, thou shalt not dread / The scatt'red foe that hopes to rise again; / For though they cannot greatly sting to hurt, / Yet look to have them buzz to offend thine ears. / First will I see the coronation, / And then to Brittany I'll cross the sea / To effect this marriage, so it please my lord.

Yes, but he's dead. Off with the traitor's head, and put it up where your father's is. And now to London in a triumphant march, to be crowned England's royal king. From there Warwick will cross the sea to France and ask for Lady Bona as your queen. That way you'll bind both countries together, and with France as your friend you won't have to fear the scattered enemy who hope to rise again; for though they can't sting hard enough to hurt you, expect them to buzz in your ears and annoy you. First I'll see the coronation, and then I'll cross the sea to Brittany to arrange this marriage, if my lord agrees.

Even as thou wilt, sweet Warwick, let it be; / For in thy shoulder do I build my seat, / And never will I undertake the thing / Wherein thy counsel and consent is wanting.— / Richard, I will create thee Duke of Gloster;— / And George, of Clarence.—Warwick, as ourself, / Shall do and undo as him pleaseth best.

Let it be just as you wish, sweet Warwick; for I build my throne on your shoulder, and I'll never undertake anything without your advice and consent. Richard, I'll make you Duke of Gloucester, and George, Duke of Clarence. Warwick, like ourself, will do and undo whatever he thinks best.
Let me be Duke of Clarence, George of Gloster, / For Gloster's dukedom is too ominous.
Let me be Duke of Clarence and George Duke of Gloucester, for the dukedom of Gloucester is too unlucky.
Tut! that's a foolish observation; / Richard, be Duke of Gloster. Now to London, / To see these honours in possession.
Nonsense! That's a foolish remark. Richard, be Duke of Gloucester. Now to London, to take possession of these honours.
Under this thick-grown brake we'll shroud ourselves, / For through this laund anon the deer will come; / And in this covert will we make our stand, / Culling the principal of all the deer.
We'll hide under this thick undergrowth, because the deer will come through this clearing soon; we'll take our position in this cover and pick out the best of the herd.
I'll stay above the hill, so both may shoot.
I'll stay up on the hill, so we can both shoot.

That cannot be; the noise of thy crossbow / Will scare the herd, and so my shoot is lost. / Here stand we both, and aim we at the best; / And, for the time shall not seem tedious, / I'll tell thee what befell me on a day / In this self place where now we mean to stand.

That won't work; the noise of your crossbow will scare the herd and my shot will be wasted. Let's both stand here and aim at the best one; and so the time doesn't drag, I'll tell you what happened to me one day in this very spot where we're about to stand.
Here comes a man; let's stay till he be past.
Here comes a man; let's wait until he's gone past.

From Scotland am I stolen, even of pure love, / To greet mine own land with my wishful sight. / No, Harry, Harry, 't is no land of thine; / Thy place is fill'd, thy sceptre wrung from thee, / Thy balm wash'd off wherewith thou wast anointed. / No bending knee will call thee Caesar now, / No humble suitors press to speak for right; / No, not a man comes for redress of thee, / For how can I help them, and not myself?

I've slipped away from Scotland, purely out of love, to greet my own country with longing eyes. No, Harry, Harry, it's not your country; your place is taken, your sceptre wrenched from you, the holy oil you were anointed with washed off. No bending knee will call you Caesar now, no humble petitioners crowd to ask for justice; no, not one man comes to you for help, for how can I help them when I can't help myself?
Ay, here's a deer whose skin's a keeper's fee. / This is the quondam king; let's seize upon him.
Yes, here's a deer whose skin is a gamekeeper's prize. This is the former king; let's seize him.
Let me embrace thee, sour adversity; / For wise men say it is the wisest course.
Let me embrace you, bitter adversity, for wise men say that's the wisest course.
Why linger we? let us lay hands upon him.
Why are we waiting? Let's grab him.
Forbear awhile; we'll hear a little more.
Hold on a moment; we'll hear a bit more.

My queen and son are gone to France for aid; / And, as I hear, the great commanding Warwick / Is thither gone to crave the French king's sister / To wife for Edward. If this news be true, / Poor queen and son, your labour is but lost, / For Warwick is a subtle orator, / And Lewis a prince soon won with moving words. / By this account then Margaret may win him, / For she's a woman to be pitied much. / Her sighs will make a batt'ry in his breast, / Her tears will pierce into a marble heart; / The tiger will be mild whiles she doth mourn, / And Nero will be tainted with remorse / To hear and see her plaints, her brinish tears. / Ay, but she's come to beg, Warwick to give; / She on his left side craving aid for Henry, / He on his right asking a wife for Edward. / She weeps and says her Henry is depos'd, / He smiles and says his Edward is install'd; / That she, poor wretch, for grief can speak no more; / Whiles Warwick tells his title, smooths the wrong, / Inferreth arguments of mighty strength, / And, in conclusion, wins the king from her, / With promise of his sister, and what else, / To strengthen and support King Edward's place. / O Margaret, thus 't will be! and thou, poor soul, / Art then forsaken, as thou went'st forlorn!

My queen and son have gone to France for help; and I hear the great, commanding Warwick has gone there to ask for the French king's sister as a wife for Edward. If this news is true, poor queen and son, your effort is wasted, for Warwick is a clever speaker and Lewis is a prince easily won by moving words. Then again, by this reckoning Margaret may win him, for she's a woman to be greatly pitied. Her sighs will batter at his heart, her tears will pierce a heart of marble; the tiger will be gentle while she mourns, and Nero would be touched with pity to hear her complaints and see her salt tears. Yes, but she's come to beg, and Warwick to give: she on his left side begging help for Henry, he on his right asking a wife for Edward. She weeps and says her Henry is deposed; he smiles and says his Edward is crowned; so that she, poor wretch, can't speak any more for grief, while Warwick explains Edward's claim, smooths over the wrong, offers powerful arguments, and in the end wins the king away from her with the promise of his sister and whatever else will strengthen and support King Edward's position. O Margaret, that's how it will be! And you, poor soul, will be abandoned, just as you went, hopeless!
Say, what art thou, that talk'st of kings and queens?
Tell me, who are you, talking about kings and queens?
More than I seem, and less than I was born to; / A man at least, for less I should not be; / And men may talk of kings, and why not I?
More than I seem, and less than I was born to be; a man at least, for I can't be less; and men may talk about kings, so why not me?
Ay, but thou talk'st as if thou wert a king.
Yes, but you talk as if you were a king.
Why, so I am, in mind; and that's enough.
Well, so I am, in my mind, and that's enough.
But, if thou be a king, where is thy crown?
But if you're a king, where's your crown?
My crown is in my heart, not on my head, / Not deck'd with diamonds and Indian stones, / Not to be seen; my crown is call'd content, / A crown it is that seldom kings enjoy.
My crown is in my heart, not on my head; not decorated with diamonds and Indian gems, not visible. My crown is called contentment, a crown that kings seldom enjoy.

Well, if you be a king crown'd with content, / Your crown content and you must be contented / To go along with us; for, as we think, / You are the king King Edward hath depos'd, / And we his subjects, sworn in all allegiance, / Will apprehend you as his enemy.

Well, if you're a king crowned with contentment, your crown, contentment, and you must be content to come with us; for we think you're the king King Edward has deposed, and we, his subjects, sworn to loyalty, will arrest you as his enemy.
But did you never swear, and break an oath?
But have you never sworn an oath and broken it?
No, never such an oath; nor will not now.
No, never an oath like that; and we won't now.
Where did you dwell when I was King of England?
Where did you live when I was King of England?
Here in this country, where we now remain.
Here in this region, where we live now.
I was anointed king at nine months old, / My father and my grandfather were kings, / And you were sworn true subjects unto me; / And tell me, then, have you not broke your oaths?
I was anointed king at nine months old; my father and grandfather were kings; and you swore to be my true subjects. So tell me, haven't you broken your oaths?
No; / For we were subjects but while you were king.
No; we were your subjects only while you were king.

Why, am I dead? do I not breathe, a man? / Ah, simple men! you know not what you swear. / Look, as I blow this feather from my face, / And as the air blows it to me again, / Obeying with my wind when I do blow, / And yielding to another when it blows, / Commanded always by the greater gust, / Such is the lightness of you common men. / But do not break your oaths; for of that sin / My mild entreaty shall not make you guilty. / Go where you will, the king shall be commanded; / And be you kings, command, and I'll obey.

Why, am I dead? Don't I still breathe, as a man? Ah, simple men! You don't know what you're swearing. Look, as I blow this feather away from my face and the air blows it back to me, obeying my breath when I blow and giving way to another when that blows, always ruled by the stronger gust: that's how fickle you common people are. But don't break your oaths; my gentle plea won't make you guilty of that sin. Go where you like; the king will obey orders. You be kings: command, and I'll obey.
We are true subjects to the king,—King Edward.
We're true subjects of the king, King Edward.
So would you be again to Henry / If he were seated as King Edward is.
And so you'd be again to Henry, if he were on the throne as King Edward is.
We charge you, in God's name and the king's / To go with us unto the officers.
We order you, in God's name and the king's, to come with us to the officers.
In God's name lead; your king's name be obey'd; / And what God will, that let your king perform; / And what he will, I humbly yield unto.
Lead on in God's name; let your king's name be obeyed. Let your king do what God wants, and I humbly submit to what he wants.

Brother of Gloster, at Saint Alban's field / This lady's husband, Sir John Grey, was slain, / His land then seiz'd on by the conqueror; / Her suit is now to repossess those lands, / Which we in justice cannot well deny, / Because in quarrel of the house of York / The worthy gentleman did lose his life.

Brother Gloucester, this lady's husband, Sir John Grey, was killed at the battle of St Albans, and his land was then seized by the victor. She is now asking to have those lands back, which in fairness we can hardly refuse, since the good gentleman lost his life fighting for the house of York.
Your highness shall do well to grant her suit; / It were dishonour to deny it her.
Your highness would do well to grant her request; it would be dishonourable to refuse.
It were no less; but yet I'll make a pause.
It would indeed; but still, I'll take my time.
[Aside to Clarence] Yea; is it so? / I see the lady hath a thing to grant / Before the king will grant her humble suit.
(Aside to Clarence) Oh, is that how it is? I see the lady has something to grant before the king will grant her humble request.
[Aside to Gloster] He knows the game; / how true he keeps the wind!
(Aside to Gloucester) He knows the hunt; see how he keeps downwind of his prey!
Widow, we will consider of your suit, / And come some other time to know our mind.
Widow, we'll consider your request; come back another time to hear our decision.
Right gracious lord, I cannot brook delay; / May it please your highness to resolve me now, / And what your pleasure is shall satisfy me.
Most gracious lord, I can't bear delay. Please decide now, your highness, and whatever pleases you will satisfy me.
[Aside to Clarence] Ay, widow? / then I'll warrant you all your lands, / An if what pleases him shall pleasure you. / Fight closer, or, good faith, you'll catch a blow.
(Aside to Clarence) Oh, will it, widow? Then I'll guarantee you all your lands, if what pleases him gives you pleasure. Guard yourself closer, or, believe me, you'll take a hit.
[Aside to Gloster] I fear her not, unless she chance to fall.
(Aside to Gloucester) I'm not worried for her, unless she happens to fall.
[Aside to CLARENCE] God forbid that, for he'll take vantages.
(Aside to Clarence) God forbid! He'll take advantage.
How many children hast thou, widow? tell me.
How many children do you have, widow? Tell me.
[Aside to Gloster] I think he means to beg a child of her.
(Aside to Gloucester) I think he means to ask her for a child.
[Aside to Clarence] Nay, whip me then; he'll rather / give her two.
(Aside to Clarence) No, whip me if he does; he'd rather give her two.
[Aside to Clarence] You shall have four if you'll be / rul'd by him.
(Aside to Clarence) You'll have four if you do as he says.
'T were pity they should lose their father's lands.
It would be a pity if they lost their father's lands.
Be pitiful, dread lord, and grant it then.
Then be merciful, dread lord, and grant them.
Lords, give us leave; I'll try this widow's wit.
Lords, leave us alone; I'll test this widow's wits.
[Aside to Clarence] Ay, good leave have you; / for you will have leave / Till youth take leave and leave you to the crutch.
(Aside to Clarence) Yes, take your leave; you'll take liberties until youth takes leave of you and leaves you to your crutch.
Now tell me, madam, do you love your children?
Now tell me, madam, do you love your children?
Ay, full as dearly as I love myself.
Yes, as dearly as I love myself.
And would you not do much to do them good?
And wouldn't you do a lot to do them good?
To do them good I would sustain some harm.
To do them good I'd put up with some harm.
Then get your husband's lands to do them good.
Then get your husband's lands back to do them good.
Therefore I came unto your majesty.
That's why I came to your majesty.
I'll tell you how these lands are to be got.
I'll tell you how these lands can be got.
So shall you bind me to your highness' service.
Then you'll bind me to your highness's service.
What service wilt thou do me if I give them?
What service will you do me if I give them to you?
What you command that rests in me to do.
Whatever you command that's in my power to do.
But you will take exceptions to my boon.
But you'll object to what I ask.
No, gracious lord, except I cannot do it.
No, gracious lord, unless I can't do it.
Ay, but thou canst do what I mean to ask.
Yes, but you can do what I mean to ask.
Why, then, I will do what your grace commands.
Why, then, I'll do what your grace commands.
He plies her hard; and much rain wears the marble.
He's pressing her hard; and a lot of rain wears down marble.
As red as fire! nay, then her wax must melt.
She's as red as fire! Well, then her wax must melt.
Why stops my lord? shall I not hear my task?
Why does my lord stop? Won't I hear my task?
An easy task; 't is but to love a king.
An easy task: it's only to love a king.
That's soon perform'd, because I am a subject.
That's easily done, since I'm his subject.
Why, then, thy husband's lands I freely give thee.
Why, then, I freely give you your husband's lands.
I take my leave with many thousand thanks.
I take my leave with many thousand thanks.
The match is made; she seals it with a curtsy.
The deal is done; she seals it with a curtsy.
But stay thee; 't is the fruits of love I mean.
But wait; it's the fruits of love I mean.
The fruits of love I mean, my loving liege.
I mean the fruits of love, my loving lord.
Ay, but, I fear me, in another sense. / What love, thinkst thou, I sue so much to get?
Yes, but I'm afraid in a different sense. What love do you think I'm so eager to get?
My love till death, my humble thanks, my prayers; / That love which virtue begs, and virtue grants.
My love till death, my humble thanks, my prayers; the love that virtue asks for and virtue gives.
No, by my troth, I did not mean such love.
No, I swear, I didn't mean that kind of love.
Why, then, you mean not as I thought you did.
Why, then, you don't mean what I thought you did.
But now you partly may perceive my mind.
But now you may partly understand what I have in mind.
My mind will never grant what I perceive / Your Highness aims at, if I aim aright.
My mind will never agree to what I see your highness is aiming at, if I've guessed right.
To tell thee plain, I aim to lie with thee.
To put it plainly, I want to sleep with you.
To tell you plain, I had rather lie in prison.
To put it plainly, I'd rather sleep in prison.
Why, then thou shalt not have thy husband's lands.
Why, then you won't have your husband's lands.
Why, then mine honesty shall be my dower, / For by that loss I will not purchase them.
Why, then my chastity will be my dowry, for I won't buy them by losing it.
Therein thou wrong'st thy children mightily.
In that you do your children a great wrong.
Herein your highness wrongs both them and me. / But, mighty lord, this merry inclination / Accords not with the sadness of my suit; / Please you dismiss me either with ay or no.
In this your highness wrongs both them and me. But, mighty lord, this playful mood doesn't suit the seriousness of my request. Please dismiss me with either yes or no.
Ay, if thou wilt say ay to my request. / No, if thou dost say no to my demand.
Yes, if you'll say yes to my request; no, if you say no to my demand.
Then no, my lord. My suit is at an end.
Then no, my lord. My suit is finished.
The widow likes him not, she knits her brows.
The widow doesn't like him; she's frowning.
He is the bluntest wooer in Christendom.
He's the bluntest wooer in Christendom.

[Aside] Her looks doth argue her replete with modesty, / Her words doth show her wit incomparable, / All her perfections challenge sovereignty; / One way or other she is for a king, / And she shall be my love, or else my queen.— / Say that King Edward take thee for his queen?

(Aside) Her looks show she's full of modesty; her words show her wit is beyond compare; all her perfections claim the right to rule. One way or another she's fit for a king, and she'll be my mistress or else my queen. (Aloud) What if King Edward took you as his queen?
'T is better said than done, my gracious lord; / I am a subject fit to jest withal, / But far unfit to be a sovereign.
That's easier said than done, my gracious lord. I'm a subject fit to joke with, but quite unfit to be a sovereign.
Sweet widow, by my state I swear to thee, / I speak no more than what my soul intends; / And that is to enjoy thee for my love.
Sweet widow, I swear to you by my crown that I mean exactly what I say, which is to have you as my love.
And that is more than I will yield unto. / I know I am too mean to be your queen, / And yet too good to be your concubine.
And that is more than I'll agree to. I know I'm too lowly to be your queen, and yet too good to be your mistress.
You cavil, widow; I did mean my queen.
You're quibbling, widow; I meant my queen.
'T will grieve your grace my sons should call you father.
It would upset your grace to have my sons call you father.

No more than when my daughters call thee mother. / Thou art a widow, and thou hast some children; / And, by God's mother, I, being but a bachelor, / Have other some; why, 't is a happy thing / To be the father unto many sons. / Answer no more, for thou shalt be my queen.

No more than it will upset you when my daughters call you mother. You're a widow and you have some children; and, by God's mother, I, though only a bachelor, have some others. Why, it's a happy thing to be father to many sons. Say no more, for you will be my queen.
The ghostly father now hath done his shrift.
The father confessor has finished hearing her confession.
When he was made a shriver, 't was for shift.
When he became a confessor, it was for a trick, to get her out of her shift.
Brothers, you muse what chat we two have had.
Brothers, you're wondering what we two have been talking about.
The widow likes it not, for she looks very sad.
The widow doesn't like it; she looks very sad.
You'd think it strange if I should marry her.
You'd think it strange if I married her.
That would be ten days' wonder, at the least.
That would be a ten days' wonder at least.
That's a day longer than a wonder lasts.
That's a day longer than a wonder usually lasts.
By so much is the wonder in extremes.
That just shows how extreme the wonder is.
Well, jest on, brothers; I can tell you both, / Her suit is granted for her husband's lands.
Well, keep joking, brothers. I can tell you both her request for her husband's lands is granted.
My gracious lord, Henry your foe is taken, / And brought your prisoner to your palace gate.
My gracious lord, your enemy Henry has been captured and brought as your prisoner to your palace gate.
See that he be convey'd unto the Tower.— / And go we, brothers, to the man that took him, / To question of his apprehension.— / Widow, go you along.—Lords, use her honourably.
See that he's taken to the Tower. And let's go, brothers, to the man who captured him, to ask him about the arrest. Widow, you come along. Lords, treat her with honour.

Ay, Edward will use women honourably. / Would he were wasted, marrow, bones, and all, / That from his loins no hopeful branch may spring, / To cross me from the golden time I look for! / And yet, between my soul's desire and me— / The lustful Edward's title buried— / Is Clarence, Henry, and his son young Edward, / And all the unlook'd-for issue of their bodies, / To take their rooms ere I can place myself; / A cold premeditation for my purpose! / Why, then I do but dream on sovereignty, / Like one that stands upon a promontory, / And spies a far-off shore where he would tread, / Wishing his foot were equal with his eye, / And chides the sea that sunders him from thence, / Saying, he'll lade it dry to have his way. / So do I wish the crown, being so far off, / And so I chide the means that keeps me from it; / And so I say I'll cut the causes off, / Flattering me with impossibilities.— / My eye's too quick, my heart o'erweens too much, / Unless my hand and strength could equal them. / Well, say there is no kingdom then for Richard, / What other pleasure can the world afford? / I'll make my heaven in a lady's lap, / And deck my body in gay ornaments, / And witch sweet ladies with my words and looks. / O miserable thought! and more unlikely / Than to accomplish twenty golden crowns. / Why, love forswore me in my mother's womb; / And, for I should not deal in her soft laws, / She did corrupt frail nature with some bribe / To shrink mine arm up like a wither'd shrub; / To make an envious mountain on my back, / Where sits deformity to mock my body; / To shape my legs of an unequal size; / To disproportion me in every part, / Like to a chaos, or an unlick'd bear-whelp / That carries no impression like the dam. / And am I then a man to be belov'd? / O, monstrous fault, to harbour such a thought! / Then, since this earth affords no joy to me / But to command, to check, to o'erbear such / As are of better person than myself, / I'll make my heaven to dream upon the crown, / And, whiles I live, to account this world but hell / Until my mis-shap'd trunk that bear this head / Be round impaled with a glorious crown. / And yet I know not how to get the crown, / For many lives stand between me and home, / And I, like one lost in a thorny wood, / That rends the thorns, and is rent with the thorns, / Seeking a way, and straying from the way, / Not knowing how to find the open air, / But toiling desperately to find it out, / Torment myself to catch the English crown; / And from that torment I will free myself, / Or hew my way out with a bloody axe. / Why, I can smile, and murther while I smile, / And cry 'Content!' to that which grieves my heart, / And wet my cheeks with artificial tears, / And frame my face to all occasions. / I'll drown more sailors than the mermaid shall, / I'll slay more gazers than the basilisk; / I'll play the orator as well as Nestor, / Deceive more slyly than Ulysses could, / And like a Sinon take another Troy. / I can add colours to the chameleon, / Change shapes with Protheus for advantages, / And set the murtherous Machiavel to school. / Can I do this, and cannot get a crown? / Tut, were it farther off, I'll pluck it down.

Yes, Edward will treat women honourably. I wish he were wasted away, marrow, bones and all, so that no promising offspring could spring from his loins to block my way to the golden time I'm hoping for! And yet, between my soul's desire and me, even with lustful Edward's claim buried, stand Clarence, Henry and his son young Edward, and all the unexpected children they may have, to take their places before I can take mine. A chilling forecast for my plans! Why, then I'm only dreaming of the crown, like someone standing on a headland who spots a distant shore he'd like to walk on, wishes his feet could go as far as his eyes, and scolds the sea that separates him from it, saying he'll bail it dry to get his way. That's how I long for the crown, so far away; that's how I scold whatever keeps me from it; and that's how I say I'll cut away the obstacles, flattering myself with impossibilities. My eye is too quick and my heart too ambitious unless my hand and strength can match them. Well, suppose there's no kingdom for Richard; what other pleasure can the world give? I'll make my heaven in a lady's lap, dress myself in fine clothes and bewitch sweet ladies with my words and looks. O miserable thought, and less likely than winning twenty golden crowns! Why, love rejected me in my mother's womb; and so that I'd have nothing to do with her gentle laws, she bribed weak nature to shrivel my arm like a withered shrub, to build a spiteful mountain on my back where deformity sits to mock my body, to shape my legs unequal in size, to put me out of proportion in every part, like chaos, or an unlicked bear cub that doesn't take after its mother. So am I a man to be loved? O monstrous mistake, even to think it! Then, since this earth gives me no joy except to command, rebuke and overpower people better-looking than me, I'll make my heaven dreaming of the crown, and as long as I live I'll count this world nothing but hell until the misshapen body that carries this head is circled with a glorious crown. And yet I don't know how to get the crown, for many lives stand between me and my goal; and like someone lost in a thorny wood, tearing at the thorns and torn by them, looking for a path and straying from it, not knowing how to reach open air but struggling desperately to find it, I torment myself to catch the English crown. And I'll free myself from that torment or hack my way out with a bloody axe. Why, I can smile, and murder while I smile, and cry 'Wonderful!' at what grieves my heart, and wet my cheeks with fake tears, and fit my face to any occasion. I'll drown more sailors than the mermaid, kill more onlookers than the basilisk; I'll speak as well as Nestor, deceive more slyly than Ulysses, and take another Troy like Sinon. I can add colours to the chameleon, change shape with Proteus when it suits me, and teach the murderous Machiavelli a lesson. Can I do all this and not get a crown? Tut, even if it were further off, I'll pull it down.
Fair Queen of England, worthy Margaret, / Sit down with us; it ill befits thy state / And birth that thou shouldst stand while Lewis doth sit.
Fair Queen of England, noble Margaret, sit down with us. It doesn't suit your rank and birth that you should stand while Lewis sits.

No, mighty King of France; now Margaret / Must strike her sail and learn a while to serve / Where kings command. I was, I must confess, / Great Albion's queen in former golden days; / But now mischance hath trod my title down / And with dishonour laid me on the ground, / Where I must take like seat unto my fortune, / And to my humble seat conform myself.

No, mighty King of France; now Margaret must lower her sails and learn to serve for a while where kings command. I confess I was queen of great England in former golden days; but now misfortune has trampled my title and laid me on the ground in disgrace, where I must take a seat that fits my fortune and adapt myself to my humble place.
Why, say, fair queen, whence springs this deep despair?
Tell me, fair queen, where does this deep despair come from?
From such a cause as fills mine eyes with tears / And stops my tongue, while heart is drown'd in cares.
From a cause that fills my eyes with tears and stops my tongue, while my heart is drowned in troubles.
Whate'er it be, be thou still like thyself, / And sit thee by our side; yield not thy neck
Whatever it is, still be yourself, and sit beside us; don't bow your neck
To fortune's yoke, but let thy dauntless mind / Still ride in triumph over all mischance. / Be plain, Queen Margaret, and tell thy grief; / It shall be eas'd if France can yield relief.
to fortune's yoke, but let your fearless mind still ride in triumph over every misfortune. Speak plainly, Queen Margaret, and tell me your grief; it will be eased if France can give relief.

Those gracious words revive my drooping thoughts, / And give my tongue-tied sorrows leave to speak. / Now, therefore, be it known to noble Lewis / That Henry, sole possessor of my love, / Is of a king become a banish'd man / And forc'd to live in Scotland a forlorn, / While proud ambitious Edward, Duke of York, / Usurps the regal title and the seat / Of England's true-anointed lawful king. / This is the cause that I, poor Margaret, / With this my son, Prince Edward, Henry's heir, / Am come to crave thy just and lawful aid; / And if thou fail us, all our hope is done. / Scotland hath will to help, but cannot help; / Our people and our peers are both misled, / Our treasure seiz'd, our soldiers put to flight, / And, as thou seest, ourselves in heavy plight.

Those kind words revive my drooping spirits and let my tongue-tied sorrows speak. So let noble Lewis know that Henry, the only owner of my love, has gone from being a king to being an exile, forced to live wretchedly in Scotland, while proud, ambitious Edward, Duke of York, usurps the royal title and throne of England's true, anointed, lawful king. That's why I, poor Margaret, have come with my son, Prince Edward, Henry's heir, to beg for your just and lawful help; and if you fail us, all our hope is finished. Scotland wants to help but can't; our people and our nobles are both misled, our treasure seized, our soldiers routed, and, as you see, we ourselves are in a sad state.
Renowned queen, with patience calm the storm / While we bethink a means to break it off.
Famous queen, calm the storm with patience while we think of a way to end it.
The more we stay, the stronger grows our foe.
The longer we wait, the stronger our enemy grows.
The more I stay, the more I'll succour thee.
The longer I wait, the more I'll help you.
O, but impatience waiteth on true sorrow!— / And see where comes the breeder of my sorrow.
O, but impatience always goes with true sorrow! And look, here comes the cause of my sorrow.
What's he approacheth boldly to our presence?
Who is this who comes so boldly into our presence?
Our Earl of Warwick, Edward's greatest friend.
Our Earl of Warwick, Edward's greatest friend.
Welcome, brave Warwick. What brings thee to France?
Welcome, brave Warwick. What brings you to France?
Ay, now begins a second storm to rise, / For this is he that moves both wind and tide.
Yes, now a second storm begins to rise, for this is the man who moves both wind and tide.

From worthy Edward, king of Albion, / My lord and sovereign, and thy vowed friend, / I come, in kindness and unfeigned love, / First, to do greetings to thy royal person; / And then, to crave a league of amity; / And lastly, to confirm that amity / With nuptial knot, if thou vouchsafe to grant / That virtuous Lady Bona, thy fair sister, / To England's king in lawful marriage.

I come from noble Edward, King of England, my lord and sovereign and your sworn friend, in kindness and sincere love: first to greet your royal person; then to ask for a treaty of friendship; and lastly to confirm that friendship with a marriage, if you'll agree to give the virtuous Lady Bona, your fair sister, to England's king in lawful marriage.
[Aside] If that go forward, Henry's hope is done.
(Aside) If that goes ahead, Henry's hope is finished.

[To BONA] And, gracious madam, in our king's behalf, / I am commanded, with your leave and favour, / Humbly to kiss your hand, and with my tongue / To tell the passion of my sovereign's heart, / Where fame, late entering at his heedful ears, / Hath plac'd thy beauty's image and thy virtue.

(To Bona) And, gracious madam, on our king's behalf I'm ordered, with your permission, to kiss your hand humbly and tell you of the love in my sovereign's heart, where report, lately reaching his attentive ears, has placed the image of your beauty and virtue.

King Lewis,—and Lady Bona,—hear me speak / Before you answer Warwick. His demand / Springs not from Edward's well-meant honest love, / But from deceit, bred by necessity; / For how can tyrants safely govern home / Unless abroad they purchase great alliance? / To prove him tyrant this reason may suffice,— / That Henry liveth still; but were he dead, / Yet here Prince Edward stands, King Henry's son. / Look therefore, Lewis, that by this league and marriage / Thou draw not on thy danger and dishonour; / For though usurpers sway the rule awhile, / Yet heavens are just, and time suppresseth wrongs.

King Lewis, and Lady Bona, hear me before you answer Warwick. His request doesn't come from Edward's honest, well-meant love, but from deceit born of need; for how can tyrants rule safely at home unless they buy powerful alliances abroad? This reason is enough to prove he's a tyrant: Henry is still alive; and even if he were dead, here stands Prince Edward, King Henry's son. So take care, Lewis, that by this treaty and marriage you don't bring danger and dishonour on yourself; for though usurpers may rule for a while, heaven is just and time puts down wrongs.
Because thy father Henry did usurp, / And thou no more art prince than she is queen.
Because your father Henry was a usurper, and you're no more a prince than she's a queen.

Then Warwick disannuls great John of Gaunt, / Which did subdue the greatest part of Spain; / And, after John of Gaunt, Henry the Fourth, / Whose wisdom was a mirror to the wisest; / And, after that wise prince, Henry the Fifth, / Who by his prowess conquered all France. / From these our Henry lineally descends.

Then Warwick cancels out great John of Gaunt, who conquered most of Spain; and after John of Gaunt, Henry the Fourth, whose wisdom was a model for the wisest; and after that wise prince, Henry the Fifth, whose valour conquered all France. Our Henry is descended in a direct line from these.

Oxford, how haps it in this smooth discourse, / You told not how Henry the Sixth hath lost / All that which Henry the Fifth had gotten? / Methinks these peers of France should smile at that. / But for the rest, you tell a pedigree / Of threescore and two years,—a silly time / To make prescription for a kingdom's worth.

Oxford, how is it that in this smooth speech you didn't mention how Henry the Sixth has lost everything Henry the Fifth won? I think these French lords would smile at that. As for the rest, you list a family tree of sixty-two years, a feeble length of time to establish a right to a kingdom.
Why, Warwick, canst thou speak against thy liege, / Whom thou obeyedst thirty and six years, / And not bewray thy treason with a blush?
Why, Warwick, can you speak against your king, whom you obeyed for thirty-six years, without a blush giving away your treason?
Can Oxford, that did ever fence the right, / Now buckler falsehood with a pedigree? / For shame Leave Henry, and call Edward king.
Can Oxford, who always defended what was right, now shield a lie with a family tree? For shame! Leave Henry and call Edward king.

Call him my king by whose injurious doom / My elder brother, the Lord Aubrey Vere, / Was done to death? and more than so, my father, / Even in the downfall of his mellow'd years, / When nature brought him to the door of death? / No, Warwick, no; while life upholds this arm, / This arm upholds the house of Lancaster.

Call him my king, by whose unjust sentence my elder brother, Lord Aubrey Vere, was put to death? And worse than that, my father too, in the decline of his ripe old age, when nature had brought him to death's door? No, Warwick, no; while there's life in this arm, this arm supports the house of Lancaster.
And I the house of York.
And I the house of York.
Queen Margaret, Prince Edward, and Oxford, / Vouchsafe at our request to stand aside / While I use further conference with Warwick.
Queen Margaret, Prince Edward and Oxford, please stand aside at our request while I talk further with Warwick.
Heavens grant that Warwick's words bewitch him not!
Heaven grant that Warwick's words don't bewitch him!
Now, Warwick, tell me, even upon thy conscience, / Is Edward your true king? for I were loath / To link with him that were not lawful chosen.
Now, Warwick, tell me honestly, on your conscience: is Edward your true king? I'd hate to ally myself with someone who wasn't lawfully chosen.
Thereon I pawn my credit and mine honour.
I stake my reputation and my honour on it.
But is he gracious in the people's eye?
But is he popular with the people?
The more that Henry was unfortunate.
All the more because Henry was unlucky.
Then further, all dissembling set aside, / Tell me for truth the measure of his love / Unto our sister Bona.
Then, further, setting all pretence aside, tell me truly how much he loves our sister Bona.

Such it seems / As may beseem a monarch like himself. / Myself have often heard him say and swear / That this his love was an eternal plant, / Whereof the root was fix'd in virtue's ground, / The leaves and fruit maintain'd with beauty's sun, / Exempt from envy, but not from disdain, / Unless the Lady Bona quit his pain.

His love seems to be what befits a monarch like him. I've often heard him say and swear that this love of his was an eternal plant, rooted in the ground of virtue, its leaves and fruit nourished by the sun of beauty, free from malice but not from scorn, unless Lady Bona relieves his pain.
Now, sister, let us hear your firm resolve.
Now, sister, let's hear your firm decision.
Your grant or your denial shall be mine. / Yet I confess [to Warwick] that often ere this day, / When I have heard your king's desert recounted, / Mine ear hath tempted judgment to desire.
Your consent or your refusal will be mine. (To Warwick) Yet I confess that often before today, when I've heard your king's merits described, my ear has tempted my judgment to desire him.

Then, Warwick, thus: our sister shall be Edward's; / And now forthwith shall articles be drawn / Touching the jointure that your king must make, / Which with her dowry shall be counterpois'd.— / Draw near, Queen Margaret, and be a witness / That Bona shall be wife to the English king.

Then, Warwick, it's settled: our sister will be Edward's. And now the terms will be drawn up at once about the settlement your king must make, to be balanced against her dowry. Come here, Queen Margaret, and witness that Bona will be the wife of the English king.
To Edward, but not to the English king.
Of Edward, but not of the English king.
Deceitful Warwick! it was thy device / By this alliance to make void my suit. / Before thy coming Lewis was Henry's friend.
Treacherous Warwick! It was your plan to cancel my request with this alliance. Before you came, Lewis was Henry's friend.

And still is friend to him and Margaret; / But if your title to the crown be weak, / As may appear by Edward's good success, / Then 't is but reason that I be releas'd / From giving aid which late I promised. / Yet shall you have all kindness at my hand / That your estate requires and mine can yield.

And I'm still a friend to him and Margaret; but if your claim to the crown is weak, as Edward's success suggests, then it's only reasonable that I should be released from giving the help I recently promised. Still, you'll have every kindness from me that your position needs and mine can give.

Henry now lives in Scotland, at his ease, / Where, having nothing, nothing can he lose. / And as for you yourself, our quondam queen, / You have a father able to maintain you, / And better 't were you troubled him than France.

Henry now lives comfortably in Scotland, where, having nothing, he can lose nothing. And as for you, our former queen, you have a father who can support you, and it would be better to trouble him than France.

Peace, impudent and shameless Warwick, / Proud setter-up and puller-down of kings! / I will not hence, till, with my talk and tears, / Both full of truth, I make King Lewis behold / Thy sly conveyance and thy lord's false love; / For both of you are birds of selfsame feather.

Quiet, impudent, shameless Warwick, proud setter-up and puller-down of kings! I won't leave until, with words and tears both full of truth, I make King Lewis see your sly trickery and your lord's false love; for you're both birds of a feather.
Warwick, this is some post to us or thee.
Warwick, this is some messenger for us or for you.
My lord ambassador, these letters are for you. / Sent from your brother Marquess Montague.— / These from our king unto your majesty.— / And, madam, these for you, from whom I know not.
My lord ambassador, these letters are for you, sent from your brother, the Marquess of Montague. These are from our king to your majesty. And these, madam, are for you, from whom I don't know.
I like it well that our fair queen and mistress / Smiles at her news while Warwick frowns at his.
I'm glad our fair queen and mistress smiles at her news while Warwick frowns at his.
Nay, mark how Lewis stamps as he were nettled; / I hope all's for the best.
And look how Lewis stamps as if he'd been stung. I hope it's all for the best.
Warwick, what are thy news?—and yours, fair queen?
Warwick, what's your news? And yours, fair queen?
Mine, such as fill my heart with unhop'd joys.
Mine is the kind that fills my heart with joy I never hoped for.
Mine, full of sorrow and heart's discontent.
Mine is full of sorrow and heartache.

What! has your king married the Lady Grey, / And now, to soothe your forgery and his, / Sends me a paper to persuade me patience? / Is this the alliance that he seeks with France? / Dare he presume to scorn us in this manner?

What! Has your king married Lady Grey, and now, to cover up your deceit and his, sends me a note to persuade me to be patient? Is this the alliance he wants with France? Does he dare to mock us like this?
I told your majesty as much before; / This proveth Edward's love and Warwick's honesty.
I told your majesty as much before. This proves Edward's love and Warwick's honesty.

King Lewis, I here protest, in sight of heaven, / And by the hope I have of heavenly bliss, / That I am clear from this misdeed of Edward's; / No more my king, for he dishonours me, / But most himself, if he could see his shame. / Did I forget that by the house of York / My father came untimely to his death? / Did I let pass the abuse done to my niece? / Did I impale him with the regal crown? / Did I put Henry from his native right? / And am I guerdon'd at the last with shame? / Shame on himself! for my desert is honour; / And to repair my honour lost for him, / I here renounce him and return to Henry.— / My noble queen, let former grudges pass, / And henceforth I am thy true servitor. / I will revenge his wrong to Lady Bona, / And replant Henry in his former state.

King Lewis, I declare here before heaven, and by my hope of heavenly bliss, that I'm innocent of Edward's wrongdoing. He's no longer my king, for he dishonours me, but himself most of all, if he could see his own shame. Did I forget that my father died before his time because of the house of York? Did I let the insult to my niece pass? Did I crown him with the royal crown? Did I put Henry out of his birthright? And am I rewarded in the end with shame? Shame on him! I deserve honour; and to repair the honour I've lost for his sake, I here renounce him and go back to Henry. My noble queen, let old grudges go; from now on I am your true servant. I'll avenge his wrong to Lady Bona and put Henry back in his former place.
Warwick, these words have turn'd my hate to love; / And I forgive and quite forget old faults, / And joy that thou becom'st King Henry's friend.
Warwick, these words have turned my hate to love; I forgive and completely forget old offences, and I'm glad you're becoming King Henry's friend.

So much his friend, ay, his unfeigned friend, / That if King Lewis vouchsafe to furnish us / With some few bands of chosen soldiers, / I'll undertake to land them on our coast / And force the tyrant from his seat by war. / 'T is not his new-made bride shall succour him; / And as for Clarence,—as my letters tell me,— / He's very likely now to fall from him, / For matching more for wanton lust than honour, / Or than for strength and safety of our country.

So much his friend, yes, his sincere friend, that if King Lewis will provide us with a few companies of picked soldiers, I'll undertake to land them on our coast and drive the tyrant from his throne by war. His new bride won't be able to help him; and as for Clarence, my letters tell me he's very likely to break with him now, for marrying out of lust rather than for honour or the strength and safety of our country.
Dear brother, how shall Bona be reveng'd / But by thy help to this distressed queen?
Dear brother, how can Bona be avenged except by your helping this distressed queen?
Renowned prince, how shall poor Henry live / Unless thou rescue him from foul despair?
Famous prince, how can poor Henry live unless you rescue him from black despair?
My quarrel and this English queen's are one.
My quarrel and this English queen's are one.
And mine, fair Lady Bona, joins with yours.
And mine, fair Lady Bona, joins with yours.
And mine with hers, and thine, and Margaret's. / Therefore, at last, I firmly am resolv'd / You shall have aid.
And mine with hers, and yours, and Margaret's. So at last I'm firmly decided: you'll have help.
Let me give humble thanks for all at once.
Let me give humble thanks for everything at once.

Then, England's messenger, return in post / And tell false Edward, thy supposed king, / That Lewis of France is sending over maskers / To revel it with him and his new bride. / Thou seest what's past; go fear thy king withal.

Then, English messenger, go back at full speed and tell false Edward, your so-called king, that Lewis of France is sending over masked dancers to revel with him and his new bride. You've seen what has happened; go and frighten your king with it.
Tell him, in hope he'll prove a widower shortly, / I'll wear the willow garland for his sake.
Tell him that, in the hope he'll soon be a widower, I'll wear the willow garland of a jilted lover for his sake.
Tell him my mourning weeds are laid aside, / And I am ready to put armour on.
Tell him my mourning clothes are put away and I'm ready to put on armour.
Tell him from me that he hath done me wrong, / And therefore I'll uncrown him ere 't be long. / There's thy reward; be gone.
Tell him from me that he has wronged me, and so I'll uncrown him before long. There's your tip; be off.

But, Warwick, / Thou and Oxford, with five thousand men, / Shall cross the seas and bid false Edward battle; / And, as occasion serves, this noble queen / And prince shall follow with a fresh supply. / Yet, ere thou go, but answer me one doubt: / What pledge have we of thy firm loyalty?

But, Warwick, you and Oxford, with five thousand men, will cross the sea and give false Edward battle; and when the moment is right, this noble queen and prince will follow with fresh troops. But before you go, answer me one doubt: what guarantee do we have of your firm loyalty?
This shall assure my constant loyalty,— / That if our queen and this young prince agree, / I'll join mine eldest daughter and my joy / To him forthwith in holy wedlock bands.
This will guarantee my constant loyalty: if our queen and this young prince agree, I'll marry my eldest daughter, my joy, to him at once in holy wedlock.

Yes, I agree, and thank you for your motion.— / Son Edward, she is fair and virtuous; / Therefore delay not, give thy hand to Warwick, / And with thy hand thy faith irrevocable / That only Warwick's daughter shall be thine.
