Yes, I agree, and thank you for the proposal. Son Edward, she's fair and virtuous, so don't delay: give your hand to Warwick, and with your hand your unbreakable promise that only Warwick's daughter will be your wife.
Yes, I accept her, for she well deserves it; / And here, to pledge my vow, I give my hand.
Yes, I accept her, for she well deserves it; and here, to pledge my vow, I give my hand.

Why stay we now? These soldiers shall be levied, / And thou, Lord Bourbon, our high admiral, / Shall waft them over with our royal fleet.— / I long till Edward fall by war's mischance / For mocking marriage with a dame of France.

Why are we waiting now? These soldiers will be raised, and you, Lord Bourbon, our high admiral, will carry them over with our royal fleet. I long for Edward to fall by the chances of war for making a mockery of marriage with a lady of France.

I came from Edward as ambassador, / But I return his sworn and mortal foe; / Matter of marriage was the charge he gave me, / But dreadful war shall answer his demand. / Had he none else to make a stale but me? / Then none but I shall turn his jest to sorrow. / I was the chief that rais'd him to the crown, / And I'll be chief to bring him down again; / Not that I pity Henry's misery, / But seek revenge on Edward's mockery.

I came from Edward as an ambassador, but I go back his sworn and deadly enemy. He sent me on a matter of marriage, but dreadful war will answer his request. Had he no one else to make a fool of but me? Then no one but me will turn his joke to sorrow. I was the main one who raised him to the crown, and I'll be the main one to bring him down again; not because I pity Henry's misery, but because I want revenge for Edward's mockery.
Now tell me, brother Clarence, what think you / Of this new marriage with the Lady Grey? / Hath not our brother made a worthy choice?
Now tell me, brother Clarence, what do you think of this new marriage to Lady Grey? Hasn't our brother made a fine choice?
Alas! you know 't is far from hence to France; / How could he stay till Warwick made return?
Alas, you know it's a long way from here to France; how could he wait until Warwick came back?
My lords, forbear this talk; here comes the King.
My lords, stop this talk; here comes the king.
I mind to tell him plainly what I think.
I intend to tell him plainly what I think.
Now, brother Clarence, how like you our choice / That you stand pensive as half malcontent?
Now, brother Clarence, how do you like our choice, that you stand there brooding, half discontented?
As well as Lewis of France, or the Earl of Warwick, / Which are so weak of courage and in judgment / That they'll take no offence at our abuse.
As much as Lewis of France or the Earl of Warwick do, who are so lacking in courage and judgment that they won't take offence at the way we've insulted them.
Suppose they take offence without a cause, / They are but Lewis and Warwick: I am Edward, / Your King and Warwick's, and must have my will.
Suppose they do take offence without cause: they're only Lewis and Warwick. I'm Edward, your king and Warwick's, and I must have my way.
And shall have your will, because our King; / Yet hasty marriage seldom proveth well.
And you shall have your way, because you're our king; but hasty marriages seldom turn out well.
Yea, brother Richard, are you offended too?
Oh, brother Richard, are you offended too?
Not I. / No; God forbid that I should wish them sever'd / Whom God hath join'd together; ay, and 't were pity / To sunder them that yoke so well together.
Not me. No; God forbid I should want to separate those whom God has joined together; yes, and it would be a pity to part two who are so well yoked together.

Setting your scorns and your mislike aside, / Tell me some reason why the Lady Grey / Should not become my wife and England's queen.— / And you too, Somerset and Montague, / Speak freely what you think.
Putting your mockery and your dislike aside, give me some reason why Lady Grey shouldn't become my wife and England's queen. And you too, Somerset and Montague, say freely what you think.
Then this is mine opinion,—that King Lewis / Becomes your enemy, for mocking him / About the marriage of the Lady Bona.
Then this is my opinion: King Lewis becomes your enemy for being made a fool of over the marriage to Lady Bona.
And Warwick, doing what you gave in charge, / Is now dishonoured by this new marriage.
And Warwick, who did what you told him to, is now dishonoured by this new marriage.
What if both Lewis and Warwick be appeas'd / By such invention as I can devise?
What if both Lewis and Warwick can be pacified by some scheme I can think up?
Yet to have join'd with France in such alliance / Would more have strength'ned this our commonwealth / 'Gainst foreign storms than any home-bred marriage.
Still, an alliance like that with France would have strengthened our country against foreign storms more than any marriage at home.
Why, knows not Montague that of itself / England is safe if true within itself?
Why, doesn't Montague know that England is safe on its own if it's loyal to itself?
But the safer when 't is back'd with France.
But safer when France backs it.

'T is better using France than trusting France. / Let us be back'd with God, and with the seas / Which he hath giv'n for fence impregnable, / And with their helps only defend ourselves; / In them and in ourselves our safety lies.

It's better to use France than to trust France. Let God be our backing, and the seas he has given us as an unbreakable wall; let us defend ourselves with their help alone. Our safety lies in them and in ourselves.
For this one speech Lord Hastings well deserves / To have the heir of the Lord Hungerford.
For that speech alone Lord Hastings well deserves to marry Lord Hungerford's heiress.
Ay, what of that? it was my will and grant; / And for this once my will shall stand for law.
Yes, what about it? It was my wish and my grant, and this once my wish will stand as law.

And yet, methinks, your grace hath not done well / To give the heir and daughter of Lord Scales / Unto the brother of your loving bride. / She better would have fitted me or Clarence; / But in your bride you bury brotherhood.

And yet, I think your grace hasn't done well to give Lord Scales's daughter and heiress to your loving bride's brother. She would have suited me or Clarence better; but in your bride you bury brotherhood.
Or else you would not have bestow'd the heir / Of the Lord Bonville on your new wife's son, / And leave your brothers to go speed elsewhere.
Or else you wouldn't have given Lord Bonville's heiress to your new wife's son and left your brothers to try their luck elsewhere.
Alas, poor Clarence! is it for a wife / That thou art malcontent? I will provide thee.
Alas, poor Clarence! Is it a wife you're unhappy about? I'll provide for you.
In choosing for yourself you show'd your judgment, / Which being shallow you shall give me leave / To play the broker in mine own behalf; / And to that end I shortly mind to leave you.
In choosing for yourself you showed your judgment, which is shallow, so you'll allow me to act as matchmaker on my own behalf; and for that purpose I intend to leave you soon.
Leave me or tarry, Edward will be king, / And not be tied unto his brother's will.
Leave me or stay, Edward will be king and not be tied to his brother's wishes.

My lords, before it pleas'd his majesty / To raise my state to title of a queen, / Do me but right, and you must all confess / That I was not ignoble of descent, / And meaner than myself have had like fortune. / But as this title honours me and mine, / So your dislikes, to whom I would be pleasing, / Doth cloud my joys with danger and with sorrow.

My lords, before it pleased his majesty to raise me to the title of queen, you must all admit, if you're fair to me, that I was not of low birth, and women of lower rank than me have had the same good fortune. But just as this title honours me and my family, so your disapproval, when I want to please you, clouds my happiness with danger and sorrow.

My love, forbear to fawn upon their frowns. / What danger or what sorrow can befall thee / So long as Edward is thy constant friend / And their true sovereign, whom they must obey? / Nay, whom they shall obey, and love thee too, / Unless they seek for hatred at my hands; / Which if they do, yet will I keep thee safe, / And they shall feel the vengeance of my wrath.

My love, don't try to win over their frowns. What danger or sorrow can come to you as long as Edward is your constant friend and their true sovereign, whom they must obey? Indeed, whom they will obey, and love you too, unless they want me to hate them; and if they do, I'll still keep you safe, and they'll feel my angry revenge.
[Aside] I hear, yet say not much, but think the more.
(Aside) I hear, and say little, but think all the more.
Now, messenger, what letters or what news / From France?
Now, messenger, what letters or news from France?
My sovereign liege, no letters, and few words, / But such as I, without your special pardon, / Dare not relate.
My sovereign lord, no letters and only a few words, but ones I don't dare repeat without your special pardon.
Go to, we pardon thee; therefore, in brief, / Tell me their words as near as thou canst guess them. / What answer makes King Lewis unto our letters?
Go on, we pardon you. So tell me briefly their words, as closely as you can remember them. What answer does King Lewis give to our letters?
At my depart these were his very words: / 'Go tell false Edward, thy supposed king, / That Lewis of France is sending over maskers / To revel it with him and his new bride.'
When I left, these were his exact words: 'Go and tell false Edward, your so-called king, that Lewis of France is sending over masked dancers to revel with him and his new bride.'
Is Lewis so brave? belike he thinks me Henry. / But what said Lady Bona to my marriage?
Is Lewis so bold? He must think I'm Henry. But what did Lady Bona say about my marriage?
These were her words, utt'red with mild disdain: / 'Tell him, in hope he'll prove a widower shortly, / I'll wear the willow garland for his sake.'
These were her words, spoken with mild scorn: 'Tell him that, in the hope he'll soon be a widower, I'll wear the willow garland for his sake.'
I blame not her, she could say little less, / She had the wrong; but what said Henry's queen? / For I have heard that she was there in place.
I don't blame her; she could hardly say less, since she was the one wronged. But what did Henry's queen say? I've heard she was there.
'Tell him' quoth she 'my mourning weeds are done, / And I am ready to put armour on.'
'Tell him,' she said, 'my mourning clothes are finished with, and I'm ready to put on armour.'
Belike she minds to play the Amazon. / But what said Warwick to these injuries?
It seems she means to play the Amazon. But what did Warwick say to these insults?
He, more incens'd against your majesty / Than all the rest, discharg'd me with these words: / 'Tell him from me that he hath done me wrong, / And therefore I'll uncrown him ere 't be long.'
He was more furious with your majesty than all the rest, and sent me off with these words: 'Tell him from me that he has wronged me, and so I'll uncrown him before long.'
Ha! durst the traitor breathe out so proud words? / Well, I will arm me, being thus forewarn'd; / They shall have wars, and pay for their presumption. / But say, is Warwick friends with Margaret?
Ha! Does the traitor dare breathe such proud words? Well, being warned like this, I'll arm myself. They'll have war and pay for their arrogance. But tell me, is Warwick friends with Margaret?
Ay, gracious sovereign; they are so link'd in friendship / That young Prince Edward marries Warwick's daughter.
Yes, gracious sovereign; they're so bound in friendship that young Prince Edward is marrying Warwick's daughter.

Belike the elder; Clarence will have the younger. / Now, brother king, farewell, and sit you fast, / For I will hence to Warwick's other daughter; / That, though I want a kingdom, yet in marriage / I may not prove inferior to yourself.— / You that love me and Warwick, follow me.

The elder one, presumably; Clarence will have the younger. Now, brother king, goodbye, and hold on tight to your throne, for I'm going to Warwick's other daughter, so that, though I lack a kingdom, at least I won't be worse off than you in marriage. Those of you who love me and Warwick, follow me.
[Aside] Not I. / My thoughts aim at a further matter; I / Stay not for the love of Edward, but the crown.
(Aside) Not me. My thoughts aim at something further. I stay not out of love for Edward, but for the crown.

Clarence and Somerset both gone to Warwick! / Yet am I arm'd against the worst can happen, / And haste is needful in this desperate case.— / Pembroke and Stafford, you in our behalf / Go levy men and make prepare for war; / They are already, or quickly will be landed. / Myself in person will straight follow you.—

Clarence and Somerset both gone over to Warwick! Still, I'm armed against the worst that can happen, and speed is needed in this desperate situation. Pembroke and Stafford, go and raise troops for us and prepare for war. They've already landed, or soon will. I'll follow you myself at once.

But, ere I go, Hastings and Montague, / Resolve my doubt. You twain, of all the rest, / Are near to Warwick by blood and by alliance; / Tell me if you love Warwick more than me? / If it be so, then both depart to him. / I rather wish you foes than hollow friends; / But if you mind to hold your true obedience, / Give me assurance with some friendly vow, / That I may never have you in suspect.

But before I go, Hastings and Montague, settle my doubt. You two, more than the rest, are close to Warwick by blood and marriage. Tell me, do you love Warwick more than me? If so, both of you go to him. I'd rather have you as enemies than as false friends; but if you mean to stay truly loyal, give me some friendly vow as a guarantee, so I'll never have to suspect you.
So God help Montague as he proves true!
May God help Montague as he proves true!
And Hastings as he favours Edward's cause!
And Hastings, as he supports Edward's cause!
Now, brother Richard, will you stand by us?
Now, brother Richard, will you stand by us?
Ay, in despite of all that shall withstand you.
Yes, in spite of everyone who stands against you.
Why, so! then am I sure of victory. / Now, therefore, let us hence; and lose no hour / Till we meet Warwick with his foreign pow'r.
Why, good! Then I'm sure of victory. So let's go now and not lose an hour until we meet Warwick and his foreign army.
Trust me, my lord, all hitherto goes well; / The common people by numbers swarm to us. / But see where Somerset and Clarence comes!—
Believe me, my lord, everything's gone well so far. The common people are swarming to us in great numbers. But look, here come Somerset and Clarence!
Speak suddenly, my lords, are we all friends?
Tell me quickly, my lords, are we all friends?
Don't worry about that, my lord.

Then, gentle Clarence, welcome unto Warwick;— / And welcome, Somerset.—I hold it cowardice / To rest mistrustful where a noble heart / Hath pawn'd an open hand in sign of love; / Else might I think that Clarence, Edward's brother, / Were but a feigned friend to our proceedings. / But welcome, sweet Clarence; my daughter shall be thine. / And now what rests but, in night's coverture, / Thy brother being carelessly encamp'd, / His soldiers lurking in the towns about, / And but attended by a simple guard, / We may surprise and take him at our pleasure? / Our scouts have found the adventure very easy; / That as Ulysses and stout Diomede / With sleight and manhood stole to Rhesus' tents, / And brought from thence the Thracian fatal steeds, / So we, well cover'd with the night's black mantle, / At unawares may beat down Edward's guard, / And seize himself,—I say not slaughter him, / For I intend but only to surprise him.— / You that will follow me to this attempt, / Applaud the name of Henry with your leader.

Then, gentle Clarence, welcome to Warwick; and welcome, Somerset. I think it's cowardly to stay suspicious when a noble heart has offered an open hand as a sign of love; otherwise I might think that Clarence, Edward's brother, was only pretending to support our cause. But welcome, sweet Clarence; my daughter will be yours. And now all that remains is this: since your brother is camped carelessly, his soldiers scattered in the towns around and only a small guard with him, we can surprise him under cover of night and take him as we please. Our scouts have found the venture very easy; so that, just as Ulysses and brave Diomedes crept by skill and courage into Rhesus's tents and brought away the fateful Thracian horses, we, well covered by night's black cloak, can catch Edward's guard unawares, beat them down and seize him. I don't say kill him; I only mean to take him by surprise. Those of you who'll follow me in this attempt, cheer the name of Henry with your leader.
Why then, let's on our way in silent sort; / For Warwick and his friends, God and Saint George!
Why then, let's go on our way quietly. For Warwick and his friends, God and Saint George!
Come on, my masters, each man take his stand; / The king by this is set him down to sleep.
Come on, gentlemen, each man take his position. The king will have sat down to sleep by now.
What, will he not to bed?
What, won't he go to bed?
Why, no; for he hath made a solemn vow / Never to lie and take his natural rest / Till Warwick or himself be quite suppress'd.
Why, no; he's made a solemn vow never to lie down and sleep properly until either Warwick or he himself is completely beaten.
To-morrow, then, belike shall be the day, / If Warwick be so near as men report.
Then tomorrow will probably be the day, if Warwick is as close as people say.
But say, I pray, what nobleman is that / That with the king here resteth in his tent?
But tell me, please, what nobleman is that resting in the tent with the king?
'T is the Lord Hastings, the king's chiefest friend.
It's Lord Hastings, the king's closest friend.
O, is it So? But why commands the king / That his chief followers lodge in towns about him, / While he himself keeps in the cold field?
Oh, is it? But why does the king order his main followers to stay in the towns around him, while he stays out in the cold field?
'T is the more honour, because more dangerous.
There's more honour in it, because it's more dangerous.
Ay, but give me worship and quietness; / I like it better than dangerous honour. / If Warwick knew in what estate he stands, / 'T is to be doubted he would waken him.
Yes, but give me dignity and quiet; I like that better than dangerous honour. If Warwick knew what position he's in, he'd probably come and wake him up.
Unless our halberds did shut up his passage.
Unless our spears blocked his way.
Ay; wherefore else guard we his royal tent / But to defend his person from night-foes?
Yes; why else do we guard his royal tent, except to protect him from enemies at night?
This is his tent; and see where, stand his guard. / Courage, my masters! honour now or never! / But follow me, and Edward shall be ours.
This is his tent; and look, there stand his guards. Courage, gentlemen! Honour now or never! Just follow me, and Edward will be ours.
What are they that fly there?
Who are those running away there?
Richard and Hastings. Let them go; here is the duke.
Richard and Hastings. Let them go; here's the duke.
The duke! why, Warwick, when we parted, / Thou call'dst me king?
The duke! Why, Warwick, when we parted you called me king.

Ay, but the case is alter'd; / When you disgrac'd me in my embassade, / Then I degraded you from being king, / And come now to create you Duke of York. / Alas! how should you govern any kingdom / That know not how to use ambassadors, / Nor how to be contented with one wife, / Nor how to use your brothers brotherly, / Nor how to study for the people's welfare, / Nor how to shroud yourself from enemies?

Yes, but things have changed. When you disgraced me during my embassy, I demoted you from being king, and now I've come to make you Duke of York. Alas! How could you govern any kingdom when you don't know how to treat ambassadors, or how to be content with one wife, or how to treat your brothers like a brother, or how to work for the people's welfare, or how to protect yourself from enemies?

Yea, brother of Clarence, art thou here too? / Nay, then I see that Edward needs must down.— / Yet, Warwick, in despite of all mischance / Of thee thyself and all thy complices, / Edward will always bear himself as king; / Though fortune's malice overthrow my state, / My mind exceeds the compass of her wheel.

Oh, brother Clarence, are you here too? Well, then I see Edward has to fall. Still, Warwick, in spite of all the bad luck you and your accomplices bring, Edward will always behave like a king. Though fortune's spite may overthrow my position, my mind is beyond the reach of her wheel.
Then for his mind be Edward England's king;
Then let Edward be England's king in his mind;

But Henry now shall wear the English crown / And be true king indeed, thou but the shadow.— / My Lord of Somerset, at my request, / See that forthwith Duke Edward be convey'd / Unto my brother, Archbishop of York. / When I have fought with Pembroke and his fellows, / I'll follow you and tell what answer / Lewis and the Lady Bona send to him.— / Now, for a while farewell, good Duke of York.

but Henry will now wear the English crown and be the real king, and you only the shadow. My Lord of Somerset, at my request see that Duke Edward is taken at once to my brother, the Archbishop of York. When I've fought Pembroke and his companions, I'll follow you and tell him what answer Lewis and Lady Bona send him. Now, goodbye for a while, good Duke of York.
What fates impose, that men must needs abide; / It boots not to resist both wind and tide.
Men must put up with what the fates impose; there's no use resisting both wind and tide.
What now remains, my lords, for us to do, / But march to London with our soldiers?
What's left for us to do now, my lords, except march to London with our soldiers?
Ay, that's the first thing that we have to do,— / To free King Henry from imprisonment / And see him seated in the regal throne.
Yes, that's the first thing we have to do: free King Henry from prison and see him sitting on the royal throne.
Madam, what makes you in this sudden change?
Madam, what has caused this sudden change in you?
Why, brother Rivers, are you yet to learn / What late misfortune is befallen King Edward?
Why, brother Rivers, haven't you heard yet what misfortune has just happened to King Edward?
What! loss of some pitch'd battle against Warwick?
What! Has he lost a pitched battle against Warwick?
No, but the loss of his own royal person.
No, but he's lost his royal person.

Ay, almost slain, for he is taken prisoner, / Either betray'd by falsehood of his guard / Or by his foe surpris'd at unawares, / And, as I further have to understand, / Is new committed to the Bishop of York, / Fell Warwick's brother and by that our foe.

Yes, almost dead, for he's been taken prisoner, either betrayed by a disloyal guard or surprised by his enemy; and, as I've also been told, he has just been handed over to the Archbishop of York, cruel Warwick's brother and therefore our enemy.
These news, I must confess, are full of grief; / Yet, gracious madam, bear it as you may. / Warwick may lose, that now hath won the day.
This news is very sad, I must admit; but, gracious madam, bear it as well as you can. Warwick, who has won today, may lose.

Till then, fair hope must hinder life's decay; / And I the rather wean me from despair, / For love of Edward's offspring in my womb. / This is it that makes me bridle passion / And bear with mildness my misfortune's cross; / Ay, ay, for this I draw in many a tear, / And stop the rising of blood-sucking sighs, / Lest with my sighs or tears I blast or drown / King Edward's fruit, true heir to the English crown.

Until then, hope must keep my life from failing; and I wean myself from despair all the more out of love for Edward's child in my womb. This is what makes me rein in my passion and bear the cross of my misfortune calmly. Yes, yes, for this I hold back many a tear and stop the blood-draining sighs, in case my sighs or tears should blight or drown King Edward's child, the true heir to the English crown.
But, madam, where is Warwick then become?
But, madam, what has become of Warwick?

I am inform'd that he comes towards London, / To set the crown once more on Henry's head. / Guess thou the rest: King Edward's friends must down; / But to prevent the tyrant's violence,— / For trust not him that hath once broken faith,— / I'll hence forthwith unto the sanctuary, / To save at least the heir of Edward's right. / There shall I rest secure from force and fraud. / Come therefore, let us fly while we may fly; / If Warwick take us, we are sure to die.

I'm told he's coming towards London to put the crown on Henry's head again. You can guess the rest: King Edward's friends must fall. But to escape the tyrant's violence, for never trust someone who has once broken his word, I'll go at once to sanctuary, to save at least the heir to Edward's right. There I'll be safe from force and trickery. Come, then, let's run while we can; if Warwick catches us, we're sure to die.

Now, my Lord Hastings, and Sir William Stanley, / Leave off to wonder why I drew you hither / Into this chiefest thicket of the park. / Thus stands the case: you know our King, my brother, / Is prisoner to the Bishop here, at whose hands / He hath good usage and great liberty, / And often, but attended with weak guard, / Comes hunting this way to disport himself. / I have advertis'd him by secret means / That if about this hour he make this way, / Under the colour of his usual game, / He shall here find his friends, with horse and men, / To set him free from his captivity.

Now, my Lord Hastings and Sir William Stanley, stop wondering why I brought you here into the thickest part of the park. This is how things stand: you know our king, my brother, is the archbishop's prisoner here; he's treated well and given a lot of freedom, and he often comes hunting this way for amusement with only a weak guard. I've secretly let him know that if he comes this way at about this time, pretending to be at his usual sport, he'll find his friends here with horses and men to free him from captivity.
This way, my lord, for this way lies the game.
This way, my lord, for the game is this way.
Nay, this way, man; see, where the huntsmen stand.— / Now, brother of Gloster, Lord Hastings, and the rest, / Stand you thus close to steal the bishop's deer?
No, this way, man; look where the huntsmen are standing. Now, brother Gloucester, Lord Hastings and the rest, are you hiding here to steal the archbishop's deer?
Brother, the time and case requireth haste; / Your horse stands ready at the park corner.
Brother, the time and situation call for speed. Your horse is ready at the corner of the park.
But where shall we go then?
To Lynn, my lord, and shipt from thence to Flanders.
To King's Lynn, my lord, and from there by ship to Flanders.
Well guess'd, believe me, for that was my meaning.
Well guessed, believe me; that was my plan.
Stanley, I will requite thy forwardness.
But wherefore stay we? 't is no time to talk.
But why are we waiting? This is no time to talk.
Huntsman, what say'st thou? wilt thou go along?
Huntsman, what do you say? Will you come along?
Better do so than tarry and be hang'd.
Better that than stay and be hanged.
Come then; away! let's have no more ado.
Come on, then; away! Let's not fuss any more.
Bishop, farewell; shield thee from Warwick's frown, / And pray that I may repossess the crown.
Goodbye, archbishop; protect yourself from Warwick's anger, and pray that I may get the crown back.

Master Lieutenant, now that God and friends / Have shaken Edward from the regal seat / And turn'd my captive state to liberty, / My fear to hope, my sorrows unto joys, / At our enlargement what are thy due fees?

Master Lieutenant, now that God and my friends have shaken Edward off the royal throne and turned my imprisonment into freedom, my fear into hope and my sorrows into joys, what fees do we owe you on our release?
Subjects may challenge nothing of their sovereigns; / But if an humble prayer may prevail, / I then crave pardon of your Majesty.
Subjects can claim nothing from their sovereigns; but if a humble request may succeed, I ask your majesty's pardon.

For what, lieutenant? for well using me? / Nay, be thou sure I'll well requite thy kindness, / For that it made my imprisonment a pleasure; / Ay, such a pleasure as incaged birds / Conceive when, after many moody thoughts, / At last by notes of household harmony / They quite forget their loss of liberty.— / But, Warwick, after God thou sett'st me free, / And chiefly therefore I thank God and thee; / He was the author, thou the instrument. / Therefore, that I may conquer fortune's spite, / By living low where fortune cannot hurt me, / And that the people of this blessed land / May not be punish'd with my thwarting stars, / Warwick, although my head still wear the crown, / I here resign my government to thee, / For thou art fortunate in all thy deeds.

For what, lieutenant? For treating me well? No, you can be sure I'll reward your kindness well, since it made my imprisonment a pleasure; yes, the kind of pleasure caged birds feel when, after many gloomy thoughts, they finally forget their lost freedom in the sound of household music. But Warwick, after God, it's you who set me free, so I thank God and you above all; he was the author, you the instrument. So, to beat fortune's spite by living humbly where fortune can't hurt me, and so that the people of this blessed land are not punished by my unlucky stars, Warwick, although my head still wears the crown, I here hand over the government to you, for you are lucky in everything you do.

Your grace hath still been fam'd for virtuous, / And now may seem as wise as virtuous / By spying and avoiding fortune's malice, / For few men rightly temper with the stars; / Yet in this one thing let me blame your grace, / For choosing me when Clarence is in place.

Your grace has always been famous for virtue, and now you may seem as wise as you are virtuous by spotting fortune's malice and avoiding it, for few men adapt themselves rightly to their stars. Yet in this one thing let me find fault with your grace: for choosing me when Clarence is here.

No, Warwick, thou art worthy of the sway, / To whom the heavens in thy nativity / Adjudg'd an olive branch and laurel crown, / As likely to be blest in peace and war; / And therefore, I yield thee my free consent.
No, Warwick, you're worthy of the power; at your birth the heavens awarded you an olive branch and a laurel crown, as one likely to be blessed in peace and war. So I freely give you my consent.
And I choose Clarence only for protector.
And I choose Clarence alone as Protector.

Warwick and Clarence, give me both your hands. / Now join your hands, and with your hands your hearts, / That no dissension hinder government. / I make you both protectors of this land, / While I myself will lead a private life / And in devotion spend my latter days, / To sin's rebuke and my Creator's praise.

Warwick and Clarence, give me both your hands. Now join your hands, and with your hands your hearts, so no quarrel hinders the government. I make you both Protectors of this land, while I myself will lead a private life and spend my last days in devotion, rebuking sin and praising my Creator.
What answers Clarence to his sovereign's will?
What does Clarence answer to his sovereign's wish?
That he consents if Warwick yield consent, / For on thy fortune I repose myself.
That he agrees if Warwick agrees, for I rely on your good fortune.

Why, then, though loath, yet I must be content. / We'll yoke together, like a double shadow / To Henry's body, and supply his place,— / I mean in bearing weight of government / While he enjoys the honour and his ease. / And, Clarence, now then it is more than needful / Forthwith that Edward be pronounc'd a traitor, / And all his lands and goods confiscated.

Why, then, though I'm reluctant, I must accept. We'll be yoked together like a double shadow to Henry's body and take his place: I mean in carrying the weight of government while he enjoys the honour and his ease. And, Clarence, it's now essential that Edward be proclaimed a traitor at once and all his lands and goods confiscated.
What else? and that succession be determin'd.
Of course; and that the succession be settled.
Ay, therein Clarence shall not want his part.
Yes, and Clarence won't lack his share in that.

But with the first of all your chief affairs, / Let me entreat—for I command no more— / That Margaret your queen, and my son Edward, / Be sent for to return from France with speed; / For, till I see them here, by doubtful fear / My joy of liberty is half eclips'd.

But as the first of all your main business, let me ask, for I command no longer, that Margaret your queen and my son Edward be sent for to return quickly from France; for until I see them here, anxious fear half darkens my joy at being free.
It shall be done, my sovereign, with all speed.
It will be done, my sovereign, with all speed.
My Lord of Somerset, what youth is that / Of whom you seem to have so tender care?
My Lord of Somerset, who is that youth you seem to take such tender care of?
My liege, it is young Henry, Earl of Richmond.
My lord, it's young Henry, Earl of Richmond.
Come hither, England's hope.—If secret powers
Come here, England's hope. If secret powers

Suggest but truth to my divining thoughts, / This pretty lad will prove our country's bliss. / His looks are full of peaceful majesty, / His head by nature fram'd to wear a crown, / His hand to wield a sceptre, and himself / Likely in time to bless a regal throne. / Make much of him, my lords; for this is he / Must help you more than you are hurt by me.

are telling my prophetic thoughts the truth, this fine boy will turn out to be our country's blessing. His looks are full of peaceful majesty; his head is shaped by nature to wear a crown, his hand to hold a sceptre, and he himself is likely in time to grace a royal throne. Look after him well, my lords; for this is the one who must help you more than I have harmed you.
That Edward is escaped from your brother, / And fled, as he hears since, to Burgundy.
That Edward has escaped from your brother and fled, as he has heard since, to Burgundy.
Unsavoury news! but how made he escape?
Unwelcome news! But how did he escape?

He was convey'd by Richard Duke of Gloster / And the Lord Hastings, who attended him / In secret ambush on the forest side, / And from the bishop's huntsmen rescued him, / For hunting was his daily exercise.

He was taken away by Richard, Duke of Gloucester, and Lord Hastings, who waited for him in a secret ambush at the edge of the forest and rescued him from the archbishop's huntsmen; for hunting was his daily exercise.
My brother was too careless of his charge.— / But let us hence, my sovereign, to provide / A salve for any sore that may betide.
My brother was too careless with his prisoner. But let's go, my sovereign, and provide a remedy for any trouble that may come.

My lord, I like not of this flight of Edward's, / For doubtless Burgundy will yield him help, / And we shall have more wars before 't be long. / As Henry's late presaging prophecy / Did glad my heart with hope of this young Richmond, / So doth my heart misgive me, in these conflicts / What may befall him, to his harm and ours; / Therefore, Lord Oxford, to prevent the worst, / Forthwith we'll send him hence to Brittany / Till storms be past of civil enmity.

My lord, I don't like this escape of Edward's, for Burgundy will certainly give him help, and we'll have more wars before long. Just as Henry's prophecy just now gladdened my heart with hope for young Richmond, so my heart fears what may happen to him in these conflicts, to his harm and ours. So, Lord Oxford, to prevent the worst, we'll send him away at once to Brittany until the storms of civil war are over.
Ay; for if Edward repossess the crown, / 'T is like that Richmond with the rest shall down.
Yes; for if Edward gets the crown back, Richmond is likely to fall with the rest.
It shall be so; he shall to Brittany. / Come therefore, let's about it speedily.
So be it; he'll go to Brittany. Come, then, let's see to it quickly.

Now, brother Richard, Lord Hastings, and the rest, / Yet thus far fortune maketh us amends, / And says that once more I shall interchange / My waned state for Henry's regal crown. / Well have we pass'd and now repass'd the seas, / And brought desired help from Burgundy. / What then remains, we being thus arriv'd / From Ravenspurg haven before the gates of York, / But that we enter as into our dukedom?

Now, brother Richard, Lord Hastings and the rest, so far fortune is making it up to us and says I'll once more exchange my fallen state for Henry's royal crown. We've crossed the sea and back safely and brought the help we wanted from Burgundy. Now that we've arrived from the harbour at Ravenspurgh at the gates of York, all that remains is to enter it as our own dukedom.
The gates made fast!—Brother, I like not this; / For many men that stumble at the threshold / Are well foretold that danger lurks within.
The gates are locked! Brother, I don't like this; many men who stumble on the doorstep are being warned that danger lies inside.
Tush, man! abodements must not now affright us; / By fair or foul means we must enter in, / For hither will our friends repair to us.
Nonsense, man! We mustn't be scared by omens now. By fair means or foul we must get in, for our friends will come to us here.
My liege, I'll knock once more to summon them.
My lord, I'll knock once more to call them.
My lords, we were forewarned of your coming / And shut the gates for safety of ourselves, / For now we owe allegiance unto Henry.
My lords, we were warned you were coming and shut the gates for our own safety, for we now owe allegiance to Henry.
But master mayor, if Henry be your king, / Yet Edward, at the least, is Duke of York.
But, Master Mayor, if Henry is your king, Edward is at least Duke of York.
True, my good lord; I know you for no less.
True, my good lord; I know you to be no less.
Why, and I challenge nothing but my dukedom, / As being well content with that alone.
Why, and I claim nothing but my dukedom, being quite content with that alone.
[Aside] But when the fox hath once got in his nose, / He'll soon find means to make the body follow.
(Aside) But once the fox has got his nose in, he'll soon find a way to make the body follow.
Why, master mayor, why stand you in a doubt? / Open the gates; we are King Henry's friends.
Why, Master Mayor, why are you hesitating? Open the gates; we're King Henry's friends.
Ay, say you so? the gates shall then be open'd.
Oh, is that so? Then the gates will be opened.
A wise, stout captain, and soon persuaded.
A wise, brave commander, and easily persuaded!
The good old man would fain that all were well, / So 't were not long of him; but, being enter'd, / I doubt not, I, but we shall soon persuade / Both him and all his brothers unto reason.
The good old man would like everything to be all right, so long as he isn't to blame; but once we're in, I have no doubt we'll soon persuade him and all his fellow aldermen to see sense.
So, master mayor; these gates must not be shut / But in the night or in the time of war. / What! fear not, man, but yield me up the keys;
So, Master Mayor, these gates must be shut only at night or in wartime. What! Don't be afraid, man; hand me the keys;
For Edward will defend the town and thee, / And all those friends that deign to follow me.
for Edward will defend the town and you, and all those friends who choose to follow me.
Brother, this is Sir John Montgomery, / Our trusty friend unless I be deceiv'd.
Brother, this is Sir John Montgomery, our loyal friend, unless I'm mistaken.
Welcome, Sir John; but why come you in arms?
Welcome, Sir John; but why have you come armed?
To help King Edward in his time of storm, / As every loyal subject ought to do.
To help King Edward in his stormy time, as every loyal subject should.
Thanks, good Montgomery; but we now forget / Our title to the crown, and only claim / Our dukedom till God please to send the rest.
Thank you, good Montgomery; but we're now forgetting our claim to the crown and claiming only our dukedom, until God chooses to send the rest.
Then fare you well, for I will hence again; / I came to serve a king, and not a duke.— / Drummer, strike up, and let us march away.
Then goodbye, for I'll go home again. I came to serve a king, not a duke. Drummer, strike up, and let's march away.
Nay, stay, Sir John, awhile, and we'll debate / By what safe means the crown may be recover'd.
No, wait a moment, Sir John, and we'll discuss safe ways to get the crown back.

What talk you of debating? in few words, / If you'll not here proclaim yourself our king, / I'll leave you to your fortune and begone / To keep them back that come to succour you. / Why shall we fight if you pretend no title?

Why talk about discussing? In short, if you won't proclaim yourself our king here, I'll leave you to your fate and go, and hold back those who are coming to help you. Why should we fight if you claim no title?
Why, brother, wherefore stand you on nice points?
Why, brother, why are you fussing over fine points?
When we grow stronger, then we'll make our claim; / Till then 't is wisdom to conceal our meaning.
When we're stronger, we'll make our claim; until then it's wise to hide our intentions.
Away with scrupulous wit! now arms must rule.
Away with cautious cleverness! Now weapons must rule.
And fearless minds climb soonest unto crowns.— / Brother, we will proclaim you out of hand; / The bruit thereof will bring you many friends.
And fearless minds climb to crowns fastest. Brother, we'll proclaim you at once; the news of it will bring you many friends.
Then be it as you will; for 't is my right, / And Henry but usurps the diadem.
Then have it your way; for it's my right, and Henry only usurps the crown.
Ay, now my sovereign speaketh like himself, / And now will I be Edward's champion.
Yes, now my sovereign speaks like himself, and now I'll be Edward's champion.
Sound, trumpet; Edward shall be here proclaim'd.— / Come, fellow-soldier, make thou proclamation.
Sound, trumpet; Edward will be proclaimed here. Come, fellow soldier, read the proclamation.
[Reads] 'Edward the Fourth, by the grace of God, / King of England and France, and Lord of Ireland,' etc.
(Reads) 'Edward the Fourth, by the grace of God, King of England and France, and Lord of Ireland,' and so on.
And whoso'er gainsays King Edward's right, / By this I challenge him to single fight.
And whoever denies King Edward's right, I challenge him to single combat with this.

Thanks, brave Montgomery, and thanks unto you all; / If fortune serve me, I'll requite this kindness. / Now for this night let's harbour here in York; / And when the morning sun shall raise his car / Above the border of this horizon / We'll forward towards Warwick and his mates, / For well I wot that Henry is no soldier.— / Ah, froward Clarence! how evil it beseems thee / To flatter Henry and forsake thy brother! / Yet, as we may, we'll meet both thee and Warwick.— / Come on, brave soldiers; doubt not of the day, / And, that once gotten, doubt not of large pay.

Thank you, brave Montgomery, and thanks to you all; if fortune favours me, I'll repay this kindness. Now let's stay here in York tonight; and when the morning sun lifts his chariot above the edge of the horizon, we'll go on towards Warwick and his allies, for I know Henry is no soldier. Ah, wayward Clarence! How badly it suits you to flatter Henry and abandon your brother! Still, we'll face both you and Warwick as best we can. Come on, brave soldiers; don't doubt we'll win the day, and once it's won, don't doubt you'll be well paid.

What counsel, lords? Edward from Belgia, / With hasty Germans and blunt Hollanders, / Hath pass'd in safety through the narrow seas, / And with his troops doth march amain to London; / And many giddy people flock to him.

What do you advise, lords? Edward has crossed the Channel safely from the Low Countries with impetuous Germans and rough Dutchmen, and is marching at full speed on London with his troops, and many fickle people are flocking to him.
Let's levy men and beat him back again.
Let's raise troops and drive him back again.
A little fire is quickly trodden out, / Which, being suffer'd, rivers cannot quench.
A little fire is quickly stamped out, which, if it's allowed to burn, rivers can't put out.

In Warwickshire I have true-hearted friends, / Not mutinous in peace, yet bold in war. / Those will I muster up;—and thou, son Clarence, / Shalt stir up in Suffolk, Norfolk, and in Kent / The knights and gentlemen to come with thee.— / Thou, brother Montague, in Buckingham, / Northampton, and in Leicestershire shalt find / Men well inclin'd to hear what thou command'st.— / And thou, brave Oxford, wondrous well belov'd, / In Oxfordshire shalt muster up thy friends.— / My sovereign, with the loving citizens, / Like to his island girt in with the ocean, / Or modest Dian circled with her nymphs, / Shall rest in London till we come to him.— / Fair lords, take leave and stand not to reply.— / Farewell, my sovereign.

In Warwickshire I have loyal friends, peaceful in peacetime but bold in war; I'll call them up. And you, son Clarence, will rouse the knights and gentlemen in Suffolk, Norfolk and Kent to come with you. You, brother Montague, will find men in Buckingham, Northampton and Leicestershire who are willing to obey your orders. And you, brave Oxford, so wonderfully well loved, will gather your friends in Oxfordshire. My sovereign, with the loyal citizens, like his island surrounded by the ocean, or chaste Diana circled by her nymphs, will stay in London until we come back to him. Fair lords, say goodbye and don't stop to answer. Farewell, my sovereign.
Farewell, my Hector, and my Troy's true hope.
Farewell, my Hector, the true hope of my Troy.
In sign of truth I kiss your highness' hand.
As a sign of my loyalty I kiss your highness's hand.
Well-meaning Clarence, may you have good fortune!
Comfort, my lord;—and so I take my leave.
Courage, my lord; and so I take my leave.
And thus [kissing Henry's hand] I seal my truth, and bid adieu.
And so (kissing Henry's hand) I seal my loyalty and say goodbye.
Sweet Oxford, and my loving Montague, / And all at once, once more a happy farewell.
Sweet Oxford, and my loving Montague, and all of you together, once more a happy farewell.
Farewell, sweet lords; let's meet at Coventry.
Farewell, sweet lords; let's meet at Coventry.
Here at the palace will I rest a while.— / Cousin of Exeter, what thinks your lordship? / Methinks the power that Edward hath in field / Should not be able to encounter mine.
I'll rest here at the palace for a while. Cousin Exeter, what does your lordship think? I think the army Edward has in the field shouldn't be able to stand up to mine.
The doubt is that he will seduce the rest.
The worry is that he'll win over the rest.

That's not my fear; my meed hath got me fame. / I have not stopp'd mine ears to their demands, / Nor posted off their suits with slow delays; / My pity hath been balm to heal their wounds, / My mildness hath allay'd their swelling griefs, / My mercy dried their water-flowing tears. / I have not been desirous of their wealth / Nor much oppress'd them with great subsidies, / Nor forward of revenge, though they much err'd; / Then, why should they love Edward more than me? / No, Exeter, these graces challenge grace; / And when the lion fawns upon the lamb / The lamb will never cease to follow him.

That's not what I fear. My good deeds have made me well known. I haven't closed my ears to the people's requests, or put off their petitions with long delays. My pity has been a balm to heal their wounds, my gentleness has eased their swelling griefs, my mercy has dried their streaming tears. I haven't wanted their wealth, or burdened them much with heavy taxes, or been quick to take revenge, though they did much wrong. So why should they love Edward more than me? No, Exeter, such kindness earns kindness; and when the lion is gentle to the lamb, the lamb will never stop following him.
Hark, hark, my lord! what shouts are these?
Listen, listen, my lord! What shouts are these?

Seize on the shame-fac'd Henry! bear him hence, / And once again proclaim us king of England.— / You are the fount that makes small brooks to flow. / Now stops thy spring; my sea shall suck them dry / And swell so much the higher by their ebb.— / Hence with him to the Tower! let him not speak.—

Seize the shamefaced Henry! Take him away, and proclaim us King of England once again. You are the spring that makes the little streams flow; now your spring is stopped, my sea will suck them dry and swell all the higher as they ebb. Off to the Tower with him! Don't let him speak.
And, lords, towards Coventry bend we our course, / Where peremptory Warwick now remains. / The sun shines hot, and, if we use delay, / Cold biting winter mars our hop'd-for hay.
And, lords, let's head for Coventry, where overbearing Warwick is now. The sun is hot, and if we delay, cold biting winter will spoil the hay we're hoping for.
Away betimes, before his forces join, / And take the great-grown traitor unawares. / Brave warriors, march amain towards Coventry.
Let's go early, before his forces join up, and take the overgrown traitor by surprise. Brave warriors, march at full speed to Coventry.
Where is the post that came from valiant Oxford?— / How far hence is thy lord, mine honest fellow?
Where's the messenger who came from brave Oxford? How far away is your lord, my good fellow?
By this at Dunsmore, marching hitherward.
At Dunsmore by now, marching this way.
How far off is our brother Montague? / Where is the post that came from Montague?
How far away is our brother Montague? Where's the messenger who came from Montague?
By this at Daintry, with a puissant troop.
At Daventry by now, with a powerful army.
Say, Somerville, what says my loving son? / And, by thy guess, how nigh is Clarence now?
Tell me, Somerville, what does my loving son-in-law say? And how near do you guess Clarence is now?
At Southam I did leave him with his forces / And do expect him here some two hours hence.
I left him at Southam with his forces, and I expect him here in about two hours.
Then Clarence is at hand; I hear his drum.
Then Clarence is close; I can hear his drum.
It is not his, my lord; here Southam lies. / The drum your honour hears marcheth from Warwick.
It isn't his, my lord; Southam lies this way. The drum your honour hears is marching from Warwick.
Who should that be? belike, unlook'd-for friends.
Who could that be? Friends we didn't expect, probably.
They are at hand, and you shall quickly know.
They're close, and you'll soon find out.
Go, trumpet, to the walls and sound a parle.
Go, trumpeter, to the walls and sound for a parley.
See how the surly Warwick mans the wall.
Look how surly Warwick has manned the wall.
O, unbid spite! Is sportful Edward come? / Where slept our scouts, or how are they seduc'd, / That we could hear no news of his repair?
O, unwelcome trouble! Has playboy Edward come? Where were our scouts sleeping, or how have they been bribed, that we heard no news of his coming?
Now, Warwick, wilt thou ope the city gates? / Speak gentle words and humbly bend thy knee, / Call Edward king and at his hands beg mercy? / And he shall pardon thee these outrages.
Now, Warwick, will you open the city gates, speak politely, kneel humbly, call Edward king and beg him for mercy? Then he'll pardon you for these outrages.
Nay, rather, wilt thou draw thy forces hence, / Confess who set thee up and pluck'd thee down? / Call Warwick patron and be penitent, / And thou shalt still remain the Duke of York.
No, rather will you take your forces away, admit who set you up and pulled you down, call Warwick your patron and repent? Then you can still remain Duke of York.
I thought, at least, he would have said the king; / Or did he make the jest against his will?
I thought at least he'd say 'king'; or did he make the joke without meaning to?
Is not a dukedom, sir, a goodly gift?
Isn't a dukedom a fine gift, sir?
Ay, by my faith, for a poor earl to give; / I'll do thee service for so good a gift.
Yes, indeed, for a poor earl to give. I'll do you a favour in return for such a good gift.
'T was I that gave the kingdom to thy brother.
It was I who gave the kingdom to your brother.
Why, then, 't is mine, if but by Warwick's gift.
Why, then, it's mine, if only by Warwick's gift.
Thou art no Atlas for so great a weight, / And, weakling, Warwick takes his gift again; / And Henry is my king, Warwick his subject.
You're no Atlas to carry such a great weight; so, weakling, Warwick takes his gift back; and Henry is my king, and Warwick is his subject.
But Warwick's king is Edward's prisoner; / And, gallant Warwick, do but answer this: / What is the body when the head is off?
But Warwick's king is Edward's prisoner. And, gallant Warwick, just answer this: what is the body when the head is cut off?

Alas! that Warwick had no more forecast, / But, whiles he thought to steal the single ten, / The king was slily finger'd from the deck! / You left poor Henry at the Bishop's palace, / And ten to one, you'll meet him in the Tower.

Alas, that Warwick didn't think further ahead! While he was trying to steal a mere ten, the king was slyly taken from the deck! You left poor Henry at the bishop's palace, and ten to one you'll meet him in the Tower.
'T is even so; yet you are Warwick still.
That's exactly it; yet you're still Warwick.
Come, Warwick, take the time; kneel down, kneel down. / Nay, when? strike now, or else the iron cools.
Come, Warwick, seize the moment; kneel, kneel. Well, when? Strike now, or the iron will cool.
I had rather chop this hand off at a blow, / And with the other fling it at thy face, / Than bear so low a sail, to strike to thee.
I'd rather chop this hand off with one blow and throw it in your face with the other than lower my sail so far as to surrender to you.

Sail how thou canst, have wind and tide thy friend, / This hand, fast wound about thy coal-black hair, / Shall, whiles thy head is warm and new cut off, / Write in the dust this sentence with thy blood, / 'Wind-changing Warwick now can change no more.'

Sail however you can, with wind and tide on your side: this hand, wound tightly in your coal-black hair, will, while your head is still warm and freshly cut off, write this sentence in the dust with your blood: 'Warwick, who changed with the wind, can change no more.'
O cheerful colours! see where Oxford comes.
O cheering flags! Look, here comes Oxford.
The gates are open; let us enter too.
The gates are open; let's go in too.

So other foes may set upon our backs. / Stand we in good array, for they no doubt / Will issue out again and bid us battle; / If not, the city being but of small defence, / We'll quietly rouse the traitors in the same.

So other enemies can attack us from behind? Let's stay in good order, for they'll no doubt come out again and offer battle; if not, since the city has weak defences, we'll soon drive the traitors out of it.
O, welcome, Oxford, for we want thy help.
O, welcome, Oxford, for we need your help.
Thou and thy brother both shall buy this treason, / Even with the dearest blood your bodies bear.
You and your brother will both pay for this treason with the most precious blood in your bodies.
The harder match'd, the greater victory; / My mind presageth happy gain and conquest.
The harder the match, the greater the victory. My mind foretells happy gain and conquest.
Two of thy name, both Dukes of Somerset, / Have sold their lives unto the House of York; / And thou shalt be the third if this sword hold.
Two of your name, both Dukes of Somerset, have paid with their lives to the house of York; and you'll be the third, if this sword holds out.
And lo, where George of Clarence sweeps along, / Of force enough to bid his brother battle; / With whom an upright zeal to right prevails, / More than the nature of a brother's love!—
And look, here comes George of Clarence, sweeping along with enough troops to fight his brother; in him an honest zeal for what is right outweighs a brother's natural love!
Come, Clarence, come; thou wilt if Warwick call.
Come, Clarence, come; you will if Warwick calls.
Father of Warwick, know you what this means?
Father-in-law Warwick, do you know what this means?

Look here, I throw my infamy at thee; / I will not ruinate my father's house, / Who gave his blood to lime the stones together, / And set up Lancaster. Why, trow'st thou, Warwick, / That Clarence is so harsh, so blunt, unnatural, / To bend the fatal instruments of war / Against his brother and his lawful king? / Perhaps thou wilt object my holy oath; / To keep that oath were more impiety / Than Jephtha's when he sacrific'd his daughter. / I am so sorry for my trespass made / That, to deserve well at my brother's hands, / I here proclaim myself thy mortal foe, / With resolution, whereso'er I meet thee— / As I will meet thee, if thou stir abroad— / To plague thee for thy foul misleading me. / And so, proud-hearted Warwick, I defy thee, / And to my brother turn my blushing cheeks.— / Pardon me, Edward, I will make amends;— / And, Richard, do not frown upon my faults, / For I will henceforth be no more unconstant.

Look, I throw my disgrace at you. I will not ruin my father's house, which he cemented together with his blood, to set up Lancaster. Why, do you really think, Warwick, that Clarence is so harsh, blunt and unnatural as to turn the deadly weapons of war against his brother and lawful king? Perhaps you'll bring up my holy oath; to keep that oath would be more wicked than Jephthah's keeping his when he sacrificed his daughter. I'm so sorry for the wrong I've done that, to earn my brother's favour, I here declare myself your deadly enemy, determined, wherever I meet you, and I will meet you if you come out, to punish you for foully misleading me. And so, proud-hearted Warwick, I defy you, and turn my blushing cheeks to my brother. Forgive me, Edward, I'll make amends; and Richard, don't frown on my faults, for from now on I'll never be fickle again.
Now, welcome more, and ten times more belov'd, / Than if thou never hadst deserv'd our hate.
Now you're more welcome, and ten times more loved, than if you'd never earned our hatred.
Welcome, good Clarence; this is brother-like.
Welcome, good Clarence; this is how a brother should behave.
O passing traitor, perjur'd and unjust!
O utter traitor, oath-breaker and unjust!
What, Warwick, wilt thou leave the town and fight, / Or shall we beat the stones about thine ears?
What, Warwick, will you leave the town and fight, or shall we knock the stones down around your ears?
Alas! I am not coop'd here for defence; / I will away towards Barnet presently, / And bid thee battle, Edward, if thou dar'st.
Alas! I'm not shut in here to defend myself. I'll go towards Barnet at once and give you battle, Edward, if you dare.
Yes, Warwick, Edward dares and leads the way.— / Lords, to the field! Saint George and victory!
Yes, Warwick, Edward dares, and leads the way. Lords, to the field! Saint George and victory!
So, lie thou there; die thou, and die our fear, / For Warwick was a bug that fear'd us all.— / Now, Montague, sit fast; I seek for thee, / That Warwick's bones may keep thine company.
So, lie there; die, and let our fear die with you, for Warwick was a bogeyman that frightened us all. Now, Montague, hold on tight; I'm coming for you, so Warwick's bones can keep you company.

Ah! who is nigh? come to me, friend or foe, / And tell me who is victor, York or Warwick. / Why ask I that? my mangled body shows; / My blood, my want of strength, my sick heart shows / That I must yield my body to the earth / And, by my fall, the conquest to my foe. / Thus yields the cedar to the axe's edge, / Whose arms gave shelter to the princely eagle, / Under whose shade the ramping lion slept, / Whose top-branch overpeer'd Jove's spreading tree, / And kept low shrubs from winter's pow'rful wind. / These eyes, that now are dimm'd with death's black veil, / Have been as piercing as the midday sun, / To search the secret treasons of the world; / The wrinkles in my brows, now fill'd with blood, / Were liken'd oft to kingly sepulchres, / For who liv'd king but I could dig his grave? / And who durst smile when Warwick bent his brow? / Lo, now my glory smear'd in dust and blood! / My parks, my walks, my manors that I had, / Even now forsake me, and of all my lands / Is nothing left me but my body's length. / Why, what is pomp, rule, reign, but earth and dust? / And live we how we can, yet die we must.

Ah! Who's near? Come to me, friend or enemy, and tell me who has won, York or Warwick. Why do I ask? My mangled body shows it; my blood, my lack of strength, my sick heart show that I must give my body to the earth and, by my fall, the victory to my enemy. So the cedar falls to the axe's edge, whose arms sheltered the princely eagle, under whose shade the rearing lion slept, whose top branch looked down on Jove's spreading oak and protected low shrubs from winter's powerful wind. These eyes, now dimmed by death's black veil, have been as piercing as the midday sun in seeking out the world's secret treasons. The wrinkles on my brow, now filled with blood, were often compared to the graves of kings; for what living king was there whose grave I couldn't dig? And who dared smile when Warwick frowned? Look, now my glory is smeared with dust and blood! My parks, my walks, the manors I owned, are leaving me even now, and of all my lands nothing is left me but the length of my body. Why, what is pomp, rule and power but earth and dust? However we live, we must die.
Ah, Warwick, Warwick! wert thou as we are, / We might recover all our loss again. / The queen from France hath brought a puissant power; / Even now we heard the news. Ah, couldst thou fly!
Ah, Warwick, Warwick! If you were as well as we are, we could still win back all we've lost. The queen has brought a powerful army from France; we heard the news just now. Ah, if only you could run!

Why, then I would not fly.—Ah, Montague! / If thou be there, sweet brother, take my hand / And with thy lips keep in my soul awhile. / Thou lov'st me not; for, brother, if thou did'st, / Thy tears would wash this cold, congealed blood / That glues my lips and will not let me speak. / Come quickly, Montague, or I am dead.

Why, even then I wouldn't run. Ah, Montague! If you're there, sweet brother, take my hand and hold my soul in a while longer with your lips. You don't love me; for, brother, if you did, your tears would wash away this cold, clotted blood that glues my lips shut and won't let me speak. Come quickly, Montague, or I'll be dead.

Ah, Warwick, Montague hath breath'd his last, / And to the latest gasp cried out for Warwick, / And said 'Commend me to my valiant brother.' / And more he would have said, and more he spoke, / Which sounded like a clamour in a vault, / That might not be distinguish'd; but at last / I well might hear, delivered with a groan,— / 'O farewell, Warwick!'

Ah, Warwick, Montague has breathed his last, and to his final gasp he called out for Warwick and said, 'Give my regards to my brave brother.' He would have said more, and did say more, but it sounded like noise echoing in a vault and couldn't be made out; but at last I clearly heard him say, with a groan, 'O farewell, Warwick!'
Sweet rest his soul!—Fly, lords, and save yourselves; / For Warwick bids you all farewell, to meet in heaven.
Rest his soul! Run, lords, and save yourselves; for Warwick bids you all farewell, to meet again in heaven.
Away, away, to meet the queen's great power!
Away, away, to meet the queen's great army!

Thus far our fortune keeps an upward course, / And we are grac'd with wreaths of victory. / But, in the midst of this bright-shining day, / I spy a black, suspicious, threatening cloud, / That will encounter with our glorious sun / Ere he attain his easeful western bed. / I mean, my lords, those powers that the Queen / Hath rais'd in Gallia have arriv'd our coast / And, as we hear, march on to fight with us.

So far our fortune keeps rising, and we're honoured with the garlands of victory. But in the middle of this bright day I can see a black, suspicious, threatening cloud that will clash with our glorious sun before he reaches his restful bed in the west. I mean, my lords, that the army the queen has raised in France has landed on our coast and, we hear, is marching to fight us.
A little gale will soon disperse that cloud / And blow it to the source from whence it came; / Thy very beams will dry those vapours up, / For every cloud engenders not a storm.
A little breeze will soon scatter that cloud and blow it back where it came from. Your own beams will dry up those mists, for not every cloud brings a storm.
The queen is valued thirty thousand strong, / And Somerset, with Oxford, fled to her; / If she have time to breathe, be well assur'd, / Her faction will be full as strong as ours.
The queen's army is reckoned at thirty thousand, and Somerset and Oxford have fled to her. If she has time to catch her breath, you can be sure her side will be just as strong as ours.

We are advertis'd by our loving friends / That they do hold their course toward Tewkesbury. / We, having now the best at Barnet field, / Will thither straight, for willingness rids way; / And, as we march, our strength will be augmented / In every county as we go along.— / Strike up the drum! cry 'Courage!' and away.

Our loyal friends tell us they're heading for Tewkesbury. Having won at Barnet, we'll go there at once, for eagerness shortens the road; and as we march, our forces will grow in every county we pass through. Strike up the drum! Shout 'Courage!' and away.

Great lords, wise men ne'er sit and wail their loss, / But cheerly seek how to redress their harms. / What though the mast be now blown overboard, / The cable broke, the holding-anchor lost, / And half our sailors swallow'd in the flood? / Yet lives our pilot still. Is 't meet that he / Should leave the helm, and like a fearful lad / With tearful eyes add water to the sea, / And give more strength to that which hath too much, / Whiles in his moan the ship splits on the rock, / Which industry and courage might have sav'd? / Ah, what a shame! ah, what a fault were this! / Say Warwick was our anchor; what of that? / And Montague our topmast; what of him? / Our slaught'red friends the tackles; what of these? / Why, is not Oxford here another anchor, / And Somerset another goodly mast? / The friends of France our shrouds and tacklings? / And, though unskilful, why not Ned and I / For once allow'd the skilful pilot's charge? / We will not from the helm to sit and weep, / But keep our course, though the rough wind say no, / From shelves and rocks that threaten us with wrack, / As good to chide the waves as speak them fair. / And what is Edward but a ruthless sea? / What Clarence but a quicksand of deceit? / And Richard but a ragged fatal rock? / All these the enemies to our poor bark? / Say you can swim; alas, 't is but a while! / Tread on the sand; why, there you quickly sink; / Bestride the rock; the tide will wash you off, / Or else you famish,—that's a threefold death. / This speak I, lords, to let you understand, / If case some one of you would fly from us, / That there's no hop'd-for mercy with the brothers / More than with ruthless waves, with sands, and rocks. / Why, courage then! what cannot be avoided / 'T were childish weakness to lament or fear.

Great lords, wise men never sit and wail over their losses, but cheerfully look for ways to repair the damage. What if the mast is blown overboard, the cable broken, the anchor lost and half our sailors swallowed by the sea? Our pilot is still alive. Is it right for him to leave the helm and, like a frightened boy, add his tears to the sea, giving more strength to what already has too much, while the ship splits on the rock as he moans, when hard work and courage might have saved it? Ah, what a shame! Ah, what a fault that would be! Say Warwick was our anchor; what of it? And Montague our topmast; what of him? Our slaughtered friends the rigging; what of them? Why, isn't Oxford here another anchor, and Somerset another fine mast, and our French friends the ropes and rigging? And though we're unskilled, why shouldn't Ned and I be allowed to take the skilled pilot's place for once? We won't leave the helm to sit and weep, but keep our course, though the rough wind says no, away from the sandbanks and rocks that threaten to wreck us. Scolding the waves does as much good as speaking kindly to them. And what is Edward but a merciless sea? What is Clarence but a quicksand of deceit? And Richard but a jagged deadly rock? All of them enemies of our poor ship. Say you can swim: alas, only for a while! Step on the sand: you'll quickly sink. Climb on the rock: the tide will wash you off, or else you'll starve; that's a triple death. I say this, lords, to make you understand, in case any of you should want to desert us, that there's no more mercy to be hoped for from those brothers than from merciless waves, sands and rocks. So, courage! It would be childish weakness to mourn or fear what can't be avoided.

Methinks, a woman of this valiant spirit / Should, if a coward heard her speak these words, / Infuse his breast with magnanimity, / And make him, naked, foil a man at arms. / I speak not this as doubting any here; / For, did I but suspect a fearful man, / He should have leave to go away betimes, / Lest in our need he might infect another / And make him of the like spirit to himself. / If any such be here—as God forbid!— / Let him depart before we need his help.

I think a woman of such brave spirit, if a coward heard her speak these words, would fill his heart with courage and make him, unarmed, defeat an armed man. I don't say this because I doubt anyone here; for if I suspected a single frightened man, he'd be allowed to leave in good time, so that when we need him he doesn't infect another and make him as fearful as himself. If there's anyone like that here, which God forbid, let him leave before we need his help.

Women and children of so high a courage, / And warriors faint! why, 't were perpetual shame.— / O, brave young prince! thy famous grandfather / Doth live again in thee; long mayst thou live / To bear his image and renew his glories!

Women and children with such great courage, and warriors fainting! Why, that would be an everlasting shame. O brave young prince! Your famous grandfather lives again in you; may you live long to carry his likeness and renew his glories!
And he that will not fight for such a hope, / Go home to bed, and like the owl by day, / If he arise, be mock'd and wonder'd at.
And anyone who won't fight for such a hope, let him go home to bed, and if he gets up, be mocked and stared at like an owl by day.
Thank you, gentle Somerset. Sweet Oxford, thank you.
And take his thanks that yet hath nothing else.
And take the thanks of one who has nothing else yet.
Prepare you, lords, for Edward is at hand / Ready to fight; therefore be resolute.
Get ready, lords, for Edward is close and ready to fight; so be resolute.
I thought no less; it is his policy / To haste thus fast, to find us unprovided.
I expected as much. It's his tactic to hurry like this, to catch us unprepared.
But he's deceiv'd; we are in readiness.
This cheers my heart, to see your forwardness.
It cheers my heart to see your eagerness.
Here pitch our battle; hence we will not budge.
Set out our battle lines here; we won't move from this spot.

Brave followers, yonder stands the thorny wood / Which, by the heaven's assistance and your strength, / Must by the roots be hewn up yet ere night. / I need not add more fuel to your fire, / For, well I wot, ye blaze to burn them out. / Give signal to the fight, and to it, lords.

Brave followers, over there stands the thorny wood which, with heaven's help and your strength, must be pulled up by the roots before nightfall. I don't need to add fuel to your fire, for I know well you're blazing to burn them out. Give the signal to fight, and at them, lords.

Lords, knights, and gentlemen, what I should say, / My tears gainsay; for every word I speak, / Ye see I drink the water of my eyes. / Therefore, no more but this: Henry, your sovereign, / Is prisoner to the foe, his state usurp'd, / His realm a slaughter-house, his subjects slain, / His statutes cancell'd, and his treasure spent; / And yonder is the wolf that makes this spoil. / You fight in justice; then, in God's name, lords, / Be valiant and give signal to the fight.

Lords, knights and gentlemen, my tears contradict what I ought to say; for with every word I speak, you can see I'm drinking the water of my eyes. So, only this: Henry, your sovereign, is the enemy's prisoner, his throne usurped, his kingdom a slaughterhouse, his subjects killed, his laws cancelled and his treasure spent; and over there is the wolf that does this damage. You're fighting for justice; so, in God's name, lords, be brave and give the signal to fight.
Now, here a period of tumultuous broils. / Away with Oxford to Hames Castle straight; / For Somerset, off with his guilty head. / Go, bear them hence; I will not hear them speak.
Now here is the end of these violent quarrels. Take Oxford away to Hammes Castle at once; as for Somerset, off with his guilty head. Go, take them away; I won't hear them speak.
For my part, I'll not trouble thee with words.
For my part, I won't trouble you with words.
Nor I, but stoop with patience to my fortune.
Nor will I; I'll bow patiently to my fortune.
So part we sadly in this troublous world, / To meet with joy in sweet Jerusalem.
So we part sadly in this troubled world, to meet with joy in the heavenly Jerusalem.
Is proclamation made that who finds Edward / Shall have a high reward, and he his life?
Has it been proclaimed that whoever finds Edward will have a large reward, and he will have his life?
It is; and lo, where youthful Edward comes!
It has; and look, here comes young Edward!

Bring forth the gallant; let us hear him speak. / What! can so young a man begin to prick?— / Edward, what satisfaction canst thou make / For bearing arms, for stirring up my subjects, / And all the trouble thou hast turn'd me to?

Bring out the young hero; let's hear him speak. What! Can someone so young start to sprout thorns already? Edward, what amends can you make for taking up arms, stirring up my subjects and all the trouble you've caused me?

Speak like a subject, proud, ambitious York! / Suppose that I am now my father's mouth; / Resign thy chair, and where I stand kneel thou, / Whilst I propose the selfsame words to thee / Which, traitor, thou wouldst have me answer to.

Speak like a subject, proud, ambitious York! Imagine I'm now speaking for my father: give up your throne, and kneel where I stand, while I put to you the very questions, traitor, that you want me to answer.
Ah, thy father had been so resolv'd!
Ah, if only your father had been so resolute!
That you might still have worn the petticoat, / And ne'er have stol'n the breech from Lancaster.
Then you could have kept wearing the petticoat and never stolen the trousers from Lancaster.
Let Aesop fable in a winter's night; / His currish riddle sorts not with this place.
Let Aesop tell his fables on a winter's night; his dog's riddles don't suit this place.
By heaven, brat, I'll plague you for that word.
By heaven, brat, I'll plague you for that word.
Ay, thou wast born to be a plague to men.
Yes, you were born to be a plague to men.
For God's sake, take away this captive scold.
For God's sake, take away this captive nag.
Nay, take away this scolding crook-back rather.
No, take away this nagging hunchback instead.
Peace, wilful boy, or I will charm your tongue.
Quiet, stubborn boy, or I'll silence your tongue.
Untutor'd lad, thou art too malapert.

I know my duty; you are all undutiful. / Lascivious Edward,—and thou perjur'd George,— / And thou misshapen Dick,—I tell ye all, / I am your better, traitors as ye are;— / And thou usurp'st my father's right and mine.

I know my duty; you're all disloyal. Lustful Edward, and you, oath-breaking George, and you, misshapen Dick, I tell you all I'm your superior, traitors that you are; and you are stealing my father's right and mine.
Take that, the likeness of this railer here.
Take that, you image of this railing woman here.
Sprawl'st thou? take that, to end thy agony.
Are you sprawling? Take that, to end your agony.
And there's for twitting me with perjury.
And that's for taunting me with breaking my oath.
Hold, Richard, hold! for we have done too much.
Stop, Richard, stop! We've done too much.
Why should she live to fill the world with words?
Why should she live to fill the world with words?
What! doth she swoon? use means for her recovery.
What! Has she fainted? Do what you can to revive her.
Clarence, excuse me to the king, my brother. / I'll hence to London on a serious matter; / Ere ye come there, be sure to hear some news.
Clarence, make my excuses to the king, my brother. I'm going to London on serious business; before you get there, you can be sure you'll hear some news.

O Ned! sweet Ned! speak to thy mother, boy. / Canst thou not speak?—O traitors! murtherers! / They that stabb'd Caesar shed no blood at all, / Did not offend, nor were not worthy blame, / If this foul deed were by to equal it. / He was a man: this, in respect, a child, / And men ne'er spend their fury on a child. / What's worse than murtherer, that I may name it? / No, no, my heart will burst, an if I speak; / And I will speak, that so my heart may burst.— / Butchers and villains! bloody cannibals! / How sweet a plant have you untimely cropp'd! / You have no children, butchers! if you had, / The thought of them would have stirr'd up remorse; / But, if you ever chance to have a child, / Look in his youth to have him so cut off / As, deathsmen, you have rid this sweet young prince!

O Ned! Sweet Ned! Speak to your mother, boy. Can't you speak? O traitors! Murderers! Those who stabbed Caesar shed no blood at all, did no wrong and deserved no blame, if this foul deed were set beside it. He was a man; this, by comparison, a child, and men never vent their fury on a child. What's worse than a murderer, so I can call you it? No, no, my heart will burst if I speak; and I will speak, so that my heart will burst. Butchers and villains! Bloody cannibals! What a sweet plant you've cut down before its time! You have no children, butchers! If you had, the thought of them would have stirred up pity; but if you ever happen to have a child, expect to see him cut off in his youth, as you, executioners, have disposed of this sweet young prince!
Away with her! go, bear her hence perforce.
Away with her! Go, take her away by force.
Nay, never bear me hence, dispatch me here; / Here sheathe thy sword, I'll pardon thee my death. / What! wilt thou not?—then, Clarence, do it thou.
