No, don't take me away; finish me here. Sheathe your sword here; I'll forgive you my death. What! Won't you? Then, Clarence, you do it.
By heaven, I will not do thee so much ease.
By heaven, I won't give you that much comfort.
Good Clarence, do; sweet Clarence, do thou do it.
Good Clarence, do; sweet Clarence, do it.
Didst thou not hear me swear I would not do it?
Didn't you hear me swear I wouldn't do it?

Ay, but thou usest to forswear thyself; / 'T was sin before, but now 't is charity. / What! wilt thou not? where is that devil's butcher, / Hard-favour'd Richard?—Richard, where art thou? / Thou art not here; murther is thy alms-deed, / Petitioners for blood thou ne'er putt'st back.

Yes, but you're in the habit of breaking your oaths. It was a sin before, but now it would be a kindness. What! Won't you? Where's that devil's butcher, ugly Richard? Richard, where are you? You're not here; murder is your act of charity; you never turn away anyone who asks for blood.
Away, I say! I charge ye, bear her hence.
Away, I say! I order you, take her away.
So come to you and yours as to this prince!
May the same happen to you and yours as to this prince!
To London, all in post, and, as I guess, / To make a bloody supper in the Tower.
To London, at full speed; and, I guess, to make a bloody supper in the Tower.

He's sudden if a thing comes in his head. / Now march we hence; discharge the common sort / With pay and thanks, and let's away to London, / And see our gentle queen how well she fares. / By this, I hope, she hath a son for me.

He acts suddenly when a thing comes into his head. Now let's march away. Dismiss the common soldiers with pay and thanks, and let's go to London to see how our gentle queen is. By now, I hope, she has had a son for me.
Good day, my lord. What! at your book so hard?
Good day, my lord. What! Studying your book so hard?
Ay, my good lord;—my lord, I should say rather. / 'T is sin to flatter; 'good' was little better. / Good Gloster and good devil were alike, / And both preposterous; therefore, not good lord.
Yes, my good lord; my lord, I should say rather. It's a sin to flatter, and 'good' was little better. 'Good Gloucester' and 'good devil' would be the same, and both absurd; so not 'good lord'.
Sirrah, leave us to ourselves; we must confer.
Fellow, leave us alone; we must talk.
So flies the reckless shepherd from the wolf; / So first the harmless sheep doth yield his fleece, / And next his throat unto the butcher's knife.— / What scene of death hath Roscius now to act?
So the careless shepherd runs away from the wolf; so the harmless sheep first gives up his fleece, and next his throat to the butcher's knife. What death scene has Roscius come to act now?
Suspicion always haunts the guilty mind; / The thief doth fear each bush an officer.
Suspicion always haunts the guilty mind; the thief fears every bush is a constable.

The bird that hath been limed in a bush / With trembling wings misdoubteth every bush; / And I, the hapless male to one sweet bird, / Have now the fatal object in my eye / Where my poor young was lim'd, was caught, and kill'd.

The bird that has been caught with birdlime in a bush fears every bush with trembling wings; and I, the unhappy father of one sweet bird, now have before my eyes the deadly thing by which my poor young one was trapped, caught and killed.
Why, what a peevish fool was that of Crete / That taught his son the office of a fowl! / And yet, for all his wings, the fool was drown'd.
Why, what a foolish idiot that man from Crete was, who taught his son to fly like a bird! And for all his wings, the fool was drowned.

I, Daedalus; my poor boy, Icarus; / Thy father, Minos, that denied our course; / The sun that sear'd the wings of my sweet boy, / Thy brother Edward; and thyself, the sea / Whose envious gulf did swallow up his life. / Ah, kill me with thy weapon, not with words! / My breast can better brook thy dagger's point / Than can my ears that tragic history. / But wherefore dost thou come? is 't for my life?

I am Daedalus; my poor boy, Icarus; your father, Minos, who blocked our way; the sun that scorched my sweet boy's wings, your brother Edward; and you yourself the sea, whose spiteful depths swallowed up his life. Ah, kill me with your weapon, not with words! My heart can stand your dagger's point better than my ears can stand that tragic story. But why have you come? Is it for my life?
Think'st thou I am an executioner?
Do you think I'm an executioner?
A persecutor, I am sure, thou art; / If murdering innocents be executing, / Why, then thou art an executioner.
A persecutor, I'm sure you are. If murdering innocent people is execution, then you're an executioner.
Thy son I kill'd for his presumption.
I killed your son for his arrogance.

Hadst thou been kill'd when first thou didst presume, / Thou hadst not liv'd to kill a son of mine. / And thus I prophesy,—that many a thousand, / Which now mistrust no parcel of my fear, / And many an old man's sigh and many a widow's, / And many an orphan's water-standing eye,— / Men for their sons', wives for their husbands' fate, / And orphans for their parents' timeless death,— / Shall rue the hour that ever thou wast born. / The owl shriek'd at thy birth, an evil sign; / The night-crow cried, aboding luckless time; / Dogs howl'd, and hideous tempest shook down trees; / The raven rook'd her on the chimney's top, / And chatt'ring pies in dismal discord sung. / Thy mother felt more than a mother's pain, / And yet brought forth less than a mother's hope, / An indigested and deformed lump, / Not like the fruit of such a goodly tree. / Teeth hadst thou in thy head when thou wast born, / To signify thou cam'st to bite the world; / And, if the rest be true which I have heard, / Thou cam'st—

If you had been killed when you first acted arrogantly, you wouldn't have lived to kill a son of mine. And so I prophesy that many thousands, who now don't suspect any of what I fear, and many an old man's sigh and many a widow's, and many an orphan's tear-filled eye, men for their sons', wives for their husbands' fate, and orphans for their parents' untimely death, will regret the hour you were ever born. The owl shrieked at your birth, an evil sign; the night-crow cried, foretelling unlucky times; dogs howled, and a hideous storm shook down trees; the raven perched on the chimney top, and chattering magpies sang in dismal discord. Your mother felt more than a mother's pain, and yet gave birth to less than a mother hopes for: a shapeless, deformed lump, not like the fruit of such a fine tree. You had teeth in your head when you were born, to show you came to bite the world; and if the rest is true that I've heard, you came—
I'll hear no more. Die, prophet, in thy speech.
I'll hear no more. Die, prophet, in the middle of your speech.
For this, amongst the rest, was I ordain'd.
I was destined for this, among other things.
Ay, and for much more slaughter after this. / O, God forgive my sins, and pardon thee!
Yes, and for much more slaughter after this. O God, forgive my sins, and pardon you!

What! will the aspiring blood of Lancaster / Sink in the ground? I thought it would have mounted. / See, how my sword weeps for the poor King's death! / O, may such purple tears be always shed / From those that wish the downfall of our house!— / If any spark of life be yet remaining, / Down, down to hell; and say I sent thee thither,

What! Will the ambitious blood of Lancaster sink into the ground? I thought it would rise. See how my sword weeps for the poor king's death! O, may such red tears always be shed from those who wish for the downfall of our house! If any spark of life is still left, down, down to hell, and say I sent you there,

I, that have neither pity, love, nor fear. / Indeed, 't is true that Henry told me of; / For I have often heard my mother say / I came into the world with my legs forward. / Had I not reason, think ye, to make haste / And seek their ruin that usurp'd our right? / The midwife wonder'd; and the women cried / 'O, Jesus bless us, he is born with teeth!' / And so I was, which plainly signified / That I should snarl and bite and play the dog. / Then, since the heavens have shap'd my body so, / Let hell make crook'd my mind to answer it. / I have no brother, I am like no brother, / And this word 'love,' which greybeards call divine, / Be resident in men like one another, / And not in me! I am myself alone.— / Clarence, beware! thou keep'st me from the light; / But I will sort a pitchy day for thee; / For I will buzz abroad such prophecies / That Edward shall be fearful of his life, / And then, to purge his fear, I'll be thy death. / King Henry and the prince his son are gone; / Clarence, thy turn is next, and then the rest, / Counting myself but bad till I be best. / I'll throw thy body in another room, / And triumph, Henry, in thy day of doom.

I, who have neither pity, love nor fear. Indeed, what Henry told me is true; for I've often heard my mother say I came into the world feet first. Don't you think I had reason to hurry and seek the ruin of those who stole our right? The midwife was amazed, and the women cried, 'O Jesus bless us, he's born with teeth!' And so I was, which clearly meant that I should snarl and bite and play the dog. Then, since the heavens have shaped my body like this, let hell twist my mind to match it. I have no brother; I'm like no brother; and let this word 'love', which old men call divine, live in men who are like one another, and not in me! I am myself alone. Clarence, beware! You keep me from the light; but I'll arrange a pitch-black day for you; for I'll spread such prophecies about that Edward will fear for his life, and then, to cure his fear, I'll be your death. King Henry and his son the prince are gone; Clarence, your turn is next, and then the rest, for I count myself nothing until I'm the best. I'll throw your body in another room, and gloat, Henry, on your day of doom.

Once more we sit in England's royal throne, / Re-purchas'd with the blood of enemies. / What valiant foemen, like to autumn's corn, / Have we mow'd down in tops of all their pride! / Three Dukes of Somerset, threefold renown'd / For hardy and undoubted champions; / Two Cliffords, as the father and the son; / And two Northumberlands,—two braver men / Ne'er spurr'd their coursers at the trumpet's sound; / With them the two brave bears, Warwick and Montague, / That in their chains fetter'd the kingly lion / And made the forest tremble when they roar'd. / Thus have we swept suspicion from our seat / And made our footstool of security.— / Come hither, Bess, and let me kiss my boy.— / Young Ned, for thee thine uncles and myself / Have in our armours watch'd the winter's night, / Went all afoot in summer's scalding heat, / That thou mightst repossess the crown in peace; / And of our labours thou shalt reap the gain.

Once more we sit on England's royal throne, bought back with our enemies' blood. What brave enemies we have mown down at the height of their pride, like corn in autumn! Three Dukes of Somerset, three times famous as bold and unquestioned champions; two Cliffords, father and son; and two Northumberlands: two braver men never spurred their horses at the sound of the trumpet; and with them the two brave bears, Warwick and Montague, who chained up the royal lion and made the forest tremble when they roared. So we've swept all threats from our throne and made security our footstool. Come here, Bess, and let me kiss my boy. Young Ned, for your sake your uncles and I have kept watch in our armour through winter nights and marched on foot in the scalding summer heat, so that you could inherit the crown in peace; and you'll reap the profit of our labours.

[Aside] I'll blast his harvest if your head were laid; / For yet I am not look'd on in the world. / This shoulder was ordain'd so thick to heave; / And heave it shall some weight or break my back.— / Work thou the way,—and that shall execute.

(Aside) I'll blight his harvest once your head is laid low; for people don't take notice of me yet. This shoulder was made so thick to lift, and it will lift some weight or break my back. (Touching his head) You plan the way, (touching his hand) and this will carry it out.
Clarence and Gloster, love my lovely queen; / And kiss your princely nephew, brothers both.
Clarence and Gloucester, love my lovely queen; and kiss your princely nephew, both of you.
The duty that I owe unto your Majesty / I seal upon the lips of this sweet babe.
I seal the duty I owe your majesty on the lips of this sweet baby.
Thanks, noble Clarence; worthy brother, thanks.
Thank you, noble Clarence; worthy brother, thank you.

And, that I love the tree from whence thou sprang'st, / Witness the loving kiss I give the fruit.— / [Aside] To say the truth, so Judas kiss'd his Master, / And cried, all hail! when as he meant all harm.

And as proof that I love the tree you grew from, see the loving kiss I give its fruit. (Aside) To tell the truth, that's how Judas kissed his master and cried 'All hail!' when he meant nothing but harm.
Now am I seated as my soul delights; / Having my country's peace and brothers' loves.
Now I'm on the throne just as my soul desires, with my country at peace and my brothers' love.
What will your Grace have done with Margaret? / Reignier, her father, to the King of France / Hath pawn'd the Sicils and Jerusalem, / And hither have they sent it for her ransom.
What does your grace want done with Margaret? Reignier, her father, has mortgaged Sicily and Jerusalem to the King of France and sent the money here for her ransom.

Away with her and waft her hence to France.— / And now what rests but that we spend the time / With stately triumphs, mirthful comic shows, / Such as befits the pleasure of the court? / Sound drums and trumpets!—farewell sour annoy! / For here, I hope, begins our lasting joy.

Away with her; ship her off to France. And now what's left but to spend the time in grand celebrations and merry comic shows, as befits the pleasures of the court? Sound drums and trumpets! Goodbye, bitter trouble! For here, I hope, our lasting joy begins.
